If you shall chance, Camillo, to visit Bohemia, on the like occasion / whereon my services are now on foot, you shall see, as I have said, / great difference betwixt our Bohemia and your Sicilia.
Camillo, if you ever happen to visit Bohemia on the same kind of errand that brings me here, you will see, as I have said, a great difference between our Bohemia and your Sicilia.
I think this coming summer the King of Sicilia means to pay Bohemia the / visitation which he justly owes him.
I think the King of Sicilia means to pay Bohemia the visit he rightly owes him this coming summer.
Wherein our entertainment shall shame us; we will be justified in our / loves. For indeed,—
And our hospitality will put us to shame. But our love will make up for it. For really,—

Verily, I speak it in the freedom of my knowledge. We cannot with such / magnificence—in so rare—I know not what to say. We will give you sleepy / drinks, that your senses, unintelligent of our insufficience, may, / though they cannot praise us, as little accuse us.

Honestly, I speak from what I know. We cannot put on such splendour, in such rare... I don't know what to say. We will give you sleeping drinks, so that your senses, not noticing how poor our entertainment is, may not praise us but will not blame us either.
You pay a great deal too dear for what's given freely.
You pay far too much for something given freely.
Believe me, I speak as my understanding instructs me and as mine / honesty puts it to utterance.
Believe me, I only say what my understanding tells me and what honesty makes me say.

Sicilia cannot show himself over-kind to Bohemia. They were trained / together in their childhoods, and there rooted betwixt them then such / an affection which cannot choose but branch now. Since their more / mature dignities and royal necessities made separation of their / society, their encounters, though not personal, have been royally / attorneyed with interchange of gifts, letters, loving embassies, that / they have seemed to be together, though absent; shook hands, as over a / vast; and embraced as it were from the ends of opposed winds. The / heavens continue their loves!

The King of Sicilia cannot be too kind to the King of Bohemia. They were brought up together as children, and a love took root between them then that cannot help but grow branches now. Since they became grown men and kings, and their royal duties separated them, they have met through deputies instead of in person, exchanging gifts, letters and loving embassies, so that they have seemed to be together though apart: they have shaken hands across a great gap and embraced, as it were, from opposite ends of the earth. May heaven keep them loving!

I think there is not in the world either malice or matter to alter it. / You have an unspeakable comfort of your young Prince Mamillius. It is a / gentleman of the greatest promise that ever came into my note.

I don't think there is any malice or any cause in the world that could change it. You have a wonderful comfort in your young Prince Mamillius. He is the most promising young gentleman I have ever come across.

I very well agree with you in the hopes of him. It is a gallant child; / one that indeed physics the subject, makes old hearts fresh. They that / went on crutches ere he was born desire yet their life to see him a / man.

I quite agree with you about his promise. He is a fine child, one who does his subjects good like medicine and makes old hearts young again. People who were on crutches before he was born want to live long enough to see him grown up.
Would they else be content to die?
Otherwise they would be happy to die?
Yes, if there were no other excuse why they should desire to live.
Yes, if they had no other reason for wanting to live.
If the king had no son, they would desire to live on crutches till he / had one.
If the king had no son, they would want to go on living on crutches until he had one.

Nine changes of the watery star hath been / The shepherd's note since we have left our throne / Without a burden. Time as long again / Would be fill'd up, my brother, with our thanks; / And yet we should, for perpetuity, / Go hence in debt: and therefore, like a cipher, / Yet standing in rich place, I multiply / With one "we thank you" many thousands more / That go before it.

The moon has changed nine times, as shepherds count it, since we left our throne empty. We could fill as long again with our thanks, my brother, and still leave for ever in your debt. So, like a nought that stands in a valuable place in a number, I multiply the thousands of thanks that came before with one more 'thank you'.
Stay your thanks a while, / And pay them when you part.
Hold your thanks for a while, and pay them when you leave.

Sir, that's tomorrow. / I am question'd by my fears, of what may chance / Or breed upon our absence; that may blow / No sneaping winds at home, to make us say / "This is put forth too truly." Besides, I have stay'd / To tire your royalty.

Sir, that will be tomorrow. I am troubled by fears of what may happen or grow at home while I am away: may no biting winds blow there to make us say 'My fears were only too right.' Besides, I have stayed long enough to weary your Majesty.
We are tougher, brother, / Than you can put us to 't.
We are tougher than that, brother. You cannot tire us out.
We'll part the time between 's then: and in that / I'll no gainsaying.
Then we'll split the difference, and I will take no refusal.

Press me not, beseech you, so, / There is no tongue that moves, none, none i' th' world, / So soon as yours, could win me: so it should now, / Were there necessity in your request, although / 'Twere needful I denied it. My affairs / Do even drag me homeward: which to hinder / Were, in your love a whip to me; my stay / To you a charge and trouble: to save both, / Farewell, our brother.

Please don't press me so. No tongue in the world could persuade me sooner than yours, and it would win me now if your request were truly needed, even if I had to refuse it. My business drags me home. To hold me back would be, for all your love, a whip to me, and my staying would be an expense and a nuisance to you. To spare us both, farewell, my brother.
Lost for words, my queen? You speak.

I had thought, sir, to have held my peace until / You had drawn oaths from him not to stay. You, sir, / Charge him too coldly. Tell him you are sure / All in Bohemia's well: this satisfaction / The by-gone day proclaimed. Say this to him, / He's beat from his best ward.

I meant to keep quiet, sir, until you had made him swear he would not stay. You ask him too coldly, sir. Tell him you are sure all is well in Bohemia: yesterday's news confirmed it. Tell him that and he has lost his best defence.

To tell he longs to see his son were strong. / But let him say so then, and let him go; / But let him swear so, and he shall not stay, / We'll thwack him hence with distaffs. / [To Polixenes] Yet of your royal presence I'll adventure / The borrow of a week. When at Bohemia / You take my lord, I'll give him my commission / To let him there a month behind the gest / Prefix'd for's parting:—yet, good deed, Leontes, / I love thee not a jar of th' clock behind / What lady she her lord. You'll stay?

If he said he longed to see his son, that would be a strong reason. But let him say so, then, and let him go. Let him swear to it and he shall not stay: we'll chase him home with our spindles. (To Polixenes) Still, I'll risk asking to borrow your royal presence for one more week. When you have my husband in Bohemia, I'll give him leave to stay there a month past the date set for his departure. And yet, truly, Leontes, I love you not a tick of the clock less than any wife loves her husband. You'll stay?

Verily! / You put me off with limber vows; but I, / Though you would seek t' unsphere the stars with oaths, / Should yet say "Sir, no going." Verily, / You shall not go. A lady's verily is / As potent as a lord's. Will go yet? / Force me to keep you as a prisoner, / Not like a guest: so you shall pay your fees / When you depart, and save your thanks. How say you? / My prisoner or my guest? By your dread "verily," / One of them you shall be.

'Truly'! You fob me off with feeble vows. But even if you tried to shake the stars from their spheres with oaths, I would still say 'Sir, you are not going.' Truly, you shall not go. A lady's 'truly' is as powerful as a lord's. Will you still go? Then you force me to keep you as a prisoner, not a guest. Then you will pay a jailer's fees when you leave, and save your thanks. What do you say? My prisoner or my guest? By your solemn 'truly', you shall be one or the other.
Your guest, then, madam. / To be your prisoner should import offending; / Which is for me less easy to commit / Than you to punish.
Your guest, then, madam. To be your prisoner would mean I had done wrong, and that would be harder for me to do than for you to punish.
Not your gaoler then, / But your kind hostess. Come, I'll question you / Of my lord's tricks and yours when you were boys. / You were pretty lordings then.
Not your jailer, then, but your kind hostess. Come, I'll question you about the tricks my husband and you got up to as boys. You must have been pretty little lords then.
We were, fair queen, / Two lads that thought there was no more behind / But such a day tomorrow as today, / And to be boy eternal.
We were, fair queen, two boys who thought there was nothing ahead but another day tomorrow just like today, and that we would be boys for ever.
Was not my lord / The verier wag o' th' two?
Wasn't my husband the naughtier of the two?

We were as twinn'd lambs that did frisk i' th' sun / And bleat the one at th' other. What we chang'd / Was innocence for innocence; we knew not / The doctrine of ill-doing, nor dream'd / That any did. Had we pursu'd that life, / And our weak spirits ne'er been higher rear'd / With stronger blood, we should have answer'd heaven / Boldly "Not guilty," the imposition clear'd / Hereditary ours.

We were like twin lambs that frisked in the sun and bleated at each other. What we exchanged was innocence for innocence. We had not learnt how to do wrong, nor dreamt that anyone did. If we had gone on living like that, and our weak spirits had never been stirred by hotter blood, we could have answered heaven boldly 'Not guilty', apart from the original sin we were born with.
By this we gather / You have tripp'd since.
From that we take it that you have slipped since.
O my most sacred lady, / Temptations have since then been born to 's! for / In those unfledg'd days was my wife a girl; / Your precious self had then not cross'd the eyes / Of my young play-fellow.
O my most sacred lady, temptations have been born to us since then! For in those unfledged days my wife was a girl, and your precious self had not yet caught the eye of my young playmate.

Grace to boot! / Of this make no conclusion, lest you say / Your queen and I are devils. Yet go on; / Th' offences we have made you do we'll answer, / If you first sinn'd with us, and that with us / You did continue fault, and that you slipp'd not / With any but with us.

Heaven help us! Don't draw any conclusion from that, or you'll be saying your queen and I are devils. But go on. We will answer for the sins we made you commit, as long as you first sinned with us, kept on sinning with us, and slipped with nobody but us.
Have you won him over yet?
At my request he would not. / Hermione, my dearest, thou never spok'st / To better purpose.
He would not stay when I asked him. Hermione, my dearest, you never spoke to better purpose.

What! have I twice said well? when was't before? / I prithee tell me. Cram 's with praise, and make 's / As fat as tame things: one good deed dying tongueless / Slaughters a thousand waiting upon that. / Our praises are our wages. You may ride 's / With one soft kiss a thousand furlongs ere / With spur we heat an acre. But to th' goal: / My last good deed was to entreat his stay. / What was my first? It has an elder sister, / Or I mistake you: O, would her name were Grace! / But once before I spoke to the purpose—when? / Nay, let me have't; I long.

What! Have I spoken well twice? When was the other time? Please tell me. Stuff us with praise and make us as fat as pets: one good deed that goes unpraised kills a thousand more that would have followed it. Praise is our wages. You can ride us a thousand furlongs with one soft kiss before you can spur us across one acre. But to the point. My last good deed was to beg him to stay. What was my first? It has an older sister, unless I misunderstand you. O, I wish her name were Grace! But once before I spoke to the purpose. When? Come, tell me; I'm longing to know.
Why, that was when / Three crabbed months had sour'd themselves to death, / Ere I could make thee open thy white hand / And clap thyself my love; then didst thou utter / "I am yours for ever."
Why, that was when three sour months had dragged themselves to death before I could make you open your white hand and give it to me as my love. Then you said 'I am yours for ever.'
'Tis Grace indeed. / Why, lo you now, I have spoke to th' purpose twice. / The one for ever earn'd a royal husband; / Th' other for some while a friend.
That was Grace indeed. Well then, you see, I have spoken to good purpose twice. The first time earned me a royal husband for ever; the second, a friend for a while.

[Aside] Too hot, too hot! / To mingle friendship far is mingling bloods. / I have tremor cordis on me. My heart dances, / But not for joy,—not joy. This entertainment / May a free face put on, derive a liberty / From heartiness, from bounty, fertile bosom, / And well become the agent: 't may, I grant: / But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers, / As now they are, and making practis'd smiles / As in a looking-glass; and then to sigh, as 'twere / The mort o' th' deer. O, that is entertainment / My bosom likes not, nor my brows. Mamillius, / Art thou my boy?

(Aside) Too hot, too hot! To mix friendship so far is to mix bloods. My heart is trembling. It dances, but not for joy, not joy. This kind of welcome may look innocent, and come from warmth, generosity and a loving heart, and suit the person who gives it: it may, I grant. But to be fondling palms and pinching fingers, as they are now, and giving each other practised smiles as if in a mirror, and then sighing like a horn at the death of a deer: O, that is a welcome my heart does not like, nor my brow. Mamillius, are you my boy?

I' fecks! / Why, that's my bawcock. What! hast smutch'd thy nose? / They say it is a copy out of mine. Come, captain, / We must be neat; not neat, but cleanly, captain: / And yet the steer, the heifer, and the calf / Are all call'd neat.—Still virginalling / Upon his palm?—How now, you wanton calf! / Art thou my calf?

Bless me! Why, that's my fine fellow. What, have you smudged your nose? They say it's a copy of mine. Come, captain, we must be neat. No, not 'neat': clean, captain. And yet bulls, cows and calves are all called neat, too. (Watching Hermione and Polixenes) Still playing on his palm like a keyboard? (To Mamillius) How now, you playful calf! Are you my calf?
Yes, if you will, my lord.
Yes, if you like, my lord.

Thou want'st a rough pash and the shoots that I have / To be full like me:—yet they say we are / Almost as like as eggs; women say so, / That will say anything. But were they false / As o'er-dy'd blacks, as wind, as waters, false / As dice are to be wish'd by one that fixes / No bourn 'twixt his and mine, yet were it true / To say this boy were like me. Come, sir page, / Look on me with your welkin eye: sweet villain! / Most dear'st! my collop! Can thy dam?—may't be? / Affection! thy intention stabs the centre: / Thou dost make possible things not so held, / Communicat'st with dreams;—how can this be?— / With what's unreal thou coactive art, / And fellow'st nothing: then 'tis very credent / Thou may'st co-join with something; and thou dost, / And that beyond commission, and I find it, / And that to the infection of my brains / And hardening of my brows.

You need a rough head and horns like mine to be fully like me. Yet they say we are almost as alike as eggs. Women say so, and they will say anything. But even if they were as false as black cloth dyed too often, as wind, as water, as false as loaded dice to a man who doesn't know his from mine, it would still be true to say this boy is like me. Come, young sir, look at me with your sky-blue eyes. Sweet rascal! Dearest! My own flesh! Can your mother... could it be? Passion! Your force pierces to the centre. You make things possible that were thought impossible, and deal with dreams. How can this be? You work together with what is unreal and keep company with nothing. Then it is very believable that you can join with something real. And you do, beyond what is allowed, and I find it, to the poisoning of my mind and the hardening of my brow.
What is the matter with the King of Sicilia?
How, my lord? / What cheer? How is't with you, best brother?
What is it, my lord? Are you all right? How are you, my dearest brother?
You look / As if you held a brow of much distraction: / Are you mov'd, my lord?
You look as if your mind is very troubled. Are you upset, my lord?

No, in good earnest. / How sometimes nature will betray its folly, / Its tenderness, and make itself a pastime / To harder bosoms! Looking on the lines / Of my boy's face, methoughts I did recoil / Twenty-three years, and saw myself unbreech'd, / In my green velvet coat; my dagger muzzled / Lest it should bite its master, and so prove, / As ornaments oft do, too dangerous. / How like, methought, I then was to this kernel, / This squash, this gentleman. Mine honest friend, / Will you take eggs for money?

No, truly. How nature sometimes gives away its own foolishness and tenderness, and becomes a joke to harder hearts! Looking at my boy's face, I thought I went back twenty-three years and saw myself not yet in breeches, in my green velvet coat, with my dagger blunted in case it bit its master and proved, as ornaments often do, too dangerous. How like this little kernel I seemed to be then, this young pea-pod, this gentleman. (To Mamillius) My honest friend, will you let yourself be fooled?
You will? Why, happy man be 's dole! My brother, / Are you so fond of your young prince as we / Do seem to be of ours?
You will? Then may good luck be yours! My brother, are you as fond of your young prince as we seem to be of ours?

If at home, sir, / He's all my exercise, my mirth, my matter: / Now my sworn friend, and then mine enemy; / My parasite, my soldier, statesman, all. / He makes a July's day short as December; / And with his varying childness cures in me / Thoughts that would thick my blood.

When I'm at home, sir, he is my whole occupation, my joy, my concern: one moment my sworn friend, the next my enemy; my flatterer, my soldier, my statesman, everything. He makes a July day as short as one in December, and with his childish changes he cures me of thoughts that would thicken my blood.

So stands this squire / Offic'd with me. We two will walk, my lord, / And leave you to your graver steps. Hermione, / How thou lov'st us show in our brother's welcome; / Let what is dear in Sicily be cheap: / Next to thyself and my young rover, he's / Apparent to my heart.

This young squire does the same for me. We two will walk off, my lord, and leave you to your more serious business. Hermione, show how much you love us by how you welcome our brother. Let the most precious things in Sicily be cheap to him. Next to you and my young rover here, he is heir to my heart.
If you would seek us, / We are yours i' the garden. Shall 's attend you there?
If you want us, we'll be yours in the garden. Shall we wait for you there?

To your own bents dispose you: you'll be found, / Be you beneath the sky. [Aside] I am angling now, / Though you perceive me not how I give line. / Go to, go to! / How she holds up the neb, the bill to him! / And arms her with the boldness of a wife / To her allowing husband!

Go where you please. You'll be found, wherever you are under the sky. (Aside) I am fishing now, though you don't see me letting out the line. Go on, go on! How she holds up her lips, her mouth to him! And arms herself with a wife's boldness, as if her husband allowed it!

Gone already! / Inch-thick, knee-deep, o'er head and ears a fork'd one!— / Go, play, boy, play. Thy mother plays, and I / Play too; but so disgrac'd a part, whose issue / Will hiss me to my grave: contempt and clamour / Will be my knell. Go, play, boy, play. There have been, / Or I am much deceiv'd, cuckolds ere now; / And many a man there is, even at this present, / Now while I speak this, holds his wife by th' arm, / That little thinks she has been sluic'd in 's absence, / And his pond fish'd by his next neighbour, by / Sir Smile, his neighbour. Nay, there's comfort in 't, / Whiles other men have gates, and those gates open'd, / As mine, against their will. Should all despair / That hath revolted wives, the tenth of mankind / Would hang themselves. Physic for't there's none; / It is a bawdy planet, that will strike / Where 'tis predominant; and 'tis powerful, think it, / From east, west, north, and south. Be it concluded, / No barricado for a belly. Know't; / It will let in and out the enemy / With bag and baggage. Many thousand of us / Have the disease, and feel't not.—How now, boy!

Gone already! Inch-thick, knee-deep, over head and ears a horned cuckold! Go and play, boy, play. Your mother plays, and I play too, but such a shameful part that its ending will hiss me to my grave. Scorn and jeering will be my funeral bell. Go and play, boy, play. There have been cuckolds before now, unless I'm much mistaken, and many a man, even at this moment, as I speak, holds his wife by the arm with no idea that she has been flooded while he was away, and his pond fished by his next-door neighbour, Sir Smile. Well, there's comfort in that: other men have gates, and those gates opened against their will, like mine. If every man with an unfaithful wife despaired, a tenth of mankind would hang themselves. There's no medicine for it. It is a lecherous planet that strikes wherever it is in the ascendant, and believe me, it is powerful east, west, north and south. In short, there is no barricade for a womb. Make no mistake: it will let the enemy in and out with all his baggage. Thousands of us have the disease and don't feel it. Well now, boy!
I am like you, they say.
Why, that's some comfort. / What! Camillo there?
Why, that's some comfort. What, is Camillo there?
Go play, Mamillius; thou'rt an honest man.
Go and play, Mamillius; you're an honest man.
Camillo, this great sir will yet stay longer.
Camillo, this great lord is going to stay longer after all.
You had much ado to make his anchor hold: / When you cast out, it still came home.
You had a hard job getting his anchor to hold. Every time you cast it out, it came back.
He would not stay at your petitions; made / His business more material.
He would not stay when you asked him. He made out his business was more important.
Didst perceive it? / [Aside] They're here with me already; whisp'ring, rounding, / "Sicilia is a so-forth." 'Tis far gone / When I shall gust it last.—How came't, Camillo, / That he did stay?

Did you see that? (Aside) They are on to me already: whispering, muttering 'The King of Sicilia is a you-know-what.' It's gone a long way if I'm the last to taste it. How did it happen, Camillo, that he stayed?
Because the good queen begged him.

At the queen's be't: "good" should be pertinent, / But so it is, it is not. Was this taken / By any understanding pate but thine? / For thy conceit is soaking, will draw in / More than the common blocks. Not noted, is't, / But of the finer natures? by some severals / Of head-piece extraordinary? lower messes / Perchance are to this business purblind? say.

'At the queen's', let it be. 'Good' would be the right word, but as things are, it is not. Has anyone with brains but you understood this? Your mind soaks things up and takes in more than common blockheads. It hasn't been noticed, has it, except by finer minds, by a few exceptional heads? The lower ranks are blind to this business, perhaps? Tell me.
Business, my lord? I think most understand / Bohemia stays here longer.
Business, my lord? I think most people understand that the King of Bohemia is staying here longer.
To satisfy your highness, and the entreaties / Of our most gracious mistress.
To please your Highness, and because our most gracious mistress begged him.

Satisfy? / Th' entreaties of your mistress? Satisfy? / Let that suffice. I have trusted thee, Camillo, / With all the nearest things to my heart, as well / My chamber-counsels, wherein, priest-like, thou / Hast cleans'd my bosom; I from thee departed / Thy penitent reform'd. But we have been / Deceiv'd in thy integrity, deceiv'd / In that which seems so.

Please? Because your mistress begged him? Please? Enough said. I have trusted you, Camillo, with everything closest to my heart, my private thoughts too. Like a priest you cleansed my heart, and I left you a reformed penitent. But we have been deceived in your honesty, deceived in what seemed to be so.

To bide upon't: thou art not honest; or, / If thou inclin'st that way, thou art a coward, / Which hoxes honesty behind, restraining / From course requir'd; or else thou must be counted / A servant grafted in my serious trust, / And therein negligent; or else a fool / That seest a game play'd home, the rich stake drawn, / And tak'st it all for jest.

To stick to the point: you are not honest. Or, if you lean that way, you are a coward, who hamstrings honesty and holds it back from what it should do. Or else you are a servant I took deep into my trust who has been careless with it. Or else a fool who watches a game played out to the end, the big stakes won, and thinks it all a joke.

My gracious lord, / I may be negligent, foolish, and fearful; / In every one of these no man is free, / But that his negligence, his folly, fear, / Among the infinite doings of the world, / Sometime puts forth. In your affairs, my lord, / If ever I were wilful-negligent, / It was my folly; if industriously / I play'd the fool, it was my negligence, / Not weighing well the end; if ever fearful / To do a thing, where I the issue doubted, / Whereof the execution did cry out / Against the non-performance, 'twas a fear / Which oft affects the wisest: these, my lord, / Are such allow'd infirmities that honesty / Is never free of. But, beseech your Grace, / Be plainer with me; let me know my trespass / By its own visage: if I then deny it, / 'Tis none of mine.

My gracious lord, I may be careless, foolish and fearful. No man is free of any of these: in the endless business of the world his carelessness, his folly or his fear sometimes shows. In your affairs, my lord, if I was ever wilfully careless, it was my folly. If I ever played the fool on purpose, it was carelessness, not thinking about the outcome. If I was ever afraid to do something when I doubted how it would end, and doing it cried out against not doing it, that was a fear that often affects the wisest. These, my lord, are accepted weaknesses that even honesty is never free of. But, I beg your Grace, be plainer with me. Let me see my offence by its own face. If I then deny it, it isn't mine.

Ha' not you seen, Camillo? / (But that's past doubt: you have, or your eye-glass / Is thicker than a cuckold's horn) or heard? / (For, to a vision so apparent, rumour / Cannot be mute) or thought? (for cogitation / Resides not in that man that does not think) / My wife is slippery? If thou wilt confess, / Or else be impudently negative, / To have nor eyes nor ears nor thought, then say / My wife's a hobby-horse, deserves a name / As rank as any flax-wench that puts to / Before her troth-plight: say't and justify't.

Haven't you seen, Camillo (but that's beyond doubt, you have, or your eyeglass is thicker than a cuckold's horn), or heard (for when something is so plain to see, rumour cannot be silent), or thought (for a man who does not think has no mind), that my wife is unfaithful? If you will admit it, or else shamelessly deny that you have eyes, ears or thoughts, then say my wife is a whore, deserving a name as foul as any flax-girl who sleeps with a man before her betrothal. Say it and stand by it.

I would not be a stander-by to hear / My sovereign mistress clouded so, without / My present vengeance taken: 'shrew my heart, / You never spoke what did become you less / Than this; which to reiterate were sin / As deep as that, though true.

I would not stand by and hear my royal mistress slandered like that without taking revenge at once. Curse me, but you never said anything that suited you less. To repeat it would be a sin as great as that one, even if it were true.

Is whispering nothing? / Is leaning cheek to cheek? is meeting noses? / Kissing with inside lip? Stopping the career / Of laughter with a sigh?—a note infallible / Of breaking honesty?—horsing foot on foot? / Skulking in corners? Wishing clocks more swift? / Hours, minutes? Noon, midnight? and all eyes / Blind with the pin and web but theirs, theirs only, / That would unseen be wicked? Is this nothing? / Why, then the world and all that's in't is nothing, / The covering sky is nothing, Bohemia nothing, / My wife is nothing, nor nothing have these nothings, / If this be nothing.

Is whispering nothing? Is leaning cheek to cheek? Is touching noses? Kissing with open lips? Stopping a laugh with a sigh, a sure sign of failing virtue? Riding foot on foot? Hiding in corners? Wishing the clocks would go faster, hours into minutes, noon into midnight? And wishing everyone else's eyes were blind with cataracts except theirs, so they could be wicked unseen? Is this nothing? Why, then the world and everything in it is nothing, the sky above is nothing, Bohemia is nothing, my wife is nothing, and these nothings have nothing in them, if this is nothing.
Good my lord, be cur'd / Of this diseas'd opinion, and betimes, / For 'tis most dangerous.
My good lord, cure yourself of this sick opinion, and quickly, for it is very dangerous.

It is; you lie, you lie: / I say thou liest, Camillo, and I hate thee, / Pronounce thee a gross lout, a mindless slave, / Or else a hovering temporizer that / Canst with thine eyes at once see good and evil, / Inclining to them both. Were my wife's liver / Infected as her life, she would not live / The running of one glass.

It is. You lie, you lie. I say you lie, Camillo, and I hate you. I call you a great lout, a mindless slave, or else a wavering time-server who can see good and evil at the same time and lean towards both. If my wife's liver were as diseased as her life, she would not live another hour.

Why, he that wears her like her medal, hanging / About his neck, Bohemia: who, if I / Had servants true about me, that bare eyes / To see alike mine honour as their profits, / Their own particular thrifts, they would do that / Which should undo more doing: ay, and thou, / His cupbearer,—whom I from meaner form / Have bench'd and rear'd to worship, who mayst see / Plainly as heaven sees earth and earth sees heaven, / How I am galled,—mightst bespice a cup, / To give mine enemy a lasting wink; / Which draught to me were cordial.

Why, the man who wears her like a medal hanging round his neck: Bohemia. If I had loyal servants around me, with eyes to look after my honour as well as their own profits and private gains, they would do something to stop any more of this. Yes, and you, his cupbearer, whom I raised from humble rank to high office, you who can see as plainly as heaven sees earth and earth sees heaven how I am wounded, you could spice a cup to give my enemy a sleep that lasts for ever. That drink would be medicine to me.

Sir, my lord, / I could do this, and that with no rash potion, / But with a ling'ring dram, that should not work / Maliciously like poison. But I cannot / Believe this crack to be in my dread mistress, / So sovereignly being honourable. / I have lov'd thee,—

Sir, my lord, I could do this, and not with a quick poison but with a slow dose that would not work openly like poison. But I cannot believe there is this flaw in my royal mistress, who is so supremely honourable. I have loved you—

Make that thy question, and go rot! / Dost think I am so muddy, so unsettled, / To appoint myself in this vexation; sully / The purity and whiteness of my sheets, / (Which to preserve is sleep, which being spotted / Is goads, thorns, nettles, tails of wasps) / Give scandal to the blood o' th' prince, my son, / (Who I do think is mine, and love as mine) / Without ripe moving to't? Would I do this? / Could man so blench?

Ask that question and go and rot! Do you think I am so muddled, so unbalanced, that I would bring this torment on myself? Stain the purity and whiteness of my sheets (keeping them clean means sleep; stained, they are goads, thorns, nettles and wasps' stings)? Cast doubt on the birth of the prince, my son, whom I think is mine and love as mine, without good reason? Would I do this? Could any man stray so far?

I must believe you, sir: / I do; and will fetch off Bohemia for't; / Provided that, when he's remov'd, your highness / Will take again your queen as yours at first, / Even for your son's sake, and thereby for sealing / The injury of tongues in courts and kingdoms / Known and allied to yours.

I must believe you, sir. I do, and I will get rid of the King of Bohemia for it, provided that, once he is out of the way, your Highness will take back your queen as you did at first, if only for your son's sake, and so stop the wagging of tongues in courts and kingdoms that know you and are allied to you.
Thou dost advise me / Even so as I mine own course have set down: / I'll give no blemish to her honour, none.
You advise me exactly as I had planned myself. I will cast no stain on her honour, none.

My lord, / Go then; and with a countenance as clear / As friendship wears at feasts, keep with Bohemia / And with your queen. I am his cupbearer. / If from me he have wholesome beverage, / Account me not your servant.

My lord, go then, and with a face as clear as friendship wears at feasts, keep company with the King of Bohemia and your queen. I am his cupbearer. If he gets a wholesome drink from me, don't count me as your servant.
This is all: / Do't, and thou hast the one half of my heart; / Do't not, thou splitt'st thine own.
That's all. Do it, and you have half my heart. Don't, and you split your own.
I will seem friendly, as thou hast advis'd me.
I will seem friendly, as you have advised me.

O miserable lady! But, for me, / What case stand I in? I must be the poisoner / Of good Polixenes, and my ground to do't / Is the obedience to a master; one / Who, in rebellion with himself, will have / All that are his so too. To do this deed, / Promotion follows. If I could find example / Of thousands that had struck anointed kings / And flourish'd after, I'd not do't. But since / Nor brass, nor stone, nor parchment, bears not one, / Let villainy itself forswear't. I must / Forsake the court: to do't, or no, is certain / To me a break-neck. Happy star reign now! / Here comes Bohemia.

O miserable lady! But as for me, what position am I in? I must poison good Polixenes, and my reason for doing it is obedience to a master who is at war with himself and wants everyone who serves him to be the same. Promotion would follow the deed. If I could find thousands of examples of men who struck down anointed kings and prospered afterwards, I still would not do it. But since not a single one is recorded in brass, stone or parchment, let villainy itself refuse it. I must leave the court: whether I do it or not, it means breaking my neck. May my lucky star rule now! Here comes the King of Bohemia.
This is strange. Methinks / My favour here begins to warp. Not speak? / Good day, Camillo.
This is strange. I think my welcome here is beginning to warp. Not speaking? Good day, Camillo.
What is the news i' th' court?
What is the news at court?

The king hath on him such a countenance / As he had lost some province, and a region / Lov'd as he loves himself. Even now I met him / With customary compliment, when he, / Wafting his eyes to the contrary, and falling / A lip of much contempt, speeds from me, and / So leaves me to consider what is breeding / That changes thus his manners.

The king has a face on him as if he had lost a province, a region he loves as much as himself. Just now I greeted him in the usual way, and he turned his eyes away, let his lip drop in contempt, hurried off, and left me to wonder what has happened to change his manner like this.
I dare not know, my lord.
I dare not know, my lord.

How, dare not? Do not? Do you know, and dare not? / Be intelligent to me? 'Tis thereabouts; / For, to yourself, what you do know, you must, / And cannot say you dare not. Good Camillo, / Your chang'd complexions are to me a mirror / Which shows me mine chang'd too; for I must be / A party in this alteration, finding / Myself thus alter'd with't.

What, dare not? Do not? Do you know, and dare not tell me? That's about it, for you must know what you know, and cannot say you dare not know it. Good Camillo, your changed looks are a mirror to me, showing that mine have changed too. I must be part of this change, since I find myself changed along with it.
There is a sickness / Which puts some of us in distemper, but / I cannot name the disease, and it is caught / Of you that yet are well.
There is a sickness that has upset some of us, but I cannot name the disease, and it was caught from you, though you are still well.

How caught of me? / Make me not sighted like the basilisk. / I have look'd on thousands who have sped the better / By my regard, but kill'd none so. Camillo,— / As you are certainly a gentleman, thereto / Clerk-like, experienc'd, which no less adorns / Our gentry than our parents' noble names, / In whose success we are gentle,—I beseech you, / If you know aught which does behove my knowledge / Thereof to be inform'd, imprison't not / In ignorant concealment.

Caught from me? Don't make me out to be a basilisk that kills with a look. I have looked at thousands of people who have done better for my favour, but killed none of them. Camillo, as you are certainly a gentleman, and learned and experienced too, which grace our rank as much as our parents' noble names that we inherit, I beg you, if you know anything I ought to be told, don't lock it up in silence.

A sickness caught of me, and yet I well? / I must be answer'd. Dost thou hear, Camillo, / I conjure thee, by all the parts of man / Which honour does acknowledge, whereof the least / Is not this suit of mine, that thou declare / What incidency thou dost guess of harm / Is creeping toward me; how far off, how near; / Which way to be prevented, if to be; / If not, how best to bear it.

A sickness caught from me, and yet I am well? I must have an answer. Do you hear, Camillo? I call on you, by everything in a man that honour recognises, not the least of which is this request of mine, to tell me what harm you guess is creeping towards me: how far off, how near, how it can be prevented if it can, and if not, how best to bear it.

Sir, I will tell you; / Since I am charg'd in honour, and by him / That I think honourable. Therefore mark my counsel, / Which must be ev'n as swiftly follow'd as / I mean to utter it, or both yourself and me / Cry lost, and so goodnight!

Sir, I will tell you, since I am called on in the name of honour, and by a man I think honourable. So listen to my advice, which you must follow as quickly as I speak it, or you and I can both say 'We are lost', and goodnight!
I am appointed him to murder you.
I have been appointed to murder you.
He thinks, nay, with all confidence he swears, / As he had seen't or been an instrument / To vice you to't, that you have touch'd his queen / Forbiddenly.
He thinks, no, he swears with total confidence, as if he had seen it or had helped persuade you to it, that you have touched his queen unlawfully.

O, then my best blood turn / To an infected jelly, and my name / Be yok'd with his that did betray the Best! / Turn then my freshest reputation to / A savour that may strike the dullest nostril / Where I arrive, and my approach be shunn'd, / Nay, hated too, worse than the great'st infection / That e'er was heard or read!

O, then let my best blood turn to infected jelly, and my name be coupled with Judas, who betrayed Christ! Let my freshest reputation turn into a stink that would strike the dullest nose wherever I go, and let people shun my approach, no, hate it, worse than the worst plague ever heard or read of!

Swear his thought over / By each particular star in heaven and / By all their influences, you may as well / Forbid the sea for to obey the moon / As or by oath remove or counsel shake / The fabric of his folly, whose foundation / Is pil'd upon his faith, and will continue / The standing of his body.

You can swear him out of it by every star in heaven and all their influences, but you might as well forbid the sea to obey the moon as hope to remove, by oath or advice, the building of his folly. Its foundation rests on his belief, and it will stand as long as his body does.

I know not: but I am sure 'tis safer to / Avoid what's grown than question how 'tis born. / If therefore you dare trust my honesty, / That lies enclosed in this trunk, which you / Shall bear along impawn'd, away tonight. / Your followers I will whisper to the business, / And will by twos and threes, at several posterns, / Clear them o' th' city. For myself, I'll put / My fortunes to your service, which are here / By this discovery lost. Be not uncertain, / For, by the honour of my parents, I / Have utter'd truth: which if you seek to prove, / I dare not stand by; nor shall you be safer / Than one condemned by the king's own mouth, / Thereon his execution sworn.

I don't know. But I am sure it is safer to avoid what has grown than to ask how it was born. So, if you dare trust my honesty, which is locked in this body of mine that you shall take with you as a pledge, leave tonight. I will whisper the business to your followers, and get them out of the city in twos and threes by different back gates. As for me, I'll put my fortunes at your service, since they are lost here now that I have told you. Do not hesitate, for by my parents' honour I have told the truth. If you try to test it, I dare not stay, and you will be no safer than a man condemned by the king's own mouth, with his execution sworn.

I do believe thee. / I saw his heart in 's face. Give me thy hand, / Be pilot to me, and thy places shall / Still neighbour mine. My ships are ready, and / My people did expect my hence departure / Two days ago. This jealousy / Is for a precious creature: as she's rare, / Must it be great; and, as his person's mighty, / Must it be violent; and as he does conceive / He is dishonour'd by a man which ever / Profess'd to him, why, his revenges must / In that be made more bitter. Fear o'ershades me. / Good expedition be my friend, and comfort / The gracious queen, part of his theme, but nothing / Of his ill-ta'en suspicion! Come, Camillo, / I will respect thee as a father if / Thou bear'st my life off hence. Let us avoid.

I believe you. I saw his heart in his face. Give me your hand. Be my pilot, and your place shall always be next to mine. My ships are ready, and my people expected me to leave two days ago. This jealousy is over a precious creature: as she is rare, it must be great; as he is mighty, it must be violent; and as he believes he is dishonoured by a man who always claimed to be his friend, his revenge must be all the more bitter. Fear overshadows me. May a quick escape be my friend, and comfort the gracious queen, who is the subject of his suspicion but has done nothing to earn it! Come, Camillo, I will honour you like a father if you carry my life away from here. Let us go.
It is in mine authority to command / The keys of all the posterns: please your highness / To take the urgent hour. Come, sir, away.
I have authority to command the keys of all the back gates. Please, your Highness, seize the moment. Come, sir, away.
Take the boy to you: he so troubles me, / 'Tis past enduring.
Take the boy away. He bothers me so much it's past bearing.
Come, my gracious lord, / Shall I be your playfellow?
Come, my gracious lord, shall I be your playmate?
You'll kiss me hard, and speak to me as if / I were a baby still. I love you better.
You'll kiss me hard and talk to me as if I were still a baby. (To the Second Lady) I like you better.
And why is that, my lord?
Not for because / Your brows are blacker; yet black brows, they say, / Become some women best, so that there be not / Too much hair there, but in a semicircle / Or a half-moon made with a pen.
Not because your eyebrows are darker. Though they say dark eyebrows suit some women best, as long as there isn't too much hair, just a semicircle or a half-moon drawn with a pen.
I learn'd it out of women's faces. Pray now, / What colour are your eyebrows?
I learnt it from women's faces. Now tell me, what colour are your eyebrows?
Nay, that's a mock. I have seen a lady's nose / That has been blue, but not her eyebrows.
No, you're teasing. I have seen a lady's nose that was blue, but not her eyebrows.
Hark ye, / The queen your mother rounds apace. We shall / Present our services to a fine new prince / One of these days, and then you'd wanton with us, / If we would have you.
Listen, the queen your mother is getting rounder fast. One of these days we will be serving a fine new prince, and then you'd be glad to play with us, if we'd have you.
She is spread of late / Into a goodly bulk: good time encounter her!
She has grown nicely big lately. May she have a safe delivery!
What wisdom stirs amongst you? Come, sir, now / I am for you again. Pray you sit by us, / And tell 's a tale.
What wise talk is going on among you? Come, sir, I'm ready for you again. Please sit by me and tell us a story.
Shall it be happy or sad?
A sad tale's best for winter. I have one / Of sprites and goblins.
A sad tale's best for winter. I have one about ghosts and goblins.
Let's have that, good sir. / Come on, sit down. Come on, and do your best / To fright me with your sprites: you're powerful at it.
Let's have that, good sir. Come on, sit down. Come on, and do your best to frighten me with your ghosts. You're good at it.
Nay, come, sit down, then on.
No, come, sit down first, then go on.
Dwelt by a churchyard. I will tell it softly, / Yond crickets shall not hear it.
Who lived by a churchyard. I'll tell it quietly: those crickets over there shan't hear it.
Come on then, / And give't me in mine ear.
Come on then, and whisper it in my ear.
Was he met there? his train? Camillo with him?
Was he seen there? His followers? Camillo with him?
Behind the tuft of pines I met them, never / Saw I men scour so on their way: I ey'd them / Even to their ships.
I met them behind the clump of pines. I never saw men hurry so on their way. I watched them all the way to their ships.

How blest am I / In my just censure, in my true opinion! / Alack, for lesser knowledge! How accurs'd / In being so blest! There may be in the cup / A spider steep'd, and one may drink, depart, / And yet partake no venom, for his knowledge / Is not infected; but if one present / Th' abhorr'd ingredient to his eye, make known / How he hath drunk, he cracks his gorge, his sides, / With violent hefts. I have drunk, and seen the spider. / Camillo was his help in this, his pander. / There is a plot against my life, my crown; / All's true that is mistrusted. That false villain / Whom I employ'd, was pre-employ'd by him. / He has discover'd my design, and I / Remain a pinch'd thing; yea, a very trick / For them to play at will. How came the posterns / So easily open?

How blessed I am in my right judgement, my true opinion! O, I wish I knew less! How cursed I am in being so blessed! There may be a spider soaked in a cup, and a man may drink and go away and take no poison, because his mind is not infected. But if someone shows him the disgusting ingredient and tells him what he has drunk, he retches violently till his throat and sides crack. I have drunk, and seen the spider. Camillo helped him in this, his go-between. There is a plot against my life and my crown. Everything I suspected is true. That false villain I hired had already been hired by him. He has revealed my plan, and I am left a pinched fool, yes, a mere toy for them to play with as they like. How did the back gates come to be so easily opened?
By his great authority, / Which often hath no less prevail'd than so / On your command.
By his great authority, which has often worked just as well when you commanded it.
I know't too well. / Give me the boy. I am glad you did not nurse him. / Though he does bear some signs of me, yet you / Have too much blood in him.
I know it too well. (To Hermione) Give me the boy. I'm glad you did not nurse him. Though he has some marks of me, there is too much of your blood in him.
Bear the boy hence, he shall not come about her, / Away with him, and let her sport herself / With that she's big with; for 'tis Polixenes / Has made thee swell thus.
Take the boy away. He shall not come near her. Away with him, and let her play with the one she's pregnant with. For it is Polixenes who has made you swell like this.
But I'd say he had not, / And I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, / Howe'er you learn th' nayward.
But I'd only have to say he had not, and I swear you would believe me, however you lean the other way.

You, my lords, / Look on her, mark her well. Be but about / To say, "she is a goodly lady," and / The justice of your hearts will thereto add / "'Tis pity she's not honest, honourable": / Praise her but for this her without-door form, / Which on my faith deserves high speech, and straight / The shrug, the hum or ha, these petty brands / That calumny doth use—O, I am out, / That mercy does; for calumny will sear / Virtue itself—these shrugs, these hum's, and ha's, / When you have said "she's goodly," come between, / Ere you can say "she's honest": but be it known, / From him that has most cause to grieve it should be, / She's an adultress!

You, my lords, look at her, look at her well. Just start to say 'She is a fine lady', and the honesty of your hearts will add 'It's a pity she's not chaste and honourable.' Praise her just for her outward looks, which I swear deserve high praise, and at once the shrug, the 'hm' or 'ha', these little marks of slander—O, I am wrong, of mercy, for slander would brand virtue itself—these shrugs, these hums and has, will come in between 'she's fine' and 'she's honest'. But let it be known, from the man who has most cause to grieve that it is so: she's an adulteress!
Should a villain say so, / The most replenish'd villain in the world, / He were as much more villain: you, my lord, / Do but mistake.
If a villain said so, the most complete villain in the world, it would make him even more of a villain. You, my lord, are only mistaken.

You have mistook, my lady, / Polixenes for Leontes. O thou thing, / Which I'll not call a creature of thy place, / Lest barbarism, making me the precedent, / Should a like language use to all degrees, / And mannerly distinguishment leave out / Betwixt the prince and beggar. I have said / She's an adultress; I have said with whom: / More, she's a traitor, and Camillo is / A federary with her; and one that knows / What she should shame to know herself / But with her most vile principal, that she's / A bed-swerver, even as bad as those / That vulgars give bold'st titles; ay, and privy / To this their late escape.

You are the one who has mistaken, my lady, Polixenes for Leontes. O you thing, I won't call you by a name that fits your rank, in case rudeness, following my example, uses the same language to all ranks and leaves out the polite difference between prince and beggar. I have said she's an adulteress. I have said with whom. More, she's a traitor, and Camillo is her accomplice, and someone who knows what she should be ashamed to know, except with her vile partner: that she's a bed-hopper, as bad as the women the common people call the boldest names. Yes, and she knew about their recent escape.

No, by my life, / Privy to none of this. How will this grieve you, / When you shall come to clearer knowledge, that / You thus have publish'd me! Gentle my lord, / You scarce can right me throughly then, to say / You did mistake.

No, by my life, I knew nothing about any of this. How it will grieve you, when you know better, that you have shamed me so publicly! My gentle lord, you will hardly be able to put me right then by saying you were mistaken.

No. If I mistake / In those foundations which I build upon, / The centre is not big enough to bear / A school-boy's top. Away with her to prison! / He who shall speak for her is afar off guilty / But that he speaks.

No. If I am wrong in the foundations I build on, the centre of the earth is not big enough to hold a schoolboy's spinning top. Away with her to prison! Anyone who speaks for her is guilty, at a distance, just by speaking.

There's some ill planet reigns: / I must be patient till the heavens look / With an aspect more favourable. Good my lords, / I am not prone to weeping, as our sex / Commonly are; the want of which vain dew / Perchance shall dry your pities. But I have / That honourable grief lodg'd here which burns / Worse than tears drown: beseech you all, my lords, / With thoughts so qualified as your charities / Shall best instruct you, measure me; and so / The king's will be perform'd.

Some evil planet is ruling. I must be patient till the heavens look on me more favourably. Good my lords, I am not inclined to weep, as women commonly are, and the lack of that useless dew may perhaps dry up your pity. But I have an honourable grief lodged here that burns worse than tears can drown. I beg you all, my lords, judge me with thoughts tempered by your charity. And so let the king's will be done.

Who is't that goes with me? Beseech your highness / My women may be with me, for you see / My plight requires it. Do not weep, good fools; / There is no cause: when you shall know your mistress / Has deserv'd prison, then abound in tears / As I come out: this action I now go on / Is for my better grace. Adieu, my lord: / I never wish'd to see you sorry; now / I trust I shall. My women, come; you have leave.

Who is coming with me? I beg your Highness, let my women be with me, for you see my condition needs it. Don't cry, you good fools. There's no reason. When you find out your mistress deserved prison, then weep floods as I come out. What I go through now is for my greater honour. Goodbye, my lord. I never wished to see you sorry, but now I believe I shall. Come, my women; you have permission.
Go, do as we command. Away!
Beseech your highness, call the queen again.
I beg your Highness, call the queen back.
Be certain what you do, sir, lest your justice / Prove violence, in the which three great ones suffer, / Yourself, your queen, your son.
Be sure of what you are doing, sir, in case your justice turns out to be violence, and three great people suffer for it: yourself, your queen and your son.
For her, my lord, / I dare my life lay down, and will do't, sir, / Please you to accept it, that the queen is spotless / I' th' eyes of heaven and to you—I mean / In this which you accuse her.
For her sake, my lord, I dare lay down my life, and will, sir, if you will accept it, that the queen is spotless in the eyes of heaven and towards you: I mean in what you accuse her of.

If it prove / She's otherwise, I'll keep my stables where / I lodge my wife; I'll go in couples with her; / Than when I feel and see her no further trust her. / For every inch of woman in the world, / Ay, every dram of woman's flesh, is false, / If she be.

If she proves otherwise, I'll keep my wife locked up like a horse in the stable. I'll go about tied to her like a pair of hounds, and trust her no further than I can see and touch her. For every inch of woman in the world, yes, every ounce of woman's flesh, is false, if she is.

It is for you we speak, not for ourselves: / You are abus'd, and by some putter-on / That will be damn'd for't: would I knew the villain, / I would land-damn him. Be she honour-flaw'd, / I have three daughters; the eldest is eleven; / The second and the third, nine and some five; / If this prove true, they'll pay for't. By mine honour, / I'll geld 'em all; fourteen they shall not see, / To bring false generations: they are co-heirs, / And I had rather glib myself than they / Should not produce fair issue.

We speak for your sake, not our own. You are deceived, and by some troublemaker who will be damned for it. If I knew the villain, I would damn him here on earth. If her honour is flawed: I have three daughters, the eldest eleven, the second and third nine and about five. If this proves true, they'll pay for it. On my honour, I'll sterilise them all. They shall not reach fourteen to bear false children. They are my heirs, and I would rather geld myself than have them produce children who are not legitimate.
Cease; no more. / You smell this business with a sense as cold / As is a dead man's nose: but I do see't and feel't, / As you feel doing thus; and see withal / The instruments that feel.
Stop; no more. You sniff at this business with a sense as cold as a dead man's nose. But I see it and feel it, as you feel me doing this (he grips him), and I see the instruments that feel.
If it be so, / We need no grave to bury honesty. / There's not a grain of it the face to sweeten / Of the whole dungy earth.
If that is so, we need no grave to bury honesty in. There's not a grain of it left to sweeten the face of the whole dungheap of the earth.
I had rather you did lack than I, my lord, / Upon this ground: and more it would content me / To have her honour true than your suspicion, / Be blam'd for't how you might.
I would rather you were not believed than I, my lord, on this matter. And it would please me more to have her honour proved true than your suspicion, however much you blamed me for it.

Why, what need we / Commune with you of this, but rather follow / Our forceful instigation? Our prerogative / Calls not your counsels, but our natural goodness / Imparts this; which, if you, or stupified / Or seeming so in skill, cannot or will not / Relish a truth, like us, inform yourselves / We need no more of your advice: the matter, / The loss, the gain, the ord'ring on't, is all / Properly ours.

Why, what need is there for us to discuss this with you at all, instead of following our own strong impulse? Our royal right does not need your advice. Only our natural goodness tells you this. And if you, either stupefied or skilfully pretending to be, cannot or will not taste a truth as we do, understand that we need no more of your advice. The matter, the loss, the gain and how to handle it all belong to us.
And I wish, my liege, / You had only in your silent judgement tried it, / Without more overture.
And I wish, my lord, you had only tested it in your own silent judgement, without making it public.

How could that be? / Either thou art most ignorant by age, / Or thou wert born a fool. Camillo's flight, / Added to their familiarity, / (Which was as gross as ever touch'd conjecture, / That lack'd sight only, nought for approbation / But only seeing, all other circumstances / Made up to th' deed) doth push on this proceeding. / Yet, for a greater confirmation / (For in an act of this importance, 'twere / Most piteous to be wild), I have dispatch'd in post / To sacred Delphos, to Apollo's temple, / Cleomenes and Dion, whom you know / Of stuff'd sufficiency: now from the oracle / They will bring all, whose spiritual counsel had, / Shall stop or spur me. Have I done well?

How could that be? Either you are very ignorant from old age, or you were born a fool. Camillo's flight, added to their familiarity, which was as plain as anything ever guessed at, lacking only being seen, with nothing missing for proof but the sight, and every other circumstance pointing to the deed, drives me to act. Still, for greater confirmation (for in an act this important it would be pitiful to be rash), I have sent Cleomenes and Dion in haste to holy Delphi, to Apollo's temple. You know they are thoroughly capable. They will bring everything from the oracle, and its holy advice will stop or spur me. Have I done well?

Though I am satisfied, and need no more / Than what I know, yet shall the oracle / Give rest to the minds of others, such as he / Whose ignorant credulity will not / Come up to th' truth. So have we thought it good / From our free person she should be confin'd, / Lest that the treachery of the two fled hence / Be left her to perform. Come, follow us; / We are to speak in public; for this business / Will raise us all.

Though I am satisfied and need nothing more than what I know, the oracle will set other minds at rest, like his (pointing to Antigonus), whose foolish trustfulness will not rise to the truth. So we have thought it good to keep her shut away from our person, in case she is left to carry out the treachery of the two who have fled. Come, follow us. We are going to speak in public, for this business will stir us all.
[Aside] To laughter, as I take it, / If the good truth were known.
(Aside) To laughter, I think, if the real truth were known.
The keeper of the prison, call to him; / Let him have knowledge who I am.
Call the keeper of the prison. Let him know who I am.
Good lady! / No court in Europe is too good for thee; / What dost thou then in prison?
Good lady! No court in Europe is too good for you. Then what are you doing in prison?
Now, good sir, / You know me, do you not?
Now, good sir, you know me, don't you?
For a worthy lady / And one who much I honour.
As a worthy lady, and one I greatly respect.
Pray you then, / Conduct me to the queen.
Then please take me to the queen.
I may not, madam. / To the contrary I have express commandment.
I may not, madam. I have strict orders against it.
Here's ado, to lock up honesty and honour from / Th' access of gentle visitors! Is't lawful, pray you, / To see her women? any of them? Emilia?
What a fuss, locking up honesty and honour from gentle visitors! Is it allowed, please, to see her women? Any of them? Emilia?
So please you, madam, / To put apart these your attendants, I / Shall bring Emilia forth.
If you please, madam, send these attendants of yours away, and I will bring Emilia out.
I pray now, call her. / Withdraw yourselves.
Call her now, please. (To her attendants) Leave us.
And, madam, / I must be present at your conference.
And, madam, I must be present while you talk.
Here's such ado to make no stain a stain / As passes colouring.
Such a fuss to make a stain out of no stain, it's beyond all excuse.
Dear gentlewoman, / How fares our gracious lady?
Dear lady, how is our gracious queen?
As well as one so great and so forlorn / May hold together: on her frights and griefs, / (Which never tender lady hath borne greater) / She is, something before her time, deliver'd.
As well as someone so great and so abandoned can hold together. Because of her frights and griefs, which no gentle lady ever bore greater, she has given birth, somewhat early.
A daughter; and a goodly babe, / Lusty, and like to live: the queen receives / Much comfort in 't; says "My poor prisoner, / I am as innocent as you."
A daughter, and a fine baby, strong and likely to live. The queen takes great comfort in her, and says 'My poor prisoner, I am as innocent as you.'

I dare be sworn. / These dangerous unsafe lunes i' th' king, beshrew them! / He must be told on't, and he shall: the office / Becomes a woman best. I'll take't upon me. / If I prove honey-mouth'd, let my tongue blister, / And never to my red-look'd anger be / The trumpet any more. Pray you, Emilia, / Commend my best obedience to the queen. / If she dares trust me with her little babe, / I'll show't the king, and undertake to be / Her advocate to th' loud'st. We do not know / How he may soften at the sight o' th' child: / The silence often of pure innocence / Persuades, when speaking fails.

I'd swear it. Curse these dangerous, mad fits of the king's! He must be told about it, and he shall. The job suits a woman best. I'll take it on. If I turn out sweet-tongued, let my tongue blister and never again trumpet my red-faced anger. Please, Emilia, give the queen my most obedient respects. If she dares trust me with her little baby, I'll show it to the king and promise to be her advocate as loudly as anyone. We don't know how he may soften at the sight of the child. The silence of pure innocence often persuades when speaking fails.

Most worthy madam, / Your honour and your goodness is so evident, / That your free undertaking cannot miss / A thriving issue: there is no lady living / So meet for this great errand. Please your ladyship / To visit the next room, I'll presently / Acquaint the queen of your most noble offer, / Who but today hammer'd of this design, / But durst not tempt a minister of honour, / Lest she should be denied.

Most worthy madam, your honour and goodness are so obvious that your generous venture cannot fail to succeed. There is no lady alive so fit for this great errand. If your ladyship will step into the next room, I'll tell the queen straight away of your most noble offer. Only today she was turning over this very plan, but dared not ask anyone of rank, in case she was refused.
Tell her, Emilia, / I'll use that tongue I have: if wit flow from 't / As boldness from my bosom, let't not be doubted / I shall do good.
Tell her, Emilia, I'll use the tongue I have. If wit flows from it as boldness does from my heart, there's no doubt I shall do some good.
Now be you blest for it! / I'll to the queen: please you come something nearer.
Bless you for it! I'll go to the queen. Please come a little nearer.
Madam, if 't please the queen to send the babe, / I know not what I shall incur to pass it, / Having no warrant.
Madam, if the queen agrees to send the baby, I don't know what punishment I'll get for letting it out, since I have no warrant.

You need not fear it, sir: / This child was prisoner to the womb, and is, / By law and process of great nature thence / Freed and enfranchis'd: not a party to / The anger of the king, nor guilty of, / If any be, the trespass of the queen.

You need not fear that, sir. This child was a prisoner in the womb, and by the law and process of great nature it has been freed and made a citizen. It is no party to the king's anger, nor guilty of the queen's offence, if there is one.
Do not you fear: upon mine honour, I / Will stand betwixt you and danger.
Don't be afraid. On my honour, I will stand between you and danger.

Nor night nor day no rest: it is but weakness / To bear the matter thus, mere weakness. If / The cause were not in being,—part o' th' cause, / She th' adultress; for the harlot king / Is quite beyond mine arm, out of the blank / And level of my brain, plot-proof. But she / I can hook to me. Say that she were gone, / Given to the fire, a moiety of my rest / Might come to me again. Who's there?

No rest night or day. It's only weakness to take the matter like this, pure weakness. If the cause were gone, or part of the cause, she, the adulteress (for the whoring king is quite beyond my reach, out of range of my mind's aim, safe from my plots)... But her I can hook. Suppose she were gone, given to the fire, then half my rest might come back to me. Who's there?
He took good rest tonight; / 'Tis hop'd his sickness is discharg'd.
He slept well last night. It's hoped his sickness is over.

To see his nobleness, / Conceiving the dishonour of his mother. / He straight declin'd, droop'd, took it deeply, / Fasten'd and fix'd the shame on't in himself, / Threw off his spirit, his appetite, his sleep, / And downright languish'd. Leave me solely: go, / See how he fares.

Think how noble he is! Understanding his mother's dishonour, he at once declined, drooped, took it to heart, fixed the shame of it on himself, lost his spirits, his appetite, his sleep, and simply wasted away. Leave me alone. Go and see how he is.

Fie, fie! no thought of him. / The very thought of my revenges that way / Recoil upon me: in himself too mighty, / And in his parties, his alliance. Let him be, / Until a time may serve. For present vengeance, / Take it on her. Camillo and Polixenes / Laugh at me; make their pastime at my sorrow: / They should not laugh if I could reach them, nor / Shall she, within my power.

No, no, don't think of him. The very thought of revenge in that direction recoils on me. He is too mighty in himself, and in his friends and allies. Let him be until the time is right. For vengeance now, take it on her. Camillo and Polixenes laugh at me and make a game of my sorrow. They would not laugh if I could reach them, and nor shall she, who is in my power.
Nay, rather, good my lords, be second to me: / Fear you his tyrannous passion more, alas, / Than the queen's life? a gracious innocent soul, / More free than he is jealous.
No, good my lords, support me instead. Alas, do you fear his tyrannous rage more than the queen's life? A gracious, innocent soul, more pure than he is jealous.
Madam, he hath not slept tonight; commanded / None should come at him.
Madam, he has not slept tonight, and has ordered that no one should come to him.

Not so hot, good sir; / I come to bring him sleep. 'Tis such as you, / That creep like shadows by him, and do sigh / At each his needless heavings,—such as you / Nourish the cause of his awaking. I / Do come with words as med'cinal as true, / Honest as either, to purge him of that humour / That presses him from sleep.

Not so hasty, good sir. I come to bring him sleep. It's people like you, creeping round him like shadows and sighing at every one of his needless groans, people like you who feed the cause of his sleeplessness. I come with words as healing as they are true, and as honest as both, to purge him of the mood that keeps him from sleep.
No noise, my lord; but needful conference / About some gossips for your highness.
No noise, my lord, only some necessary talk about godparents for your Highness's child.
How! / Away with that audacious lady! Antigonus, / I charg'd thee that she should not come about me. / I knew she would.
What! Away with that impudent woman! Antigonus, I ordered you not to let her come near me. I knew she would.
I told her so, my lord, / On your displeasure's peril and on mine, / She should not visit you.
I told her so, my lord, on pain of your displeasure and of mine: she was not to visit you.
From all dishonesty he can. In this, / Unless he take the course that you have done, / Commit me for committing honour—trust it, / He shall not rule me.
He can keep me from anything dishonest. In this, unless he does what you have done and imprisons me for doing honour, believe me, he shall not control me.
La you now, you hear. / When she will take the rein I let her run; / But she'll not stumble.
There, you hear. When she takes the reins, I let her run. But she won't stumble.

Good my liege, I come,— / And, I beseech you hear me, who professes / Myself your loyal servant, your physician, / Your most obedient counsellor, yet that dares / Less appear so, in comforting your evils, / Than such as most seem yours—I say I come / From your good queen.

My good lord, I come (and I beg you to hear me, who claims to be your loyal servant, your doctor, your most obedient adviser, yet who dares to seem less so by not soothing your faults than those who seem most devoted to you), I say I come from your good queen.
Good queen, my lord, good queen: I say, good queen, / And would by combat make her good, so were I / A man, the worst about you.
Good queen, my lord, good queen. I say good queen, and if I were a man, even the weakest one around you, I would prove her good in a duel.

Let him that makes but trifles of his eyes / First hand me: on mine own accord I'll off; / But first I'll do my errand. The good queen, / (For she is good) hath brought you forth a daughter; / Here 'tis; commends it to your blessing.

Let anyone who cares nothing for his eyes lay hands on me first. I'll go of my own accord, but first I'll do my errand. The good queen, for she is good, has given birth to a daughter for you. Here she is. She commends it to your blessing.
Out! / A mankind witch! Hence with her, out o' door: / A most intelligencing bawd!
Out! A mannish witch! Away with her, out of the door! A spying, scheming bawd!
Not so. / I am as ignorant in that as you / In so entitling me; and no less honest / Than you are mad; which is enough, I'll warrant, / As this world goes, to pass for honest.
Not so. I know as little about that as you do in calling me that, and I am no less honest than you are mad, which I promise is enough, the way this world goes, to pass for honest.

Traitors! / Will you not push her out? [To Antigonus] Give her the bastard, / Thou dotard! Thou art woman-tir'd, unroosted / By thy Dame Partlet here. Take up the bastard, / Take't up, I say; give't to thy crone.

Traitors! Won't you push her out? (To Antigonus) Give her the bastard, you old fool! You're henpecked, knocked off your perch by your Dame Partlet here. Pick up the bastard, pick it up, I say. Give it to your old hag.
For ever / Unvenerable be thy hands, if thou / Tak'st up the princess by that forced baseness / Which he has put upon 't!
May your hands be dishonoured for ever if you pick up the princess under that false, low name he has forced on her!
So I would you did; then 'twere past all doubt / You'd call your children yours.
I wish you were afraid of yours. Then there would be no doubt you'd call your children yours.
I am none, by this good light.
I'm not one, by this good daylight.

Nor I; nor any / But one that's here, and that's himself. For he / The sacred honour of himself, his queen's, / His hopeful son's, his babe's, betrays to slander, / Whose sting is sharper than the sword's; and will not, / (For, as the case now stands, it is a curse / He cannot be compell'd to't) once remove / The root of his opinion, which is rotten / As ever oak or stone was sound.

Nor am I, nor is anyone here but one, and that's himself. For he betrays to slander, whose sting is sharper than a sword's, his own sacred honour, his queen's, his promising son's and his baby's, and will not (and as things stand it's a curse that he can't be forced to) once pull up the root of his belief, which is as rotten as any oak or stone was ever sound.

A callat / Of boundless tongue, who late hath beat her husband, / And now baits me! This brat is none of mine; / It is the issue of Polixenes. / Hence with it, and together with the dam / Commit them to the fire.

A scold with an endless tongue, who has just beaten her husband and now baits me! This brat is not mine. It is the child of Polixenes. Away with it, and throw it and its mother into the fire together.

It is yours; / And, might we lay th' old proverb to your charge, / So like you 'tis the worse. Behold, my lords, / Although the print be little, the whole matter / And copy of the father: eye, nose, lip, / The trick of 's frown, his forehead; nay, the valley, / The pretty dimples of his chin and cheek; his smiles; / The very mould and frame of hand, nail, finger: / And thou, good goddess Nature, which hast made it / So like to him that got it, if thou hast / The ordering of the mind too, 'mongst all colours / No yellow in 't, lest she suspect, as he does, / Her children not her husband's!

It is yours, and, as the old proverb says, it's so like you it's the worse for it. Look, my lords: although the print is small, it is a complete copy of the father. Eye, nose, lip, the way he frowns, his forehead; even the hollow, the pretty dimples of his chin and cheek; his smiles; the very shape of hand, nail and finger. And you, good goddess Nature, who have made her so like the man who fathered her, if you have charge of the mind too, put no yellow of jealousy in it among all its colours, in case she suspects, as he does, that her children are not her husband's!
A gross hag! / And, losel, thou art worthy to be hang'd / That wilt not stay her tongue.
A foul hag! (To Antigonus) And, you good-for-nothing, you deserve to be hanged for not stopping her tongue.
Hang all the husbands / That cannot do that feat, you'll leave yourself / Hardly one subject.
If you hang all the husbands who can't do that, you'll hardly have one subject left.
A most unworthy and unnatural lord / Can do no more.
A most unworthy and unnatural lord could do no worse.

I care not. / It is an heretic that makes the fire, / Not she which burns in 't. I'll not call you tyrant; / But this most cruel usage of your queen, / Not able to produce more accusation / Than your own weak-hing'd fancy, something savours / Of tyranny, and will ignoble make you, / Yea, scandalous to the world.

I don't care. It is the one who lights the fire who is the heretic, not the woman who burns in it. I won't call you a tyrant. But this cruel treatment of your queen, without being able to produce any accusation but your own unhinged imagination, smacks somewhat of tyranny, and will disgrace you, yes, make you a scandal to the world.
On your allegiance, / Out of the chamber with her! Were I a tyrant, / Where were her life? She durst not call me so, / If she did know me one. Away with her!
On your allegiance, get her out of the room! If I were a tyrant, where would her life be? She wouldn't dare call me one if she really thought I was. Away with her!

I pray you, do not push me; I'll be gone. / Look to your babe, my lord; 'tis yours: Jove send her / A better guiding spirit! What needs these hands? / You that are thus so tender o'er his follies, / Will never do him good, not one of you. / So, so. Farewell; we are gone.

Please don't push me. I'll go. Look after your baby, my lord. It's yours. May Jove give her a better guiding spirit! What need for these hands? You who are so tender towards his follies will never do him any good, not one of you. There, there. Farewell; I'm going.

Thou, traitor, hast set on thy wife to this. / My child? Away with't. Even thou, that hast / A heart so tender o'er it, take it hence, / And see it instantly consum'd with fire; / Even thou, and none but thou. Take it up straight: / Within this hour bring me word 'tis done, / And by good testimony, or I'll seize thy life, / With that thou else call'st thine. If thou refuse / And wilt encounter with my wrath, say so; / The bastard brains with these my proper hands / Shall I dash out. Go, take it to the fire; / For thou set'st on thy wife.

You traitor, you put your wife up to this. My child? Away with it! You, who have such a tender heart for it, take it away and see it burnt at once. You and nobody else. Pick it up now. Within the hour bring me word it's done, with good witnesses, or I'll take your life and everything else you call yours. If you refuse and want to face my anger, say so, and I'll dash out the bastard's brains with my own hands. Go, take it to the fire, for you set your wife on.
I did not, sir: / These lords, my noble fellows, if they please, / Can clear me in 't.
I did not, sir. These lords, my noble colleagues, can clear me of it, if they will.
