We can: my royal liege, / He is not guilty of her coming hither.
We can. My royal lord, he is not to blame for her coming here.

Beseech your highness, give us better credit: / We have always truly serv'd you; and beseech / So to esteem of us. And on our knees we beg, / As recompense of our dear services / Past and to come, that you do change this purpose, / Which being so horrible, so bloody, must / Lead on to some foul issue. We all kneel.

I beg your Highness, trust us more. We have always served you truly, and we beg you to think so of us. On our knees we beg you, as a reward for our loyal service past and to come, to change this plan, which is so horrible and bloody that it must lead to something foul. We all kneel.

I am a feather for each wind that blows. / Shall I live on to see this bastard kneel / And call me father? better burn it now / Than curse it then. But be it; let it live. / It shall not neither. [To Antigonus] You, sir, come you hither, / You that have been so tenderly officious / With Lady Margery, your midwife, there, / To save this bastard's life—for 'tis a bastard, / So sure as this beard's grey. What will you adventure / To save this brat's life?

I am a feather blown by every wind. Shall I live to see this bastard kneel and call me father? Better burn it now than curse it then. But so be it: let it live. No, it shall not either. (To Antigonus) You, sir, come here, you who have been so tenderly busy with Lady Margery, your midwife there, to save this bastard's life (for it is a bastard, as sure as this beard is grey). What will you risk to save this brat's life?
Anything, my lord, / That my ability may undergo, / And nobleness impose: at least thus much: / I'll pawn the little blood which I have left / To save the innocent. Anything possible.
Anything, my lord, that my strength can bear and honour requires. At least this much: I'll pledge what little blood I have left to save the innocent. Anything possible.
It shall be possible. Swear by this sword / Thou wilt perform my bidding.
It shall be possible. Swear on this sword that you will do what I command.

Mark, and perform it, seest thou? for the fail / Of any point in't shall not only be / Death to thyself, but to thy lewd-tongu'd wife, / Whom for this time we pardon. We enjoin thee, / As thou art liegeman to us, that thou carry / This female bastard hence, and that thou bear it / To some remote and desert place, quite out / Of our dominions; and that there thou leave it, / Without more mercy, to it own protection / And favour of the climate. As by strange fortune / It came to us, I do in justice charge thee, / On thy soul's peril and thy body's torture, / That thou commend it strangely to some place / Where chance may nurse or end it. Take it up.

Listen, and do it, do you see? If you fail in any detail, it will mean death not only for you but for your foul-tongued wife, whom we pardon for now. We command you, as our sworn subject, to carry this female bastard away from here, take it to some remote and deserted place quite outside our kingdom, and leave it there, without any more mercy, to its own protection and the kindness of the weather. As it came to us by strange fortune, I charge you in justice, at the risk of your soul and body's torture, to leave it as a stranger in some place where chance may nurse it or end it. Pick it up.

I swear to do this, though a present death / Had been more merciful. Come on, poor babe: / Some powerful spirit instruct the kites and ravens / To be thy nurses! Wolves and bears, they say, / Casting their savageness aside, have done / Like offices of pity. Sir, be prosperous / In more than this deed does require! And blessing / Against this cruelty, fight on thy side, / Poor thing, condemn'd to loss!

I swear to do it, though instant death would have been more merciful. Come on, poor baby. May some powerful spirit teach the kites and ravens to be your nurses! Wolves and bears, they say, have put their savageness aside and done such kindly duties. (To Leontes) Sir, may you prosper more than this deed deserves! (To the baby) And may blessing fight on your side against this cruelty, poor thing, condemned to be lost!
No, I'll not rear / Another's issue.
No, I won't bring up another man's child.
Please your highness, posts / From those you sent to th' oracle are come / An hour since: Cleomenes and Dion, / Being well arriv'd from Delphos, are both landed, / Hasting to th' court.
If it please your Highness, messengers came an hour ago from the men you sent to the oracle. Cleomenes and Dion have arrived safely from Delphi, landed, and are hurrying to court.
So please you, sir, their speed / Hath been beyond account.
If you please, sir, their speed has been beyond belief.

Twenty-three days / They have been absent: 'tis good speed; foretells / The great Apollo suddenly will have / The truth of this appear. Prepare you, lords; / Summon a session, that we may arraign / Our most disloyal lady; for, as she hath / Been publicly accus'd, so shall she have / A just and open trial. While she lives, / My heart will be a burden to me. Leave me, / And think upon my bidding.

They have been away twenty-three days. That's good speed. It means great Apollo wants the truth of this to be known quickly. Get ready, lords. Call a court session so that we can put our most disloyal lady on trial. For as she has been publicly accused, so she shall have a just and open trial. While she lives, my heart will be a burden to me. Leave me, and think about what I have ordered.
The climate's delicate; the air most sweet, / Fertile the isle, the temple much surpassing / The common praise it bears.
The climate is mild, the air very sweet, the island fertile, and the temple far beyond the praise it usually gets.

I shall report, / For most it caught me, the celestial habits / (Methinks I so should term them) and the reverence / Of the grave wearers. O, the sacrifice! / How ceremonious, solemn, and unearthly, / It was i' th' offering!

I shall report, for it struck me most, the heavenly robes (I think that's the right word for them) and the reverence of the solemn priests who wore them. O, the sacrifice! How ceremonious, solemn and unearthly the offering was!
But of all, the burst / And the ear-deaf'ning voice o' th' oracle, / Kin to Jove's thunder, so surprised my sense / That I was nothing.
But above everything, the blast and ear-deafening voice of the oracle, like Jove's thunder, so overwhelmed my senses that I was nothing.
If the event o' th' journey / Prove as successful to the queen,—O, be't so!— / As it hath been to us rare, pleasant, speedy, / The time is worth the use on't.
If the outcome of the journey proves as good for the queen (O, let it!) as it has been rare, pleasant and quick for us, the time was well spent.
Great Apollo / Turn all to th' best! These proclamations, / So forcing faults upon Hermione, / I little like.
Great Apollo turn everything to the best! I don't like these proclamations that force faults on Hermione.

The violent carriage of it / Will clear or end the business: when the oracle, / (Thus by Apollo's great divine seal'd up) / Shall the contents discover, something rare / Even then will rush to knowledge. Go. Fresh horses! / And gracious be the issue!

The violent haste of it will clear up the business or end it. When the oracle, sealed up like this by Apollo's great priest, reveals its contents, something extraordinary will come to light. Go. Fresh horses! And may it end well!

This sessions (to our great grief we pronounce) / Even pushes 'gainst our heart: the party tried / The daughter of a king, our wife, and one / Of us too much belov'd. Let us be clear'd / Of being tyrannous, since we so openly / Proceed in justice, which shall have due course, / Even to the guilt or the purgation. / Produce the prisoner.

This trial, we say with great grief, pushes against our very heart. The accused is the daughter of a king, our wife, and someone we loved too much. Let us be cleared of tyranny, since we proceed so openly in justice, which shall take its proper course to a verdict of guilty or a clearing of her name. Bring in the prisoner.
It is his highness' pleasure that the queen / Appear in person here in court. Silence!
It is his Highness's wish that the queen appear in person here in court. Silence!

[Reads] "Hermione, queen to the worthy Leontes, king of Sicilia, / thou art here accused and arraigned of high treason, in committing / adultery with Polixenes, king of Bohemia; and conspiring with Camillo / to take away the life of our sovereign lord the king, thy royal / husband: the pretence whereof being by circumstances partly laid open, / thou, Hermione, contrary to the faith and allegiance of a true subject, / didst counsel and aid them, for their better safety, to fly away by / night."

(Reads) 'Hermione, queen to the worthy Leontes, King of Sicilia, you are accused and put on trial here for high treason, for committing adultery with Polixenes, King of Bohemia, and conspiring with Camillo to take the life of our sovereign lord the king, your royal husband. When this plan was partly uncovered by circumstances, you, Hermione, against the faith and loyalty of a true subject, advised and helped them to escape by night for their greater safety.'

Since what I am to say must be but that / Which contradicts my accusation, and / The testimony on my part no other / But what comes from myself, it shall scarce boot me / To say "Not guilty". Mine integrity, / Being counted falsehood, shall, as I express it, / Be so receiv'd. But thus, if powers divine / Behold our human actions, as they do, / I doubt not, then, but innocence shall make / False accusation blush, and tyranny / Tremble at patience. You, my lord, best know, / Who least will seem to do so, my past life / Hath been as continent, as chaste, as true, / As I am now unhappy; which is more / Than history can pattern, though devis'd / And play'd to take spectators. For behold me, / A fellow of the royal bed, which owe / A moiety of the throne, a great king's daughter, / The mother to a hopeful prince, here standing / To prate and talk for life and honour 'fore / Who please to come and hear. For life, I prize it / As I weigh grief, which I would spare. For honour, / 'Tis a derivative from me to mine, / And only that I stand for. I appeal / To your own conscience, sir, before Polixenes / Came to your court, how I was in your grace, / How merited to be so; since he came, / With what encounter so uncurrent I / Have strain'd t' appear thus: if one jot beyond / The bound of honour, or in act or will / That way inclining, harden'd be the hearts / Of all that hear me, and my near'st of kin / Cry fie upon my grave!

Since all I can say must simply contradict the charge, and the only evidence on my side comes from me, it will hardly help me to say 'Not guilty'. My honesty, being counted as falsehood, will be taken as falsehood when I speak it. But if the gods watch our human actions, as they do, I have no doubt that innocence will make false accusation blush and tyranny tremble at patience. You, my lord, know best, though you will least seem to, that my past life has been as self-controlled, as chaste and as true as I am now unhappy, which is more than any story can match, even one invented and acted to move an audience. For look at me: partner in the royal bed, owner of half the throne, a great king's daughter, mother of a promising prince, standing here to chatter and plead for my life and honour in front of anyone who cares to come and listen. As for life, I value it as I value grief, which I would gladly be spared. As for honour, it passes from me to my children, and that is all I stand up for. I appeal to your own conscience, sir: before Polixenes came to your court, how I stood in your favour and how I deserved to; and since he came, what improper behaviour I have stooped to that I should appear like this. If I went one jot beyond the bounds of honour, in act or in will, let the hearts of everyone who hears me be hardened, and my nearest relatives cry 'Shame!' on my grave.
I ne'er heard yet / That any of these bolder vices wanted / Less impudence to gainsay what they did / Than to perform it first.
I never yet heard that any of these bold vices lacked the nerve to deny what they did any less than they had the nerve to do it.
That's true enough; / Though 'tis a saying, sir, not due to me.
That's true enough, though it's a saying, sir, that does not apply to me.

More than mistress of / Which comes to me in name of fault, I must not / At all acknowledge. For Polixenes, / With whom I am accus'd, I do confess / I lov'd him as in honour he requir'd, / With such a kind of love as might become / A lady like me; with a love even such, / So and no other, as yourself commanded: / Which not to have done, I think had been in me / Both disobedience and ingratitude / To you and toward your friend, whose love had spoke, / Ever since it could speak, from an infant, freely, / That it was yours. Now, for conspiracy, / I know not how it tastes, though it be dish'd / For me to try how: all I know of it / Is that Camillo was an honest man; / And why he left your court, the gods themselves, / Wotting no more than I, are ignorant.

I must not admit to any more faults than are truly mine. As for Polixenes, whom I am accused with, I confess I loved him as his honour required, with the kind of love that suits a lady like me, exactly the love, no more and no other, that you yourself commanded. Not to have given it would, I think, have been disobedience and ingratitude to you and to your friend, whose love has openly declared itself yours ever since he could speak, from a baby. Now, as for conspiracy, I don't know what it tastes like, though it is served up for me to try. All I know of it is that Camillo was an honest man. And why he left your court, the gods themselves don't know, if they know no more than I do.
You knew of his departure, as you know / What you have underta'en to do in 's absence.
You knew he was leaving, just as you know what you have agreed to do while he's away.
Sir, / You speak a language that I understand not: / My life stands in the level of your dreams, / Which I'll lay down.
Sir, you speak a language I don't understand. My life is a target for your dreams, and I'll give it up to them.

Your actions are my dreams. / You had a bastard by Polixenes, / And I but dream'd it. As you were past all shame / (Those of your fact are so) so past all truth, / Which to deny concerns more than avails; for as / Thy brat hath been cast out, like to itself, / No father owning it (which is, indeed, / More criminal in thee than it), so thou / Shalt feel our justice; in whose easiest passage / Look for no less than death.

Your actions are my dreams. You had a bastard by Polixenes, and I only dreamt it. As you were past all shame (those who do what you did always are), so you are past all truth. Denying it costs you more than it gains. For just as your brat has been thrown out, as it deserves, with no father to own it (which is more your crime than its), so you shall feel our justice, and in its mildest form, expect nothing less than death.

Sir, spare your threats: / The bug which you would fright me with, I seek. / To me can life be no commodity. / The crown and comfort of my life, your favour, / I do give lost, for I do feel it gone, / But know not how it went. My second joy, / And first-fruits of my body, from his presence / I am barr'd, like one infectious. My third comfort, / Starr'd most unluckily, is from my breast, / (The innocent milk in its most innocent mouth) / Hal'd out to murder; myself on every post / Proclaim'd a strumpet; with immodest hatred / The child-bed privilege denied, which 'longs / To women of all fashion; lastly, hurried / Here to this place, i' th' open air, before / I have got strength of limit. Now, my liege, / Tell me what blessings I have here alive, / That I should fear to die. Therefore proceed. / But yet hear this: mistake me not: no life, / I prize it not a straw, but for mine honour, / Which I would free, if I shall be condemn'd / Upon surmises, all proofs sleeping else / But what your jealousies awake, I tell you / 'Tis rigour, and not law. Your honours all, / I do refer me to the oracle: / Apollo be my judge!

Sir, spare your threats. The bogeyman you would frighten me with is what I seek. Life can be no benefit to me. The crown and comfort of my life, your love, I count as lost, for I feel it gone, but don't know how it went. My second joy, the first child of my body, I am barred from, as if I were infectious. My third comfort, born under the unluckiest star, is dragged from my breast, with the innocent milk in its innocent mouth, to be murdered. I myself am proclaimed a whore on every post. With shameless hatred I am denied the rest after childbirth that belongs to women of every rank. And last, I am rushed here to this place, into the open air, before I have got my strength back. Now, my lord, tell me what blessings I have left alive that I should fear to die. So go on. But hear this, don't misunderstand me. It is not my life I care about (I don't value it a straw) but my honour, which I want to clear. If I am condemned on suspicion, with every other proof asleep except what your jealousy wakes up, I tell you it is cruelty, not law. Your honours all, I appeal to the oracle. Let Apollo be my judge!
This your request / Is altogether just: therefore bring forth, / And in Apollo's name, his oracle:
This request of yours is entirely just. So, in Apollo's name, bring out his oracle.
The Emperor of Russia was my father. / O that he were alive, and here beholding / His daughter's trial! that he did but see / The flatness of my misery; yet with eyes / Of pity, not revenge!
The Emperor of Russia was my father. O, if only he were alive and here, watching his daughter's trial! If only he could see the depth of my misery, but with eyes of pity, not revenge!

You here shall swear upon this sword of justice, / That you, Cleomenes and Dion, have / Been both at Delphos, and from thence have brought / This seal'd-up oracle, by the hand deliver'd / Of great Apollo's priest; and that since then / You have not dared to break the holy seal, / Nor read the secrets in't.

You shall swear here on this sword of justice that you, Cleomenes and Dion, have both been to Delphi and brought back this sealed oracle, handed to you by great Apollo's priest, and that since then you have not dared to break the holy seal or read the secrets inside.
Break up the seals and read.
Break the seals and read it.

[Reads] "Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true / subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent babe truly begotten; / and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost be not / found."

(Reads) 'Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a loyal subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent baby truly his own; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost is not found.'
Now blessed be the great Apollo!
Now blessed be the great Apollo!
Ay, my lord, even so / As it is here set down.
Yes, my lord, exactly as it is written here.
There is no truth at all i' th' oracle: / The sessions shall proceed: this is mere falsehood.
There is no truth at all in the oracle. The trial shall go on. This is pure falsehood.
My lord the king, the king!
My lord the king, the king!
O sir, I shall be hated to report it. / The prince your son, with mere conceit and fear / Of the queen's speed, is gone.
O sir, I shall be hated for reporting it. The prince your son, from sheer imagination and fear about what would happen to the queen, is gone.
Apollo's angry, and the heavens themselves / Do strike at my injustice.
Apollo is angry, and the heavens themselves are striking at my injustice.
This news is mortal to the queen. Look down / And see what death is doing.
This news is deadly to the queen. Look down and see what death is doing.
Take her hence: / Her heart is but o'ercharg'd; she will recover. / I have too much believ'd mine own suspicion. / Beseech you tenderly apply to her / Some remedies for life.
Take her away. Her heart is only overburdened. She will recover. I have believed my own suspicion too much. I beg you, gently give her something to revive her.

Apollo, pardon / My great profaneness 'gainst thine oracle! / I'll reconcile me to Polixenes, / New woo my queen, recall the good Camillo, / Whom I proclaim a man of truth, of mercy; / For, being transported by my jealousies / To bloody thoughts and to revenge, I chose / Camillo for the minister to poison / My friend Polixenes: which had been done, / But that the good mind of Camillo tardied / My swift command, though I with death and with / Reward did threaten and encourage him, / Not doing it and being done. He, most humane / And fill'd with honour, to my kingly guest / Unclasp'd my practice, quit his fortunes here, / Which you knew great, and to the certain hazard / Of all incertainties himself commended, / No richer than his honour. How he glisters / Thorough my rust! And how his piety / Does my deeds make the blacker!

Apollo, pardon my great sacrilege against your oracle! I'll make my peace with Polixenes, woo my queen again, and call back good Camillo, whom I declare a man of truth and mercy. For, carried away by my jealousy to bloody thoughts and revenge, I chose Camillo to poison my friend Polixenes. And it would have been done, if Camillo's good mind had not delayed my hasty order, though I threatened him with death if he did not do it and promised him reward if he did. He, most humane and full of honour, revealed my plot to my royal guest, left his fortunes here, which you knew were great, and gave himself up to the certain risks of every uncertainty, with nothing but his honour to his name. How he shines through my rust! And how his goodness makes my deeds look blacker!
Woe the while! / O, cut my lace, lest my heart, cracking it, / Break too!
Alas the day! O, cut my laces, or my heart, cracking them, will break too!
What fit is this, good lady?
What fit is this, good lady?

What studied torments, tyrant, hast for me? / What wheels? racks? fires? what flaying? boiling / In leads or oils? What old or newer torture / Must I receive, whose every word deserves / To taste of thy most worst? Thy tyranny, / Together working with thy jealousies, / Fancies too weak for boys, too green and idle / For girls of nine. O, think what they have done, / And then run mad indeed, stark mad! for all / Thy by-gone fooleries were but spices of it. / That thou betray'dst Polixenes, 'twas nothing; / That did but show thee, of a fool, inconstant / And damnable ingrateful; nor was't much / Thou wouldst have poison'd good Camillo's honour, / To have him kill a king; poor trespasses, / More monstrous standing by: whereof I reckon / The casting forth to crows thy baby daughter, / To be or none or little, though a devil / Would have shed water out of fire ere done't, / Nor is't directly laid to thee the death / Of the young prince, whose honourable thoughts, / Thoughts high for one so tender, cleft the heart / That could conceive a gross and foolish sire / Blemish'd his gracious dam: this is not, no, / Laid to thy answer: but the last—O lords, / When I have said, cry Woe!—the queen, the queen, / The sweet'st, dear'st creature's dead, and vengeance for't / Not dropp'd down yet.

What carefully devised tortures have you for me, tyrant? What wheels? Racks? Fires? What flaying, boiling in lead or oil? What old or new torture must I suffer, when every word I say deserves the very worst you can do? Your tyranny, working together with your jealousy, fancies too weak for boys, too green and silly for girls of nine, O, think what they have done, and then go mad indeed, stark mad! For all your past follies were only a taste of it. That you betrayed Polixenes was nothing: that only showed you up as a fickle and damnably ungrateful fool. Nor was it much that you would have poisoned good Camillo's honour by making him kill a king: small offences, next to something more monstrous. And among those I count throwing out your baby daughter to the crows as nothing or little, though a devil would have wept tears out of fire before doing it. Nor is the death of the young prince directly blamed on you, whose honourable thoughts, high thoughts for one so young, broke his heart when he understood that a coarse and foolish father had stained his gracious mother. No, that is not charged to you. But the last thing (O lords, when I have said it, cry 'Woe!'): the queen, the queen, the sweetest, dearest creature, is dead, and vengeance for it has not yet fallen.

I say she's dead: I'll swear't. If word nor oath / Prevail not, go and see: if you can bring / Tincture, or lustre, in her lip, her eye, / Heat outwardly or breath within, I'll serve you / As I would do the gods. But, O thou tyrant! / Do not repent these things, for they are heavier / Than all thy woes can stir. Therefore betake thee / To nothing but despair. A thousand knees / Ten thousand years together, naked, fasting, / Upon a barren mountain, and still winter / In storm perpetual, could not move the gods / To look that way thou wert.

I say she's dead. I'll swear to it. If neither word nor oath convinces you, go and see. If you can bring colour or shine to her lip or her eye, warmth to her body or breath inside it, I'll serve you as I would the gods. But, O you tyrant, don't repent these things, for they are too heavy for all your sorrows to shift. So give yourself up to nothing but despair. A thousand people kneeling for ten thousand years together, naked and fasting, on a barren mountain in constant winter and endless storm, could not move the gods to look in your direction.
Go on, go on: / Thou canst not speak too much; I have deserv'd / All tongues to talk their bitterest.
Go on, go on. You can't say too much. I have deserved every tongue to speak its bitterest.
Say no more: / Howe'er the business goes, you have made fault / I' th' boldness of your speech.
Say no more. However the matter stands, you were wrong to speak so boldly.

I am sorry for 't: / All faults I make, when I shall come to know them, / I do repent. Alas, I have show'd too much / The rashness of a woman: he is touch'd / To th' noble heart. What's gone and what's past help, / Should be past grief. Do not receive affliction / At my petition; I beseech you, rather / Let me be punish'd, that have minded you / Of what you should forget. Now, good my liege, / Sir, royal sir, forgive a foolish woman: / The love I bore your queen—lo, fool again! / I'll speak of her no more, nor of your children. / I'll not remember you of my own lord, / Who is lost too. Take your patience to you, / And I'll say nothing.

I am sorry for it. Whenever I find out my faults, I repent of them. Alas, I have shown too much of a woman's rashness. He is hurt to his noble heart. What's gone and can't be helped should be past grieving. Don't take my words as a torment. I beg you, rather let me be punished, for reminding you of what you should forget. Now, my good lord, sir, royal sir, forgive a foolish woman. The love I bore your queen... There, a fool again! I'll speak no more of her, nor of your children. I won't remind you of my own husband, who is lost too. Arm yourself with patience, and I'll say nothing.

Thou didst speak but well / When most the truth, which I receive much better / Than to be pitied of thee. Prithee, bring me / To the dead bodies of my queen and son: / One grave shall be for both. Upon them shall / The causes of their death appear, unto / Our shame perpetual. Once a day I'll visit / The chapel where they lie, and tears shed there / Shall be my recreation. So long as nature / Will bear up with this exercise, so long / I daily vow to use it. Come, and lead me / To these sorrows.

You only spoke well when you spoke the truth, and I take that much better than your pity. Please take me to the bodies of my queen and son. One grave shall hold them both. On it shall be written the causes of their death, to our everlasting shame. Once a day I'll visit the chapel where they lie, and weeping there shall be my only pastime. As long as nature can bear this exercise, I vow to do it every day. Come, and lead me to these sorrows.
Thou art perfect, then, our ship hath touch'd upon / The deserts of Bohemia?
You're sure, then, that our ship has landed on the deserted coast of Bohemia?
Ay, my lord, and fear / We have landed in ill time: the skies look grimly, / And threaten present blusters. In my conscience, / The heavens with that we have in hand are angry, / And frown upon 's.
Yes, my lord, and I fear we've landed at a bad time. The skies look grim and threaten storms any moment. In my opinion, heaven is angry with what we are doing and frowns on us.
Their sacred wills be done! Go, get aboard; / Look to thy bark: I'll not be long before / I call upon thee.
Their holy will be done! Go, get on board. Look after your ship. I won't be long before I call for you.
Make your best haste, and go not / Too far i' th' land: 'tis like to be loud weather; / Besides, this place is famous for the creatures / Of prey that keep upon 't.
Be as quick as you can, and don't go too far inland. It's likely to be stormy. Besides, this place is known for the wild beasts of prey that live here.
Go thou away: / I'll follow instantly.
Go on. I'll follow straight away.
I am glad at heart / To be so rid o' th' business.
I'm glad at heart to be rid of this business.

Come, poor babe. / I have heard, but not believ'd, the spirits of the dead / May walk again: if such thing be, thy mother / Appear'd to me last night; for ne'er was dream / So like a waking. To me comes a creature, / Sometimes her head on one side, some another. / I never saw a vessel of like sorrow, / So fill'd and so becoming: in pure white robes, / Like very sanctity, she did approach / My cabin where I lay: thrice bow'd before me, / And, gasping to begin some speech, her eyes / Became two spouts. The fury spent, anon / Did this break from her: "Good Antigonus, / Since fate, against thy better disposition, / Hath made thy person for the thrower-out / Of my poor babe, according to thine oath, / Places remote enough are in Bohemia, / There weep, and leave it crying. And, for the babe / Is counted lost for ever, Perdita / I prithee call't. For this ungentle business, / Put on thee by my lord, thou ne'er shalt see / Thy wife Paulina more." And so, with shrieks, / She melted into air. Affrighted much, / I did in time collect myself and thought / This was so, and no slumber. Dreams are toys, / Yet for this once, yea, superstitiously, / I will be squar'd by this. I do believe / Hermione hath suffer'd death, and that / Apollo would, this being indeed the issue / Of King Polixenes, it should here be laid, / Either for life or death, upon the earth / Of its right father. Blossom, speed thee well! / There lie; and there thy character: there these;

Come, poor baby. I have heard, but not believed, that the spirits of the dead can walk again. If it's true, your mother appeared to me last night, for no dream was ever so like being awake. A figure came to me, with her head leaning first one way, then the other. I never saw a vessel of sorrow so full and so beautiful. In pure white robes, like holiness itself, she came to the cabin where I lay, bowed three times before me, and, gasping to begin a speech, her eyes became two fountains. When the fit was spent, this broke from her: 'Good Antigonus, since fate, against your better nature, has made you the one to throw out my poor baby, as you swore to, there are remote enough places in Bohemia. Weep there, and leave it crying. And because the baby is counted lost for ever, please call her Perdita. For this unkind business, put on you by my husband, you will never see your wife Paulina again.' And so, with shrieks, she melted into air. Badly frightened, I gradually pulled myself together and thought this was real and no dream. Dreams are trifles, but this once, yes, superstitiously, I will be ruled by this one. I believe Hermione has died, and that Apollo wants this child, being truly King Polixenes's, to be laid here, to live or die, on its true father's soil. Little blossom, good luck to you! Lie there, and there's your written account; there, these things,

Which may if fortune please, both breed thee, pretty, / And still rest thine. The storm begins: poor wretch, / That for thy mother's fault art thus expos'd / To loss and what may follow! Weep I cannot, / But my heart bleeds, and most accurs'd am I / To be by oath enjoin'd to this. Farewell! / The day frowns more and more. Thou'rt like to have / A lullaby too rough. I never saw / The heavens so dim by day. A savage clamour! / Well may I get aboard! This is the chase: / I am gone for ever.

which may, if fortune wills, pay for your upbringing, pretty one, and still leave something over. The storm is beginning. Poor wretch, exposed like this to loss and whatever follows, for your mother's fault! I cannot weep, but my heart bleeds, and I am most cursed to be bound by oath to do this. Farewell! The day frowns more and more. You're likely to have too rough a lullaby. I never saw the sky so dark by day. A savage roar! I'd better get on board! This is the hunt: I'm gone for ever.

I would there were no age between ten and three-and-twenty, or that / youth would sleep out the rest; for there is nothing in the between but / getting wenches with child, wronging the ancientry, stealing, / fighting—Hark you now! Would any but these boiled brains of nineteen / and two-and-twenty hunt this weather? They have scared away two of my / best sheep, which I fear the wolf will sooner find than the master: if / anywhere I have them, 'tis by the sea-side, browsing of ivy. Good luck, / an 't be thy will, what have we here?

I wish there were no age between ten and twenty-three, or that young men would sleep through it, for there's nothing in between but getting girls pregnant, insulting their elders, stealing, fighting... Listen to that! Would anyone but these hot-headed nineteen- and twenty-two-year-olds go hunting in this weather? They have scared off two of my best sheep, which I'm afraid the wolf will find before their owner does. If they're anywhere, it's by the seaside, nibbling ivy. Good luck, if it's your will! What have we here?

Mercy on 's, a bairn! A very pretty bairn! A boy or a child, I wonder? / A pretty one; a very pretty one. Sure, some scape. Though I am not / bookish, yet I can read waiting-gentlewoman in the scape. This has / been some stair-work, some trunk-work, some behind-door-work. They / were warmer that got this than the poor thing is here. I'll take it up / for pity: yet I'll tarry till my son come; he halloed but even now. / Whoa-ho-hoa!

Mercy on us, a baby! A very pretty baby! A boy or a girl, I wonder? A pretty one, a very pretty one. Surely some mistake from a fling. Though I'm no scholar, I can read a lady's maid in this escapade. This has been some business on the back stairs, in a trunk, behind a door. Whoever made this was warmer than the poor thing is here. I'll pick it up out of pity. But I'll wait till my son comes. He shouted a moment ago. Whoa-ho-hoa!
What, art so near? If thou'lt see a thing to talk on when thou art dead / and rotten, come hither. What ail'st thou, man?
What, are you so near? If you want to see something you'll still be talking about when you're dead and rotten, come here. What's the matter with you, man?
I have seen two such sights, by sea and by land! But I am not to say it / is a sea, for it is now the sky: betwixt the firmament and it, you / cannot thrust a bodkin's point.
I have seen two such sights, at sea and on land! But I can't call it the sea, because it's the sky now. You couldn't stick a pin between the heavens and the waves.

I would you did but see how it chafes, how it rages, how it takes up / the shore! But that's not to the point. O, the most piteous cry of the / poor souls! sometimes to see 'em, and not to see 'em. Now the ship / boring the moon with her mainmast, and anon swallowed with yest and / froth, as you'd thrust a cork into a hogshead. And then for the land / service, to see how the bear tore out his shoulder-bone, how he cried / to me for help, and said his name was Antigonus, a nobleman. But to / make an end of the ship, to see how the sea flap-dragon'd it: but / first, how the poor souls roared, and the sea mocked them, and how the / poor gentleman roared, and the bear mocked him, both roaring louder / than the sea or weather.

I wish you could see how it rages and storms, how it swallows the shore! But that's not the point. O, the pitiful cries of the poor souls! Sometimes you could see them, sometimes not. One moment the ship was poking the moon with her mainmast, the next swallowed in foam and froth, like a cork thrown into a barrel. And then on land, to see how the bear tore out his shoulder-bone, how he cried to me for help and said his name was Antigonus, a nobleman. But to finish with the ship, to see how the sea gulped it down: but first, how the poor souls roared, and the sea mocked them, and how the poor gentleman roared, and the bear mocked him, both roaring louder than the sea or the storm.
Name of mercy, when was this, boy?
For mercy's sake, when was this, boy?
Now, now. I have not winked since I saw these sights: the men are not / yet cold under water, nor the bear half dined on the gentleman. He's at / it now.
Now, just now. I haven't blinked since I saw these sights. The men aren't cold under the water yet, and the bear isn't half finished dining on the gentleman. He's at it now.
Would I had been by to have helped the old man!
I wish I had been there to help the old man!
I would you had been by the ship side, to have helped her: there your / charity would have lacked footing.
I wish you had been by the ship to help her. Your charity would have had nothing to stand on there.

Heavy matters, heavy matters! But look thee here, boy. Now bless / thyself: thou met'st with things dying, I with things new-born. Here's / a sight for thee. Look thee, a bearing-cloth for a squire's child! Look / thee here; take up, take up, boy; open't. So, let's see. It was told me / I should be rich by the fairies. This is some changeling: open't. / What's within, boy?

Sad things, sad things! But look here, boy. Now bless yourself: you met with things dying, I with things newborn. Here's a sight for you. Look, a christening cloth fit for a gentleman's child! Look here. Pick it up, pick it up, boy. Open it. So, let's see. I was told by fortune-tellers that the fairies would make me rich. This is some fairy changeling. Open it. What's inside, boy?
You're a made old man. If the sins of your youth are forgiven you, / you're well to live. Gold! all gold!
You're a made man, old man. If the sins of your youth are forgiven, you'll live well. Gold! All gold!

This is fairy gold, boy, and 'twill prove so. Up with it, keep it / close: home, home, the next way. We are lucky, boy, and to be so still / requires nothing but secrecy. Let my sheep go: come, good boy, the next / way home.

This is fairy gold, boy, and it will prove so. Pick it up, keep it hidden. Home, home, the quickest way. We are lucky, boy, and to stay that way we need only keep it secret. Let my sheep go. Come, good boy, the quickest way home.

Go you the next way with your findings. I'll go see if the bear be gone / from the gentleman, and how much he hath eaten. They are never curst / but when they are hungry: if there be any of him left, I'll bury it.

You go the quickest way with your find. I'll go and see if the bear has left the gentleman, and how much he's eaten. They're only fierce when they're hungry. If there's anything left of him, I'll bury it.
That's a good deed. If thou mayest discern by that which is left of him / what he is, fetch me to th' sight of him.
That's a good deed. If you can tell from what's left of him who he is, fetch me to see him.
Marry, will I; and you shall help to put him i' th' ground.
I certainly will, and you shall help put him in the ground.
'Tis a lucky day, boy, and we'll do good deeds on 't.
It's a lucky day, boy, and we'll do good deeds on it.

I that please some, try all: both joy and terror / Of good and bad, that makes and unfolds error, / Now take upon me, in the name of Time, / To use my wings. Impute it not a crime / To me or my swift passage, that I slide / O'er sixteen years, and leave the growth untried / Of that wide gap, since it is in my power / To o'erthrow law, and in one self-born hour / To plant and o'erwhelm custom. Let me pass / The same I am, ere ancient'st order was / Or what is now received. I witness to / The times that brought them in; so shall I do / To th' freshest things now reigning, and make stale / The glistering of this present, as my tale / Now seems to it. Your patience this allowing, / I turn my glass, and give my scene such growing / As you had slept between. Leontes leaving / Th' effects of his fond jealousies, so grieving / That he shuts up himself, imagine me, / Gentle spectators, that I now may be / In fair Bohemia, and remember well, / I mentioned a son o' th' king's, which Florizel / I now name to you; and with speed so pace / To speak of Perdita, now grown in grace / Equal with wondering. What of her ensues / I list not prophesy; but let Time's news / Be known when 'tis brought forth. A shepherd's daughter, / And what to her adheres, which follows after, / Is th' argument of Time. Of this allow, / If ever you have spent time worse ere now; / If never, yet that Time himself doth say / He wishes earnestly you never may.

I, who please some and test everyone, who am joy and terror to good and bad alike, who make mistakes and reveal them, now take it on myself, as Time, to use my wings. Don't count it a crime of mine, or of my swift passing, that I slide over sixteen years and leave what happened in that wide gap untold, since it is in my power to overturn law, and in a single hour of my own making to plant and overthrow custom. Let me pass as the same I was before the oldest order existed, or what is accepted now. I saw the times that brought them in, and I shall do the same to the newest things in fashion now, and make the glitter of the present as stale as my story seems now. If you will allow it, I turn my hourglass and move my play on as if you had slept in between. Leaving Leontes, who is grieving so much over the results of his foolish jealousy that he shuts himself away, imagine me, gentle audience, now in lovely Bohemia. And remember that I mentioned a son of the king's, whom I now name to you as Florizel. And now let me hurry on to speak of Perdita, grown in grace to be the wonder of everyone. What happens to her I don't care to prophesy, but let Time's news be known when it is born. A shepherd's daughter, and what comes with her, is the subject of Time's story. Allow this, if you have ever spent time worse before now. If never, then Time himself says he earnestly wishes you never may.
I pray thee, good Camillo, be no more importunate: 'tis a sickness / denying thee anything; a death to grant this.
Please, good Camillo, don't press me any more. It makes me sick to refuse you anything, but it would kill me to grant this.

It is fifteen years since I saw my country. Though I have for the most / part been aired abroad, I desire to lay my bones there. Besides, the / penitent king, my master, hath sent for me; to whose feeling sorrows I / might be some allay, or I o'erween to think so,—which is another spur / to my departure.

It is fifteen years since I saw my country. Though I have lived abroad most of my life, I want to lay my bones there. Besides, the repentant king, my master, has sent for me. I might be some comfort in his deep sorrow, or I flatter myself that I might, which is another spur to my leaving.

As thou lov'st me, Camillo, wipe not out the rest of thy services by / leaving me now: the need I have of thee, thine own goodness hath made; / better not to have had thee than thus to want thee. Thou, having made / me businesses which none without thee can sufficiently manage, must / either stay to execute them thyself, or take away with thee the very / services thou hast done, which if I have not enough considered (as too / much I cannot) to be more thankful to thee shall be my study; and my / profit therein the heaping friendships. Of that fatal country Sicilia, / prithee speak no more; whose very naming punishes me with the / remembrance of that penitent, as thou call'st him, and reconciled king, / my brother; whose loss of his most precious queen and children are even / now to be afresh lamented. Say to me, when sawest thou the Prince / Florizel, my son? Kings are no less unhappy, their issue not being / gracious, than they are in losing them when they have approved their / virtues.

If you love me, Camillo, don't wipe out all your other services by leaving me now. Your own goodness has made me need you. It would be better never to have had you than to lose you like this. You have started business for me that nobody but you can manage properly, so you must either stay and carry it out yourself, or take away with you the very services you have done. If I have not thanked you enough (and I cannot thank you too much), I'll make it my study to be more thankful, and my profit will be more of your friendship. Please say no more about that fatal country Sicilia. The very name punishes me by reminding me of that repentant king, as you call him, my brother, now reconciled, whose loss of his most precious queen and children is still to be mourned afresh. Tell me, when did you last see Prince Florizel, my son? Kings are as unhappy when their children turn out badly as when they lose them after they have proved their worth.

Sir, it is three days since I saw the prince. What his happier affairs / may be, are to me unknown, but I have missingly noted he is of late / much retired from court, and is less frequent to his princely exercises / than formerly he hath appeared.

Sir, it is three days since I saw the prince. What pleasanter affairs he has, I don't know, but I have noticed his absence lately: he spends much less time at court and at his princely exercises than he used to.

I have considered so much, Camillo, and with some care; so far that I / have eyes under my service which look upon his removedness; from whom I / have this intelligence, that he is seldom from the house of a most / homely shepherd, a man, they say, that from very nothing, and beyond / the imagination of his neighbours, is grown into an unspeakable estate.

I have noticed that too, Camillo, and with some concern, so much that I have spies in my service watching his absences. From them I've learnt that he is hardly ever away from the house of a very humble shepherd, a man who, they say, has grown from nothing to an incredible fortune, beyond anything his neighbours can imagine.
I have heard, sir, of such a man, who hath a daughter of most rare / note: the report of her is extended more than can be thought to begin / from such a cottage.
I have heard of such a man, sir, who has a daughter of quite extraordinary reputation. Talk of her spreads further than you would think could start from such a cottage.

That's likewise part of my intelligence: but, I fear, the angle that / plucks our son thither. Thou shalt accompany us to the place, where we / will, not appearing what we are, have some question with the shepherd; / from whose simplicity I think it not uneasy to get the cause of my / son's resort thither. Prithee, be my present partner in this business, / and lay aside the thoughts of Sicilia.

That is part of my report too. But I fear it's the hook that pulls our son there. You shall come with us to the place, where, without showing who we are, we will question the shepherd. He's simple, so I think it won't be hard to get from him why my son goes there. Please be my partner in this business now, and put aside your thoughts of Sicilia.
My best Camillo! We must disguise ourselves.
My best Camillo! We must disguise ourselves.

When daffodils begin to peer, / With, hey! the doxy over the dale, / Why, then comes in the sweet o' the year, / For the red blood reigns in the winter's pale. / The white sheet bleaching on the hedge, / With, hey! the sweet birds, O, how they sing! / Doth set my pugging tooth on edge; / For a quart of ale is a dish for a king. / The lark, that tirra-lirra chants, / With, hey! with, hey! the thrush and the jay, / Are summer songs for me and my aunts, / While we lie tumbling in the hay. / I have served Prince Florizel, and in my time wore three-pile, but now / I am out of service. / But shall I go mourn for that, my dear? / The pale moon shines by night: / And when I wander here and there, / I then do most go right. / If tinkers may have leave to live, / And bear the sow-skin budget, / Then my account I well may give / And in the stocks avouch it. / My traffic is sheets; when the kite builds, look to lesser linen. My / father named me Autolycus; who being, I as am, littered under Mercury, / was likewise a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles. With die and drab I / purchased this caparison, and my revenue is the silly cheat. Gallows / and knock are too powerful on the highway. Beating and hanging are / terrors to me. For the life to come, I sleep out the thought of it. A / prize! a prize!

(Singing) When daffodils begin to peep, with hey, the girl over the valley, why then comes in the sweet of the year, for the red blood rules where winter's pale used to. The white sheet bleaching on the hedge, with hey, the sweet birds, O, how they sing! sets my thieving tooth on edge, for a quart of ale is a dish for a king. The lark that sings tirra-lirra, with hey, with hey, the thrush and the jay, are summer songs for me and my girlfriends while we lie tumbling in the hay. I have served Prince Florizel, and in my time wore the finest velvet, but now I'm out of work. (Singing) But shall I go and mourn for that, my dear? The pale moon shines by night, and when I wander here and there I'm most on the right road. If tinkers are allowed to live and carry their pigskin bags, then I can well give an account of myself, and swear to it in the stocks. My trade is sheets: when the kite is building its nest, watch your smaller linen. My father named me Autolycus. Being born, as I was, under Mercury, the god of thieves, I was likewise a snapper-up of trifles nobody watches. Dice and whores bought me these rags, and my income is cheating fools. The gallows and a beating are too great a risk on the highway. Beating and hanging terrify me. As for the life to come, I sleep away the thought of it. A prize! A prize!
Let me see: every 'leven wether tods; every tod yields pound and odd / shilling; fifteen hundred shorn, what comes the wool to?
Let me see: every eleven sheep give a tod of wool, every tod yields a pound and some shillings; fifteen hundred sheared, what does the wool come to?
[Aside] If the springe hold, the cock's mine.
(Aside) If the snare holds, the bird is mine.

I cannot do't without counters. Let me see; what am I to buy for our / sheep-shearing feast? "Three pound of sugar, five pound of currants, / rice"—what will this sister of mine do with rice? But my father hath / made her mistress of the feast, and she lays it on. She hath made me / four-and-twenty nosegays for the shearers, three-man song-men all, and / very good ones; but they are most of them means and basses, but one / puritan amongst them, and he sings psalms to hornpipes. I must have / saffron to colour the warden pies; "mace; dates", none, that's out of / my note; "nutmegs, seven; a race or two of ginger", but that I may beg; / "four pound of prunes, and as many of raisins o' th' sun."

I can't do it without counters. Let me see, what am I to buy for our sheep-shearing feast? 'Three pounds of sugar, five pounds of currants, rice.' What will this sister of mine do with rice? But my father has made her mistress of the feast, and she's going all out. She has made twenty-four posies for the shearers, all singers of three-part songs, and very good ones, but they're mostly tenors and basses, except one Puritan among them, and he sings psalms to dance tunes. I must have saffron to colour the pear pies. 'Mace; dates': no, that's not on my list. 'Nutmegs, seven; a root or two of ginger,' but I can beg that; 'four pounds of prunes, and as many raisins dried in the sun.'
[Grovelling on the ground] O that ever I was born!
(Grovelling on the ground) O, that I was ever born!
O, help me, help me! Pluck but off these rags; and then, death, death!
O, help me, help me! Just pull off these rags, and then death, death!
Alack, poor soul! thou hast need of more rags to lay on thee, rather / than have these off.
Alas, poor soul! You need more rags put on you, not these taken off.
O sir, the loathsomeness of them offends me more than the stripes I / have received, which are mighty ones and millions.
O sir, their filthiness offends me more than the blows I've had, which were mighty ones, and millions of them.
Alas, poor man! a million of beating may come to a great matter.
Alas, poor man! A million blows can add up to a lot.
I am robbed, sir, and beaten; my money and apparel ta'en from me, and / these detestable things put upon me.
I've been robbed, sir, and beaten. My money and clothes were taken from me, and these disgusting things put on me.
What, by a horseman or a footman?
What, by a man on horseback or on foot?
A footman, sweet sir, a footman.
On foot, sweet sir, on foot.
Indeed, he should be a footman by the garments he has left with thee: / if this be a horseman's coat, it hath seen very hot service. Lend me / thy hand, I'll help thee: come, lend me thy hand.
Yes, he must have been a footpad, by the clothes he's left you. If this is a horseman's coat, it's seen some very hot service. Give me your hand. I'll help you. Come, give me your hand.
O, good sir, softly, good sir. I fear, sir, my shoulder blade is out.
O, good sir, softly, good sir. I'm afraid, sir, my shoulder blade is out.
Softly, dear sir! [Picks his pocket] good sir, softly. You ha' done / me a charitable office.
Softly, dear sir! (He picks the Clown's pocket) Good sir, softly. You have done me a kind service.
Dost lack any money? I have a little money for thee.
Do you need any money? I have a little money for you.

No, good sweet sir; no, I beseech you, sir: I have a kinsman not past / three-quarters of a mile hence, unto whom I was going. I shall there / have money or anything I want. Offer me no money, I pray you; that / kills my heart.

No, good sweet sir, no, I beg you, sir. I have a relative not more than three-quarters of a mile from here, where I was going. I shall have money there, or anything I need. Don't offer me money, please; that breaks my heart.
What manner of fellow was he that robbed you?
What sort of fellow was it that robbed you?

A fellow, sir, that I have known to go about with troll-my-dames. I / knew him once a servant of the prince; I cannot tell, good sir, for / which of his virtues it was, but he was certainly whipped out of the / court.

A fellow, sir, that I have known to go round with a gambling game. I knew him once as a servant of the prince. I can't say, good sir, which of his virtues it was for, but he was certainly whipped out of court.
His vices, you would say; there's no virtue whipped out of the court. / They cherish it to make it stay there; and yet it will no more but / abide.
His vices, you mean. No virtue gets whipped out of court. They cherish virtue to make it stay there, and yet it only ever visits.

Vices, I would say, sir. I know this man well. He hath been since an / ape-bearer, then a process-server, a bailiff. Then he compassed a / motion of the Prodigal Son, and married a tinker's wife within a mile / where my land and living lies; and, having flown over many knavish / professions, he settled only in rogue. Some call him Autolycus.

Vices, I mean, sir. I know this man well. Since then he has been a man with a performing monkey, then a server of summonses, a bailiff. Then he got hold of a puppet show of the Prodigal Son, and married a tinker's wife within a mile of where my land and living are. After flitting through many crooked trades, he settled down as a rogue. Some call him Autolycus.
Out upon him! prig, for my life, prig: he haunts wakes, fairs, and / bear-baitings.
Curse him! A thief, I swear, a thief. He hangs around church festivals, fairs and bear-baitings.
Very true, sir; he, sir, he; that's the rogue that put me into this / apparel.
Very true, sir. He, sir, he. That's the rogue that put me in these clothes.
Not a more cowardly rogue in all Bohemia. If you had but looked big and / spit at him, he'd have run.
There isn't a more cowardly rogue in all Bohemia. If you had only looked big and spat at him, he'd have run.
I must confess to you, sir, I am no fighter. I am false of heart that / way; and that he knew, I warrant him.
I must confess to you, sir, I'm no fighter. My heart's weak that way, and he knew it, I'm sure.
Sweet sir, much better than I was. I can stand and walk: I will even / take my leave of you and pace softly towards my kinsman's.
Sweet sir, much better than I was. I can stand and walk. I'll even say goodbye to you and walk slowly to my relative's.
Shall I bring thee on the way?
Shall I take you on your way?
No, good-faced sir; no, sweet sir.
No, kind-faced sir; no, sweet sir.
Then fare thee well. I must go buy spices for our sheep-shearing.
Then goodbye. I must go and buy spices for our sheep-shearing.
Good luck to you, sweet sir!

Your purse is not hot enough to purchase your spice. I'll be with you / at your sheep-shearing too. If I make not this cheat bring out / another, and the shearers prove sheep, let me be unrolled, and my name / put in the book of virtue!

Your purse isn't warm enough now to buy your spice. I'll be with you at your sheep-shearing too. If I don't make this trick lead to another, and the shearers turn out to be sheep, let my name be struck off the roll of rogues and written in the book of virtue!
Jog on, jog on, the footpath way, / And merrily hent the stile-a: / A merry heart goes all the day, / Your sad tires in a mile-a.
(Singing) Jog on, jog on, along the footpath, and merrily jump over the stile. A merry heart goes all day long; a sad one tires in a mile.

These your unusual weeds to each part of you / Do give a life, no shepherdess, but Flora / Peering in April's front. This your sheep-shearing / Is as a meeting of the petty gods, / And you the queen on 't.

These unusual clothes of yours give life to every part of you. You are no shepherdess, but Flora, goddess of flowers, peeping out at the start of April. This sheep-shearing of yours is like a meeting of the minor gods, and you are its queen.

Sir, my gracious lord, / To chide at your extremes it not becomes me; / O, pardon that I name them! Your high self, / The gracious mark o' th' land, you have obscur'd / With a swain's wearing, and me, poor lowly maid, / Most goddess-like prank'd up. But that our feasts / In every mess have folly, and the feeders / Digest it with a custom, I should blush / To see you so attir'd; swoon, I think, / To show myself a glass.

Sir, my gracious lord, it isn't my place to scold you for your excesses. O, forgive me for mentioning them! You have hidden your high self, the gracious model of the land, in a peasant's clothes, and dressed me, a poor humble girl, like a goddess. If it weren't that our feasts have foolery in every course, and the guests are used to swallowing it, I would blush to see you dressed like that, and faint, I think, to see myself in a mirror.
I bless the time / When my good falcon made her flight across / Thy father's ground.
I bless the time when my good falcon flew across your father's land.

Now Jove afford you cause! / To me the difference forges dread. Your greatness / Hath not been us'd to fear. Even now I tremble / To think your father, by some accident, / Should pass this way, as you did. O, the Fates! / How would he look to see his work, so noble, / Vilely bound up? What would he say? Or how / Should I, in these my borrow'd flaunts, behold / The sternness of his presence?

May Jove give you cause to! The difference in our rank makes me afraid. Your greatness has never been used to fear. Even now I tremble to think your father might come this way by chance, as you did. O, the Fates! How would he look to see his own noble work, his son, so vilely bound up? What would he say? Or how could I, in this borrowed finery, face the sternness of his presence?

Apprehend / Nothing but jollity. The gods themselves, / Humbling their deities to love, have taken / The shapes of beasts upon them. Jupiter / Became a bull and bellow'd; the green Neptune / A ram and bleated; and the fire-rob'd god, / Golden Apollo, a poor humble swain, / As I seem now. Their transformations / Were never for a piece of beauty rarer, / Nor in a way so chaste, since my desires / Run not before mine honour, nor my lusts / Burn hotter than my faith.

Expect nothing but fun. The gods themselves, lowering their godhead for love, have taken the shapes of beasts. Jupiter became a bull and bellowed; green Neptune a ram, and bleated; and the god in robes of fire, golden Apollo, a poor humble shepherd, as I seem now. Their transformations were never for a rarer beauty, nor in such a chaste way, since my desires don't run ahead of my honour, nor my lust burn hotter than my faith.

O, but, sir, / Your resolution cannot hold when 'tis / Oppos'd, as it must be, by the power of the king: / One of these two must be necessities, / Which then will speak, that you must change this purpose, / Or I my life.
O, but, sir, your resolve cannot hold when it is opposed, as it must be, by the king's power. One of two things will then have to happen: either you must change your plan, or I must lose my life.

Thou dearest Perdita, / With these forc'd thoughts, I prithee, darken not / The mirth o' th' feast. Or I'll be thine, my fair, / Or not my father's. For I cannot be / Mine own, nor anything to any, if / I be not thine. To this I am most constant, / Though destiny say no. Be merry, gentle. / Strangle such thoughts as these with anything / That you behold the while. Your guests are coming: / Lift up your countenance, as it were the day / Of celebration of that nuptial which / We two have sworn shall come.

Dearest Perdita, please don't darken the fun of the feast with these far-fetched thoughts. Either I'll be yours, my fair one, or not my father's. For I cannot be my own, or anything to anyone, if I am not yours. I am firmly fixed on this, even if destiny says no. Be merry, gentle one. Strangle thoughts like these with anything you see around you. Your guests are coming. Lift up your face, as if it were the day of the wedding that we two have sworn shall come.
O lady Fortune, / Stand you auspicious!
O Lady Fortune, be kind to us!
See, your guests approach: / Address yourself to entertain them sprightly, / And let's be red with mirth.
Look, your guests are coming. Get ready to entertain them in high spirits, and let's be red-faced with fun.

Fie, daughter! When my old wife liv'd, upon / This day she was both pantler, butler, cook, / Both dame and servant; welcom'd all; serv'd all; / Would sing her song and dance her turn; now here / At upper end o' th' table, now i' th' middle; / On his shoulder, and his; her face o' fire / With labour, and the thing she took to quench it / She would to each one sip. You are retired, / As if you were a feasted one, and not / The hostess of the meeting: pray you, bid / These unknown friends to 's welcome, for it is / A way to make us better friends, more known. / Come, quench your blushes, and present yourself / That which you are, mistress o' th' feast. Come on, / And bid us welcome to your sheep-shearing, / As your good flock shall prosper.

For shame, daughter! When my old wife was alive, on this day she was pantry-maid, butler and cook, mistress and servant. She welcomed everyone, served everyone, sang her song and danced her turn, now at the top of the table, now in the middle, leaning on his shoulder and his, her face on fire with work, and she would sip to each one with the drink she took to cool it. You keep in the background, as if you were a guest and not the hostess of the party. Please welcome these strangers to us, for that's the way to make us better friends and better acquainted. Come, put out your blushes and show yourself for what you are, mistress of the feast. Come on, and welcome us to your sheep-shearing, as you want your good flock to thrive.

[To Polixenes] Sir, welcome. / It is my father's will I should take on me / The hostess-ship o' the day. / [To Camillo] You're welcome, sir. / Give me those flowers there, Dorcas. Reverend sirs, / For you there's rosemary and rue; these keep / Seeming and savour all the winter long. / Grace and remembrance be to you both! / And welcome to our shearing!

(To Polixenes) Sir, welcome. It is my father's wish that I take on the duties of hostess today. (To Camillo) You're welcome, sir. Give me those flowers there, Dorcas. Reverend sirs, here's rosemary and rue for you. These keep their look and their scent all winter long. Grace and remembrance be with you both! And welcome to our shearing!
Shepherdess— / A fair one are you—well you fit our ages / With flowers of winter.
Shepherdess (and a lovely one you are), you suit our ages well with winter flowers.

Sir, the year growing ancient, / Not yet on summer's death nor on the birth / Of trembling winter, the fairest flowers o' th' season / Are our carnations and streak'd gillyvors, / Which some call nature's bastards: of that kind / Our rustic garden's barren; and I care not / To get slips of them.

Sir, as the year grows old, not yet at summer's death nor at the birth of shivering winter, the loveliest flowers of the season are our carnations and striped gillyflowers, which some call nature's bastards. Our country garden has none of that kind, and I don't care to get cuttings of them.
Wherefore, gentle maiden, / Do you neglect them?
Why, gentle maiden, do you neglect them?
For I have heard it said / There is an art which, in their piedness, shares / With great creating nature.
Because I have heard it said that in their streaks there is an art of breeding that shares the work with great creating nature.

Say there be; / Yet nature is made better by no mean / But nature makes that mean. So, over that art / Which you say adds to nature, is an art / That nature makes. You see, sweet maid, we marry / A gentler scion to the wildest stock, / And make conceive a bark of baser kind / By bud of nobler race. This is an art / Which does mend nature, change it rather, but / The art itself is nature.

Suppose there is. Yet nature is improved by no means but nature makes that means. So, above the art that you say adds to nature, there is an art that nature makes. You see, sweet girl, we marry a gentler shoot to the wildest stock, and make a tree of humbler kind conceive by a bud of nobler breed. This is an art that improves nature, or rather changes it, but the art itself is nature.
Then make your garden rich in gillyvors, / And do not call them bastards.
Then fill your garden with gillyflowers, and don't call them bastards.

I'll not put / The dibble in earth to set one slip of them; / No more than, were I painted, I would wish / This youth should say 'twere well, and only therefore / Desire to breed by me. Here's flowers for you: / Hot lavender, mints, savory, marjoram, / The marigold, that goes to bed with th' sun / And with him rises weeping. These are flowers / Of middle summer, and I think they are given / To men of middle age. You're very welcome.

I won't push a spade into the earth to plant a single cutting of them, any more than, if I wore make-up, I would want this young man to say it looked well and desire to have children with me only for that. Here are flowers for you: hot lavender, mint, savory, marjoram, the marigold that goes to bed with the sun and rises with him, weeping dew. These are midsummer flowers, and I think they are given to men of middle age. You're very welcome.
I should leave grazing, were I of your flock, / And only live by gazing.
If I were one of your flock, I would stop grazing and live only by gazing.

Out, alas! / You'd be so lean that blasts of January / Would blow you through and through. [To Florizel] Now, my fair'st friend, / I would I had some flowers o' th' spring, that might / Become your time of day; and yours, and yours, / That wear upon your virgin branches yet / Your maidenheads growing. O Proserpina, / From the flowers now that, frighted, thou let'st fall / From Dis's waggon! daffodils, / That come before the swallow dares, and take / The winds of March with beauty; violets dim, / But sweeter than the lids of Juno's eyes / Or Cytherea's breath; pale primroses, / That die unmarried ere they can behold / Bright Phoebus in his strength (a malady / Most incident to maids); bold oxlips and / The crown imperial; lilies of all kinds, / The flower-de-luce being one. O, these I lack, / To make you garlands of; and my sweet friend, / To strew him o'er and o'er!

Oh dear! You'd be so thin that January winds would blow right through you. (To Florizel) Now, my fairest friend, I wish I had some spring flowers that might suit your time of life; (to the shepherdesses) and yours, and yours, who still carry your maidenhood on your young branches. O Proserpina, if only I had the flowers that you let fall in fright from Pluto's chariot! Daffodils, that come before the swallow dares, and take the March winds with their beauty; violets, dim, but sweeter than Juno's eyelids or the breath of Venus; pale primroses, that die unmarried before they can see the bright sun in his strength (an illness common in young girls); bold oxlips and the crown imperial; lilies of every kind, the iris being one. O, I lack these to make garlands for you, and to scatter over and over my sweet friend!

No, like a bank for love to lie and play on; / Not like a corse; or if, not to be buried, / But quick, and in mine arms. Come, take your flowers. / Methinks I play as I have seen them do / In Whitsun pastorals. Sure this robe of mine / Does change my disposition.

No, like a bank for love to lie and play on. Not like a corpse; or if so, not to be buried, but alive, in my arms. Come, take your flowers. I think I'm acting the way I've seen them do in Whitsun plays. This dress of mine must be changing my nature.

What you do / Still betters what is done. When you speak, sweet, / I'd have you do it ever. When you sing, / I'd have you buy and sell so, so give alms, / Pray so; and, for the ord'ring your affairs, / To sing them too. When you do dance, I wish you / A wave o' th' sea, that you might ever do / Nothing but that, move still, still so, / And own no other function. Each your doing, / So singular in each particular, / Crowns what you are doing in the present deeds, / That all your acts are queens.

Whatever you do improves on what has been done. When you speak, sweet, I'd have you speak for ever. When you sing, I'd have you buy and sell like that, give to the poor like that, pray like that, and give orders to your household singing too. When you dance, I wish you were a wave of the sea, so that you might do nothing but that, move always, always like that, and have no other task. Every single thing you do, so special in every detail, crowns what you are doing at the moment, so that all your acts are queens.

O Doricles, / Your praises are too large. But that your youth, / And the true blood which peeps fairly through 't, / Do plainly give you out an unstained shepherd, / With wisdom I might fear, my Doricles, / You woo'd me the false way.

O Doricles, your praises are too great. If your youth, and the honest blood that shows so fairly through it, did not plainly mark you as an innocent shepherd, I might wisely fear, my Doricles, that you were wooing me dishonestly.
I think you have / As little skill to fear as I have purpose / To put you to 't. But, come; our dance, I pray. / Your hand, my Perdita. So turtles pair / That never mean to part.
I think you have as little cause to fear as I have intention to give you any. But come, our dance, please. Your hand, my Perdita. This is how turtle-doves pair, who never mean to part.
This is the prettiest low-born lass that ever / Ran on the green-sward. Nothing she does or seems / But smacks of something greater than herself, / Too noble for this place.
This is the prettiest low-born girl who ever ran across the green. Nothing she does or seems to be but tastes of something greater than herself, too noble for this place.
He tells her something / That makes her blood look out. Good sooth, she is / The queen of curds and cream.
He's telling her something that makes her blush. Truly, she is the queen of curds and cream.
Come on, strike up the music.
Mopsa must be your mistress: marry, garlic, to mend her kissing with!
Mopsa must be your partner. Well, take garlic, to sweeten her kisses!
Not a word, a word; we stand upon our manners. / Come, strike up.
Not a word, not a word. We must mind our manners. Come, strike up.
Pray, good shepherd, what fair swain is this / Which dances with your daughter?
Please, good shepherd, who is the handsome young man dancing with your daughter?

They call him Doricles; and boasts himself / To have a worthy feeding. But I have it / Upon his own report, and I believe it. / He looks like sooth. He says he loves my daughter. / I think so too; for never gaz'd the moon / Upon the water as he'll stand and read, / As 'twere, my daughter's eyes. And, to be plain, / I think there is not half a kiss to choose / Who loves another best.

They call him Doricles, and he boasts of having good land with pasture. But I only have his word for it, and I believe it. He looks honest. He says he loves my daughter. I think so too, for the moon never gazed on the water the way he'll stand and read my daughter's eyes. And to be honest, I don't think there's half a kiss between them in who loves the other best.
So she does anything, though I report it / That should be silent. If young Doricles / Do light upon her, she shall bring him that / Which he not dreams of.
So she does everything, though I'm the one saying it who should keep quiet. If young Doricles gets her, she will bring him something he doesn't dream of.

O master, if you did but hear the pedlar at the door, you would never / dance again after a tabor and pipe; no, the bagpipe could not move you. / He sings several tunes faster than you'll tell money. He utters them as / he had eaten ballads, and all men's ears grew to his tunes.

O master, if you could only hear the pedlar at the door, you would never dance to drum and pipe again; no, even the bagpipe couldn't move you. He sings several tunes faster than you can count money. He pours them out as if he'd eaten ballads, and everyone's ears are glued to his songs.
He could never come better: he shall come in. I love a ballad but even / too well, if it be doleful matter merrily set down, or a very pleasant / thing indeed and sung lamentably.
He couldn't have come at a better time. He shall come in. I love a ballad almost too much, if it's sad stuff set to a merry tune, or something really cheerful sung mournfully.

He hath songs for man or woman of all sizes. No milliner can so fit his / customers with gloves. He has the prettiest love-songs for maids, so / without bawdry, which is strange; with such delicate burdens of dildos / and fadings, "jump her and thump her"; and where some stretch-mouthed / rascal would, as it were, mean mischief and break a foul gap into the / matter, he makes the maid to answer "Whoop, do me no harm, good man"; / puts him off, slights him, with "Whoop, do me no harm, good man."

He has songs for men or women of every size. No shop can fit its customers with gloves so well. He has the prettiest love songs for girls, without any rudeness, which is strange, with such dainty refrains of 'dildos' and 'fadings', 'jump her and thump her'. And where some big-mouthed rascal might mean mischief and break in with something filthy, he makes the girl answer 'Whoop, do me no harm, good man.' She puts him off and snubs him with 'Whoop, do me no harm, good man.'
Believe me, thou talkest of an admirable conceited fellow. Has he any / unbraided wares?
Believe me, you're talking about a wonderfully clever fellow. Has he got any fresh goods?

He hath ribbons of all the colours i' th' rainbow; points, more than / all the lawyers in Bohemia can learnedly handle, though they come to / him by th' gross; inkles, caddisses, cambrics, lawns; why he sings 'em / over as they were gods or goddesses; you would think a smock were a / she-angel, he so chants to the sleeve-hand and the work about the / square on 't.

He has ribbons of every colour in the rainbow; laces, more than all the lawyers in Bohemia can learnedly handle, though they come to him by the gross; tapes, braids, cambrics, fine linens. He sings about them as if they were gods or goddesses. You'd think a smock was a she-angel, the way he sings about the cuff and the embroidery on the front.
Prithee bring him in; and let him approach singing.
Please bring him in, and let him come in singing.
Forewarn him that he use no scurrilous words in 's tunes.
Warn him not to use any dirty words in his songs.
You have of these pedlars that have more in them than you'd think, / sister.
There are some of these pedlars who have more in them than you'd think, sister.
Ay, good brother, or go about to think.
Yes, good brother, or would want to think.

Lawn as white as driven snow, / Cypress black as e'er was crow, / Gloves as sweet as damask roses, / Masks for faces and for noses, / Bugle-bracelet, necklace amber, / Perfume for a lady's chamber, / Golden quoifs and stomachers / For my lads to give their dears, / Pins and poking-sticks of steel, / What maids lack from head to heel. / Come buy of me, come; come buy, come buy; / Buy, lads, or else your lasses cry. / Come, buy.

(Singing) Linen as white as driven snow, crape as black as any crow, gloves as sweet as damask roses, masks for faces and for noses, bead bracelets, amber necklaces, perfume for a lady's bedroom, golden caps and bodices for my lads to give their sweethearts, pins and steel rods for ironing ruffs, everything girls need from head to heel. Come and buy from me, come; come buy, come buy. Buy, lads, or else your girls will cry. Come and buy.
If I were not in love with Mopsa, thou shouldst take no money of me; / but being enthralled as I am, it will also be the bondage of certain / ribbons and gloves.
If I weren't in love with Mopsa, you wouldn't get a penny out of me. But being as enslaved as I am, it will mean buying certain ribbons and gloves as well.
I was promised them against the feast; but they come not too late now.
I was promised them for the feast, but they're not too late now.
He hath promised you more than that, or there be liars.
He has promised you more than that, or people are liars.
He hath paid you all he promised you. Maybe he has paid you more, which / will shame you to give him again.
He has paid you all he promised you. Maybe he's paid you more, which you'll be ashamed to give back to him.

Is there no manners left among maids? Will they wear their plackets / where they should bear their faces?
