Is there not milking-time, when you / are going to bed, or kiln-hole, to whistle of these secrets, but you / must be tittle-tattling before all our guests? 'Tis well they are / whispering. Clamour your tongues, and not a word more.

Have girls got no manners left? Will they show their petticoats where they should show their faces? Isn't there milking time, or bedtime, or the fireside, to whisper these secrets, without tittle-tattling in front of all our guests? It's a good thing they're whispering. Stop your tongues, and not another word.
I have done. Come, you promised me a tawdry lace and a pair of sweet / gloves.
I've finished. Come, you promised me a showy lace and a pair of scented gloves.
Have I not told thee how I was cozened by the way and lost all my / money?
Haven't I told you how I was cheated on the road and lost all my money?
And indeed, sir, there are cozeners abroad; therefore it behoves men to / be wary.
And indeed, sir, there are cheats about, so men should be careful.
Fear not thou, man. Thou shalt lose nothing here.
Don't worry, man. You'll lose nothing here.
I hope so, sir; for I have about me many parcels of charge.
I hope so, sir, for I'm carrying many valuable packages.
What have you got here? Ballads?
Pray now, buy some. I love a ballad in print alife, for then we are / sure they are true.
Please, buy some. I love a printed ballad with all my heart, because then we can be sure they're true.
Here's one to a very doleful tune. How a usurer's wife was brought to / bed of twenty money-bags at a burden, and how she longed to eat adders' / heads and toads carbonadoed.
Here's one to a very sad tune: how a moneylender's wife gave birth to twenty moneybags at once, and how she craved adders' heads and grilled toads.
Very true, and but a month old.
Very true, and only a month old.
Bless me from marrying a usurer!
Heaven save me from marrying a moneylender!
Here's the midwife's name to't, one Mistress Taleporter, and five or / six honest wives that were present. Why should I carry lies abroad?
Here's the midwife's name on it, one Mistress Taleporter, and five or six honest wives who were there. Why would I go round telling lies?
Come on, lay it by; and let's first see more ballads. We'll buy the / other things anon.
Come on, put it aside, and let's see more ballads first. We'll buy the other things later.

Here's another ballad, of a fish that appeared upon the coast on / Wednesday the fourscore of April, forty thousand fathom above water, / and sung this ballad against the hard hearts of maids. It was thought / she was a woman, and was turned into a cold fish for she would not / exchange flesh with one that loved her. The ballad is very pitiful, and / as true.

Here's another ballad, about a fish that appeared off the coast on Wednesday the eightieth of April, forty thousand fathoms above the water, and sang this ballad against the hard hearts of girls. It was thought she had been a woman, and was turned into a cold fish because she would not have sex with a man who loved her. The ballad is very sad, and just as true.
Is it true too, think you?
Do you think that's true too?
Five justices' hands at it, and witnesses more than my pack will hold.
Five magistrates have signed it, and there are more witnesses than my pack will hold.
This is a merry ballad; but a very pretty one.
This is a merry ballad, but a very pretty one.
Why, this is a passing merry one and goes to the tune of "Two maids / wooing a man." There's scarce a maid westward but she sings it. 'Tis in / request, I can tell you.
Why, this is an extremely merry one, and goes to the tune of 'Two girls wooing a man'. There's hardly a girl in the west who doesn't sing it. It's very popular, I can tell you.
We can both sing it: if thou'lt bear a part, thou shalt hear; 'tis in / three parts.
We can both sing it. If you'll take a part, you'll hear it. It's in three parts.
We had the tune on 't a month ago.
We learnt the tune a month ago.
I can bear my part; you must know 'tis my occupation: have at it with / you.
I can take my part. You must know singing is my trade. Here goes.
Get you hence, for I must go / Where it fits not you to know.
(Singing) Go away, for I must go where it's not right for you to know.
It becomes thy oath full well / Thou to me thy secrets tell.
(Singing) It suits your oath very well for you to tell your secrets to me.
Me too! Let me go thither.
(Singing) Me too! Let me go there.
Or thou goest to th' grange or mill.
(Singing) Are you going to the farm or the mill?
If to either, thou dost ill.
(Singing) If to either, you are doing wrong.
Thou hast sworn my love to be.
(Singing) You have sworn to be my love.
Thou hast sworn it more to me. / Then whither goest? Say, whither?
(Singing) You've sworn it more to me. Then where are you going? Say, where?

We'll have this song out anon by ourselves. My father and the gentlemen / are in sad talk, and we'll not trouble them. Come, bring away thy pack / after me. Wenches, I'll buy for you both. Pedlar, let's have the first / choice. Follow me, girls.

We'll finish this song later by ourselves. My father and the gentlemen are having a serious talk, and we won't disturb them. Come, bring your pack after me. Girls, I'll buy for you both. Pedlar, let's have first pick. Follow me, girls.
[Aside] And you shall pay well for 'em.
(Aside) And you'll pay well for them.

Will you buy any tape, / Or lace for your cape, / My dainty duck, my dear-a? / Any silk, any thread, / Any toys for your head, / Of the new'st and fin'st, fin'st wear-a? / Come to the pedlar; / Money's a meddler / That doth utter all men's ware-a.

(Singing) Will you buy any tape, or lace for your cape, my dainty duck, my dear? Any silk, any thread, any trinkets for your head, of the newest and finest, finest wear? Come to the pedlar. Money is a go-between that sells all men's goods.

Master, there is three carters, three shepherds, three neat-herds, / three swine-herds, that have made themselves all men of hair. They call / themselves saltiers, and they have dance which the wenches say is a / gallimaufry of gambols, because they are not in 't; but they themselves / are o' the mind (if it be not too rough for some that know little but / bowling) it will please plentifully.

Master, there are three carters, three shepherds, three cowherds and three swineherds who have dressed themselves up all in hair. They call themselves 'saltiers' (satyrs), and they have a dance which the girls say is a hotchpotch of capers, because they aren't in it. But they themselves think (if it isn't too rough for some who know nothing but bowls) it will please very much.
Away! we'll none on 't. Here has been too much homely foolery already. / I know, sir, we weary you.
Away! We'll have none of it. There's been too much homely foolery already. I know, sir, we are tiring you.
You weary those that refresh us: pray, let's see these four threes of / herdsmen.
You tire those who refresh us. Please, let's see these four threes of herdsmen.
One three of them, by their own report, sir, hath danced before the / king; and not the worst of the three but jumps twelve foot and a half / by th' square.
One three of them, by their own account, sir, have danced before the king, and the worst of the three jumps twelve and a half feet, measured exactly.
Leave your prating: since these good men are pleased, let them come in; / but quickly now.
Stop your chattering. Since these good men are pleased, let them come in. But quickly now.
Why, they stay at door, sir.
Why, they're waiting at the door, sir.

O, father, you'll know more of that hereafter. / [To Camillo] Is it not too far gone? 'Tis time to part them. / He's simple and tells much. [To Florizel] How now, fair shepherd! / Your heart is full of something that does take / Your mind from feasting. Sooth, when I was young / And handed love, as you do, I was wont / To load my she with knacks: I would have ransack'd / The pedlar's silken treasury and have pour'd it / To her acceptance. You have let him go, / And nothing marted with him. If your lass / Interpretation should abuse, and call this / Your lack of love or bounty, you were straited / For a reply, at least if you make a care / Of happy holding her.

(To the Shepherd) O, old man, you'll hear more of that later. (To Camillo) Hasn't it gone too far? It's time to part them. He's simple and tells a lot. (To Florizel) Well, handsome shepherd! Your heart is full of something that takes your mind off the feast. Truly, when I was young and courted as you do, I used to load my girl with trinkets. I would have ransacked the pedlar's silk treasury and poured it out for her to accept. You have let him go and bought nothing from him. If your girl took it the wrong way and called it a lack of love or generosity, you would be hard put to answer, at least if you care about keeping her happy.

Old sir, I know / She prizes not such trifles as these are: / The gifts she looks from me are pack'd and lock'd / Up in my heart, which I have given already, / But not deliver'd. O, hear me breathe my life / Before this ancient sir, who, it should seem, / Hath sometime lov'd. I take thy hand! this hand, / As soft as dove's down and as white as it, / Or Ethiopian's tooth, or the fann'd snow that's bolted / By th' northern blasts twice o'er.

Old sir, I know she does not value trifles like these. The gifts she expects from me are packed and locked up in my heart, which I have given her already, but not formally handed over. (To Perdita) O, hear me breathe out my life before this old gentleman, who, it seems, was once in love. I take your hand, this hand, as soft as a dove's down and as white, or as an African's tooth, or the snow that the northern winds have sifted twice over.
What follows this? / How prettily the young swain seems to wash / The hand was fair before! I have put you out. / But to your protestation. Let me hear / What you profess.
What comes next? How prettily the young shepherd seems to wash a hand that was fair already! I have interrupted you. But go back to your declaration. Let me hear what you vow.
Do, and be a witness to it.
And this neighbour of mine, too?

And he, and more / Than he, and men, the earth, the heavens, and all: / That were I crown'd the most imperial monarch, / Thereof most worthy, were I the fairest youth / That ever made eye swerve, had force and knowledge / More than was ever man's, I would not prize them / Without her love; for her employ them all; / Commend them and condemn them to her service, / Or to their own perdition.

And he, and more than he, and men, the earth, the heavens and everything. If I were crowned the most powerful monarch, and most worthy of it, if I were the handsomest young man who ever turned heads, had more strength and knowledge than any man ever had, I would not value any of it without her love. I would use it all for her, giving it up to her service or to its own destruction.
But my daughter, / Say you the like to him?
But, my daughter, do you say the same to him?
I cannot speak / So well, nothing so well; no, nor mean better: / By th' pattern of mine own thoughts I cut out / The purity of his.
I cannot speak as well, nothing like as well, nor mean anything better. I measure the purity of his thoughts by the pattern of my own.
Take hands, a bargain! / And, friends unknown, you shall bear witness to't. / I give my daughter to him, and will make / Her portion equal his.
Join hands. It's a bargain! And, friends we don't know, you shall be witnesses to it. I give my daughter to him, and will make her dowry equal to his wealth.
O, that must be / I' th' virtue of your daughter: one being dead, / I shall have more than you can dream of yet; / Enough then for your wonder. But come on, / Contract us 'fore these witnesses.
O, that must be your daughter's own worth. When one man is dead, I shall have more than you can dream of yet, enough to make you wonder then. But come on, betroth us in front of these witnesses.
Come, your hand; / And, daughter, yours.
Come, your hand; and, daughter, yours.
Soft, swain, awhile, beseech you; / Have you a father?
Wait, young shepherd, a moment, please. Do you have a father?
I have; but what of him?
I do. But what about him?

Methinks a father / Is at the nuptial of his son a guest / That best becomes the table. Pray you once more, / Is not your father grown incapable / Of reasonable affairs? is he not stupid / With age and alt'ring rheums? can he speak? hear? / Know man from man? dispute his own estate? / Lies he not bed-rid? and again does nothing / But what he did being childish?

I think a father is the guest who best suits the table at his son's wedding. Tell me again, please: hasn't your father become unfit to deal with reasonable business? Isn't he stupid with age and the illnesses that change a man? Can he speak? Hear? Tell one man from another? Manage his own affairs? Isn't he bedridden, and doing nothing but what he did as a child?
No, good sir; / He has his health, and ampler strength indeed / Than most have of his age.
No, good sir. He is healthy, and in fact stronger than most men his age.

By my white beard, / You offer him, if this be so, a wrong / Something unfilial: reason my son / Should choose himself a wife, but as good reason / The father, all whose joy is nothing else / But fair posterity, should hold some counsel / In such a business.

By my white beard, if that's so, you are doing him a wrong that is hardly fitting for a son. It is reasonable that my son should choose his own wife, but just as reasonable that the father, whose whole joy lies in fine descendants, should have some say in such a business.
I yield all this; / But for some other reasons, my grave sir, / Which 'tis not fit you know, I not acquaint / My father of this business.
I grant all that. But for some other reasons, my serious sir, which it is not right for you to know, I am not telling my father about this business.
Let him, my son: he shall not need to grieve / At knowing of thy choice.
Let him, my son. He won't have any cause to grieve when he knows your choice.
Come, come, he must not. / Mark our contract.
Come, come, he must not. Witness our contract.

[Discovering himself] Mark your divorce, young sir, / Whom son I dare not call; thou art too base / To be acknowledged: thou a sceptre's heir, / That thus affects a sheep-hook! Thou, old traitor, / I am sorry that, by hanging thee, I can / But shorten thy life one week. And thou, fresh piece / Of excellent witchcraft, whom of force must know / The royal fool thou cop'st with,—

(Revealing himself) Witness your divorce, young sir, whom I dare not call my son. You are too low to be acknowledged: you, heir to a sceptre, who wants a shepherd's crook like this! You, old traitor, I am sorry that by hanging you I can only shorten your life by a week. And you, young piece of excellent witchcraft, who must have known the royal fool you were dealing with—

I'll have thy beauty scratch'd with briers and made / More homely than thy state. For thee, fond boy, / If I may ever know thou dost but sigh / That thou no more shalt see this knack (as never / I mean thou shalt), we'll bar thee from succession; / Not hold thee of our blood, no, not our kin, / Far than Deucalion off. Mark thou my words. / Follow us to the court. Thou churl, for this time, / Though full of our displeasure, yet we free thee / From the dead blow of it. And you, enchantment, / Worthy enough a herdsman; yea, him too / That makes himself, but for our honour therein, / Unworthy thee. If ever henceforth thou / These rural latches to his entrance open, / Or hoop his body more with thy embraces, / I will devise a death as cruel for thee / As thou art tender to 't.

I'll have your beauty scratched with briars and made plainer than your rank. As for you, foolish boy, if I ever find out that you so much as sigh that you will never see this trinket again (as I mean you never shall), we'll bar you from the throne and not count you of our blood, no, not even our kin, further off than Deucalion, the first man. Mark my words. Follow us to court. You peasant, this time, though you're full of our displeasure, we free you from its death blow. And you, enchantress, good enough for a herdsman, yes, even for him, who makes himself unworthy of you, if it weren't for our honour: if from now on you ever open these country latches to let him in, or wrap his body in your embraces, I will invent a death for you as cruel as you are tender.

Even here undone. / I was not much afeard, for once or twice / I was about to speak, and tell him plainly / The selfsame sun that shines upon his court / Hides not his visage from our cottage, but / Looks on alike. [To Florizel] Will't please you, sir, be gone? / I told you what would come of this. Beseech you, / Of your own state take care. This dream of mine— / Being now awake, I'll queen it no inch farther, / But milk my ewes, and weep.

Ruined, right here. I wasn't very frightened. Once or twice I was going to speak and tell him plainly that the same sun that shines on his court doesn't hide its face from our cottage, but looks on both alike. (To Florizel) Will you please go, sir? I told you what would come of this. I beg you, look after your own position. This dream of mine, now I'm awake, I'll play the queen not an inch further, but milk my sheep and weep.
Why, how now, father! / Speak ere thou diest.
Why, what's the matter, old man? Speak before you die.

I cannot speak, nor think, / Nor dare to know that which I know. O sir, / You have undone a man of fourscore three, / That thought to fill his grave in quiet; yea, / To die upon the bed my father died, / To lie close by his honest bones; but now / Some hangman must put on my shroud and lay me / Where no priest shovels in dust. O cursed wretch, / That knew'st this was the prince, and wouldst adventure / To mingle faith with him! Undone, undone! / If I might die within this hour, I have liv'd / To die when I desire.

I can't speak, or think, or dare to know what I know. (To Florizel) O sir, you have ruined a man of eighty-three, who hoped to go to his grave in peace, yes, to die in the bed my father died in, to lie beside his honest bones. But now some hangman will dress me in my shroud and lay me where no priest shovels in earth. (To Perdita) O cursed wretch, who knew this was the prince, and dared to pledge yourself to him! Ruined, ruined! If I could die within this hour, I would have lived to die when I wanted.
Why look you so upon me? / I am but sorry, not afeard; delay'd, / But nothing alt'red: what I was, I am: / More straining on for plucking back; not following / My leash unwillingly.

Why do you look at me like that? I am only sorry, not afraid; delayed, but not changed at all. What I was, I am, straining forward all the more for being pulled back, not following my leash unwillingly.

Gracious my lord, / You know your father's temper: at this time / He will allow no speech (which I do guess / You do not purpose to him) and as hardly / Will he endure your sight as yet, I fear: / Then, till the fury of his highness settle, / Come not before him.

My gracious lord, you know your father's temper. At this moment he will let you say nothing (which I guess you don't intend to anyway), and I fear he can hardly bear the sight of you yet. So until his Highness's fury settles, don't go before him.
I not purpose it. / I think Camillo?
I don't intend to. Camillo, I think?
How often have I told you 'twould be thus! / How often said my dignity would last / But till 'twere known!
How often I told you it would be like this! How often I said my high rank would last only until it was known!

It cannot fail but by / The violation of my faith; and then / Let nature crush the sides o' th' earth together / And mar the seeds within! Lift up thy looks. / From my succession wipe me, father; I / Am heir to my affection.

It cannot fail except by my breaking faith, and if I do, let nature crush the sides of the earth together and destroy every seed inside it! Lift up your face. Strike me out of the succession, father. I am heir to my love.
I am, and by my fancy. If my reason / Will thereto be obedient, I have reason; / If not, my senses, better pleas'd with madness, / Do bid it welcome.
I do, and with my love. If my reason will obey it, I have reason. If not, my senses, happier with madness, welcome it.

So call it: but it does fulfil my vow. / I needs must think it honesty. Camillo, / Not for Bohemia, nor the pomp that may / Be thereat glean'd; for all the sun sees or / The close earth wombs, or the profound seas hides / In unknown fathoms, will I break my oath / To this my fair belov'd. Therefore, I pray you, / As you have ever been my father's honour'd friend, / When he shall miss me,—as, in faith, I mean not / To see him any more,—cast your good counsels / Upon his passion: let myself and fortune / Tug for the time to come. This you may know, / And so deliver, I am put to sea / With her whom here I cannot hold on shore; / And, most opportune to her need, I have / A vessel rides fast by, but not prepar'd / For this design. What course I mean to hold / Shall nothing benefit your knowledge, nor / Concern me the reporting.

Call it that. But it keeps my vow, so I must think it honesty. Camillo, not for Bohemia, nor for the splendour that could be gathered from it, nor for everything the sun sees, or the earth holds in its womb, or the deep seas hide in unknown depths, will I break my oath to my fair beloved here. So I beg you, since you have always been my father's honoured friend, when he misses me (and truly I don't mean to see him any more), calm his anger with your good advice. Let me and fortune fight it out for the future. This much you may know, and tell him: I have gone to sea with her, since I cannot keep her here on shore. And, most luckily for her need, I have a ship riding at anchor close by, though not fitted out for this purpose. Where I mean to go will do your knowledge no good, nor do I want it reported.
O my lord, / I would your spirit were easier for advice, / Or stronger for your need.
O my lord, I wish your spirit were more open to advice, or stronger for what you need.
Hark, Perdita. [Takes her aside] / [To Camillo] I'll hear you by and by.
Listen, Perdita. (He takes her aside. To Camillo) I'll hear you in a moment.

He's irremovable, / Resolv'd for flight. Now were I happy if / His going I could frame to serve my turn, / Save him from danger, do him love and honour, / Purchase the sight again of dear Sicilia / And that unhappy king, my master, whom / I so much thirst to see.

He can't be moved; he's determined to run away. Now I would be happy if I could shape his going to serve my purpose: save him from danger, do him love and honour, and win back the sight of dear Sicilia and that unhappy king, my master, whom I so long to see.
Now, good Camillo, / I am so fraught with curious business that / I leave out ceremony.
Now, good Camillo, I am so loaded with urgent business that I leave out the formalities.
Sir, I think / You have heard of my poor services, i' th' love / That I have borne your father?
Sir, I think you have heard of my small services, done out of the love I have for your father?
Very nobly / Have you deserv'd: it is my father's music / To speak your deeds, not little of his care / To have them recompens'd as thought on.
You have deserved very nobly. It is music to my father to speak of your deeds, and no small concern of his to have them rewarded as well as he thinks of them.

Well, my lord, / If you may please to think I love the king, / And, through him, what's nearest to him, which is / Your gracious self, embrace but my direction, / If your more ponderous and settled project / May suffer alteration. On mine honour, / I'll point you where you shall have such receiving / As shall become your highness; where you may / Enjoy your mistress; from the whom, I see, / There's no disjunction to be made, but by, / As heavens forfend, your ruin. Marry her, / And with my best endeavours in your absence / Your discontenting father strive to qualify / And bring him up to liking.

Well, my lord, if you are willing to believe that I love the king, and through him what's closest to him, which is your gracious self, just accept my direction, if your weighty, settled plan can be changed. On my honour, I'll show you where you will get a welcome fit for your Highness, where you may enjoy your love, from whom I see there's no separating you, except, heaven forbid, by your ruin. Marry her, and while you are away I'll do my best to calm your displeased father and bring him round to approving.
How, Camillo, / May this, almost a miracle, be done? / That I may call thee something more than man, / And after that trust to thee.
How, Camillo, can this near-miracle be done? Tell me, so that I can call you something more than a man, and trust you from then on.
Have you thought on / A place whereto you'll go?
Have you thought of a place to go?
Not any yet. / But as th' unthought-on accident is guilty / To what we wildly do, so we profess / Ourselves to be the slaves of chance, and flies / Of every wind that blows.
Not yet. But since an unexpected accident is to blame for what we wildly do, we admit we are the slaves of chance, and flies blown by every wind.

Then list to me: / This follows, if you will not change your purpose, / But undergo this flight, make for Sicilia, / And there present yourself and your fair princess, / For so, I see, she must be, 'fore Leontes: / She shall be habited as it becomes / The partner of your bed. Methinks I see / Leontes opening his free arms and weeping / His welcomes forth; asks thee, the son, forgiveness, / As 'twere i' th' father's person; kisses the hands / Of your fresh princess; o'er and o'er divides him / 'Twixt his unkindness and his kindness. Th' one / He chides to hell, and bids the other grow / Faster than thought or time.

Then listen to me. If you won't change your plan but will go ahead with this escape, this is what follows. Sail for Sicilia, and present yourself and your fair princess (for I see that's what she must be) to Leontes. She shall be dressed as suits the partner of your bed. I think I see Leontes opening his generous arms and weeping out his welcomes, asking you, the son, for forgiveness, as if you were your father, kissing the hands of your young princess, torn again and again between his unkindness and his kindness: one he curses to hell, and the other he tells to grow faster than thought or time.
Worthy Camillo, / What colour for my visitation shall I / Hold up before him?
Worthy Camillo, what excuse for my visit shall I give him?

Sent by the king your father / To greet him and to give him comforts. Sir, / The manner of your bearing towards him, with / What you (as from your father) shall deliver, / Things known betwixt us three, I'll write you down, / The which shall point you forth at every sitting / What you must say; that he shall not perceive / But that you have your father's bosom there / And speak his very heart.

Say you were sent by the king your father to greet him and comfort him. Sir, I'll write down for you how to behave towards him, and what you are to tell him as if from your father, things known only to the three of us. It will show you at every meeting what you must say, so that he will think you have your father's confidence there and speak his very heart.
I am bound to you: / There is some sap in this.
I am in your debt. There is some life in this.

A course more promising / Than a wild dedication of yourselves / To unpath'd waters, undream'd shores, most certain / To miseries enough: no hope to help you, / But as you shake off one to take another: / Nothing so certain as your anchors, who / Do their best office if they can but stay you / Where you'll be loath to be. Besides, you know / Prosperity's the very bond of love, / Whose fresh complexion and whose heart together / Affliction alters.

A course more promising than a wild surrender of yourselves to pathless waters and undreamt-of shores, certain to bring miseries enough, with no hope of help except shaking off one trouble only to take on another, nothing so certain as your anchors, which do their best work if they can just hold you where you'll hate to be. Besides, you know that prosperity is the very bond of love, and hardship changes both its fresh face and its heart.
One of these is true: / I think affliction may subdue the cheek, / But not take in the mind.
One of these is true. I think hardship may conquer the cheek, but not capture the mind.
Yea, say you so? / There shall not at your father's house, these seven years / Be born another such.
Yes, do you say so? There won't be another like her born in your father's house for seven years.
My good Camillo, / She is as forward of her breeding as / She is i' th' rear our birth.
My good Camillo, she is as far ahead of her upbringing as she is behind us in birth.
I cannot say 'tis pity / She lacks instructions, for she seems a mistress / To most that teach.
I can't say it's a pity she lacks education, for she seems a teacher to most who teach.
Your pardon, sir; for this / I'll blush you thanks.
Pardon me, sir. For this I'll thank you with a blush.

My prettiest Perdita! / But, O, the thorns we stand upon! Camillo, / Preserver of my father, now of me, / The medicine of our house, how shall we do? / We are not furnish'd like Bohemia's son, / Nor shall appear in Sicilia.

My prettiest Perdita! But, O, the thorns we're standing on! Camillo, saviour of my father, now of me, the medicine of our house, what shall we do? We aren't equipped like the King of Bohemia's son, and won't look like one in Sicilia.

My lord, / Fear none of this. I think you know my fortunes / Do all lie there: it shall be so my care / To have you royally appointed as if / The scene you play were mine. For instance, sir, / That you may know you shall not want,—one word.

My lord, don't worry about any of this. I think you know my fortunes all lie there. I'll take care to have you royally fitted out, as if the play you act were mine. For example, sir, so that you know you'll want for nothing, a word with you.

Ha, ha! what a fool Honesty is! and Trust, his sworn brother, a very / simple gentleman! I have sold all my trumpery. Not a counterfeit stone, / not a ribbon, glass, pomander, brooch, table-book, ballad, knife, tape, / glove, shoe-tie, bracelet, horn-ring, to keep my pack from fasting. / They throng who should buy first, as if my trinkets had been hallowed / and brought a benediction to the buyer: by which means I saw whose / purse was best in picture; and what I saw, to my good use I remembered. / My clown (who wants but something to be a reasonable man) grew so in / love with the wenches' song that he would not stir his pettitoes till / he had both tune and words; which so drew the rest of the herd to me / that all their other senses stuck in ears: you might have pinched a / placket, it was senseless; 'twas nothing to geld a codpiece of a purse; / I would have filed keys off that hung in chains: no hearing, no / feeling, but my sir's song, and admiring the nothing of it. So that in / this time of lethargy I picked and cut most of their festival purses; / and had not the old man come in with a whoobub against his daughter and / the king's son, and scared my choughs from the chaff, I had not left a / purse alive in the whole army.

Ha, ha! What a fool Honesty is! And Trust, his sworn brother, a very simple gentleman! I have sold all my junk. Not a fake jewel, ribbon, mirror, scent ball, brooch, notebook, ballad, knife, tape, glove, shoelace, bracelet or horn ring left to keep my pack from starving. They crowded to see who could buy first, as if my trinkets were holy and brought the buyer a blessing. That way I saw whose purse looked fattest, and I remembered what I saw for my own good use. My clown (who only lacks something to be a reasonable man) fell so in love with the girls' song that he wouldn't move his little trotters till he had the tune and the words. That drew the rest of the herd to me so that all their other senses were stuck in their ears. You could have pinched a petticoat and they'd have felt nothing. It was nothing to cut a purse off a codpiece. I could have filed off keys hanging on chains. No hearing, no feeling, but my master's song, and admiring the nothing of it. So in this sleepy time I picked and cut most of their festival purses. And if the old man hadn't come in with a hubbub against his daughter and the king's son and scared my crows off the grain, I wouldn't have left a purse alive in the whole army.
Nay, but my letters, by this means being there / So soon as you arrive, shall clear that doubt.
No, but my letters, getting there by this means as soon as you arrive, will clear up that doubt.
And those that you'll procure from king Leontes?
And those you'll get from King Leontes?
Happy be you! / All that you speak shows fair.
Bless you! Everything you say looks hopeful.
[Seeing Autolycus] Who have we here? / We'll make an instrument of this; omit / Nothing may give us aid.
(Seeing Autolycus) Who have we here? We'll make use of him. We mustn't leave out anything that may help us.
[Aside] If they have overheard me now,—why, hanging.
(Aside) If they've overheard me now, why, it's hanging.
How now, good fellow! why shakest thou so? Fear not, man; here's no / harm intended to thee.
Well, good fellow! Why are you shaking? Don't be afraid, man. Nobody means you any harm.
I am a poor fellow, sir.
I am a poor fellow, sir.

Why, be so still; here's nobody will steal that from thee: yet, for the / outside of thy poverty we must make an exchange; therefore discase thee / instantly,—thou must think there's a necessity in't—and change garments / with this gentleman: though the pennyworth on his side be the worst, / yet hold thee, there's some boot.

Well, stay that way. Nobody here will steal that from you. Still, we must swap the outside of your poverty. So undress at once (you must believe it's necessary) and change clothes with this gentleman. Though he gets the worse bargain, still, here, take this; there's something extra.
I am a poor fellow, sir: [Aside] I know ye well enough.
I am a poor fellow, sir. (Aside) I know you well enough.
Nay, prithee dispatch: the gentleman is half flayed already.
No, please, hurry. The gentleman is half skinned already.
Are you in earnest, sir? [Aside] I smell the trick on't.
Are you in earnest, sir? (Aside) I smell a trick in this.
Indeed, I have had earnest; but I cannot with conscience take it.
Indeed, I've had earnest money, but I can't in conscience take it.

Fortunate mistress,—let my prophecy / Come home to you!—you must retire yourself / Into some covert. Take your sweetheart's hat / And pluck it o'er your brows, muffle your face, / Dismantle you; and, as you can, disliken / The truth of your own seeming; that you may / (For I do fear eyes over) to shipboard / Get undescried.

Lucky lady (may my prophecy come true for you!), you must go off into some hiding place. Take your sweetheart's hat and pull it down over your brows, muffle your face, change your clothes, and as best you can disguise your true appearance, so that (for I fear there are watchers) you can get on board unseen.
I see the play so lies / That I must bear a part.
I see the play is set up so that I must take a part.
No remedy. / Have you done there?
It can't be helped. Have you finished there?
Should I now meet my father, / He would not call me son.
If I met my father now, he wouldn't call me his son.
Nay, you shall have no hat. [Giving it to Perdita] / Come, lady, come. Farewell, my friend.
No, you shall have no hat. (He gives it to Perdita) Come, lady, come. Farewell, my friend.
O Perdita, what have we twain forgot? / Pray you a word.
O Perdita, what have we two forgotten? A word, please.

[Aside] What I do next, shall be to tell the king / Of this escape, and whither they are bound; / Wherein my hope is I shall so prevail / To force him after: in whose company / I shall re-view Sicilia; for whose sight / I have a woman's longing.

(Aside) What I'll do next is tell the king about this escape and where they're going. I hope I'll persuade him to follow them, and in his company I'll see Sicilia again, which I long to see like a pregnant woman longs for food.
Fortune speed us! / Thus we set on, Camillo, to the sea-side.
Fortune speed us! So we set off for the seaside, Camillo.

I understand the business, I hear it. To have an open ear, a quick eye, / and a nimble hand, is necessary for a cut-purse; a good nose is / requisite also, to smell out work for the other senses. I see this is / the time that the unjust man doth thrive. What an exchange had this / been without boot! What a boot is here with this exchange! Sure the / gods do this year connive at us, and we may do anything extempore. The / prince himself is about a piece of iniquity, stealing away from his / father with his clog at his heels: if I thought it were a piece of / honesty to acquaint the king withal, I would not do't: I hold it the / more knavery to conceal it; and therein am I constant to my profession.

I understand the business. I heard it. An open ear, a quick eye and a nimble hand are necessary for a pickpocket. A good nose is needed too, to sniff out work for the other senses. I see this is the time when the dishonest man prospers. What a swap this would have been even without anything extra! And what an extra there is with this swap! The gods must be winking at us this year, and we can do anything on the spur of the moment. The prince himself is up to some wickedness, stealing away from his father with his ball and chain at his heels. If I thought it would be honest to tell the king, I wouldn't do it. I consider it more knavish to keep it quiet, and in that I'm true to my profession.
Aside, aside; here is more matter for a hot brain: every lane's end, / every shop, church, session, hanging, yields a careful man work.
Aside, aside. Here's more work for a busy brain. Every lane's end, every shop, church, court session and hanging gives a careful man work.
See, see; what a man you are now! There is no other way but to tell the / king she's a changeling, and none of your flesh and blood.
Look, look, what a man you are now! There's nothing for it but to tell the king she's a changeling and not your flesh and blood.

She being none of your flesh and blood, your flesh and blood has not / offended the king; and so your flesh and blood is not to be punished by / him. Show those things you found about her, those secret things, all / but what she has with her: this being done, let the law go whistle, I / warrant you.

Since she's not your flesh and blood, your flesh and blood hasn't offended the king, so your flesh and blood can't be punished by him. Show him those things you found with her, those secret things, all except what she has with her. Do that, and the law can whistle for you, I promise.
I will tell the king all, every word, yea, and his son's pranks too; / who, I may say, is no honest man neither to his father nor to me, to go / about to make me the king's brother-in-law.
I'll tell the king everything, every word, yes, and his son's pranks too. I can say he's been no honest man to his father or to me, trying to make me the king's brother-in-law.
Indeed, brother-in-law was the farthest off you could have been to him, / and then your blood had been the dearer by I know how much an ounce.
Indeed, brother-in-law was the furthest off you could have been from him, and then your blood would have been worth I don't know how much more an ounce.
Well, let us to the king: there is that in this fardel will make him / scratch his beard.
Well, let's go to the king. There's something in this bundle that will make him scratch his beard.
[Aside] I know not what impediment this complaint may be to the / flight of my master.
(Aside) I don't know how much this complaint may hinder my master's escape.
Pray heartily he be at' palace.
Pray hard that he's at the palace.
[Aside] Though I am not naturally honest, I am so sometimes by / chance. Let me pocket up my pedlar's excrement. [Takes off his false / beard.] How now, rustics! whither are you bound?
(Aside) Though I'm not honest by nature, I am sometimes by chance. Let me pocket my pedlar's beard. (He takes off his false beard) Well now, peasants! Where are you going?
To the palace, an it like your worship.
To the palace, if it please your worship.
Your affairs there, what, with whom, the condition of that fardel, the / place of your dwelling, your names, your ages, of what having, / breeding, and anything that is fitting to be known? discover!
Your business there: what, with whom, what's in that bundle, where you live, your names, your ages, your wealth, your upbringing, and anything else fit to be known? Reveal it!
We are but plain fellows, sir.

A lie; you are rough and hairy. Let me have no lying. It becomes none / but tradesmen, and they often give us soldiers the lie; but we pay them / for it with stamped coin, not stabbing steel; therefore they do not / give us the lie.

A lie: you're rough and hairy. Let me have no lying. It only suits tradesmen, and they often give us soldiers the lie. But we pay them for it in stamped coin, not stabbing steel, so they don't give it us, they sell it.
Your worship had like to have given us one, if you had not taken / yourself with the manner.
Your worship nearly gave us one yourself, if you hadn't caught yourself in the act.
Are you a courtier, an 't like you, sir?
Are you a courtier, if you please, sir?

Whether it like me or no, I am a courtier. Seest thou not the air of / the court in these enfoldings? hath not my gait in it the measure of / the court? receives not thy nose court-odour from me? reflect I not on / thy baseness court-contempt? Think'st thou, for that I insinuate, or / toaze from thee thy business, I am therefore no courtier? I am courtier / cap-a-pe, and one that will either push on or pluck back thy business / there. Whereupon I command thee to open thy affair.

Whether it pleases me or not, I am a courtier. Don't you see the air of the court in these clothes? Doesn't my walk have the rhythm of the court? Doesn't your nose catch the court smell from me? Don't I reflect court contempt on your lowliness? Do you think that because I worm my way in and tease your business out of you, I'm no courtier? I'm a courtier from head to foot, and one who can push your business on there or pull it back. So I command you to tell me your business.
My business, sir, is to the king.
My business, sir, is with the king.
What advocate hast thou to him?
Who is your advocate with him?
I know not, an 't like you.
I don't know, if you please.
Advocate's the court-word for a pheasant. Say you have none.
'Advocate' is the court word for a pheasant. Say you haven't one.
None, sir; I have no pheasant, cock nor hen.
None, sir. I have no pheasant, cock or hen.
How bless'd are we that are not simple men! / Yet nature might have made me as these are, / Therefore I will not disdain.
How blessed we are who are not simple men! Yet nature might have made me like them, so I won't scorn them.
This cannot be but a great courtier.
He must be a great courtier.
His garments are rich, but he wears them not handsomely.
His clothes are rich, but he doesn't wear them well.
He seems to be the more noble in being fantastical: a great man, I'll / warrant; I know by the picking on's teeth.
He seems all the more noble for being odd. A great man, I'll bet. I can tell by the way he picks his teeth.
The fardel there? What's i' th' fardel? Wherefore that box?
That bundle there? What's in the bundle? Why that box?
Sir, there lies such secrets in this fardel and box which none must / know but the king; and which he shall know within this hour, if I may / come to th' speech of him.
Sir, there are secrets in this bundle and box that no one must know but the king, and he'll know them within the hour, if I can get to speak to him.
Age, thou hast lost thy labour.
Old man, you've wasted your effort.
The king is not at the palace; he is gone aboard a new ship to purge / melancholy and air himself: for, if thou beest capable of things / serious, thou must know the king is full of grief.
The king isn't at the palace. He has gone aboard a new ship to clear his melancholy and get some air. For, if you can understand serious things, you must know the king is full of grief.
So 'tis said, sir; about his son, that should have married a shepherd's / daughter.
So they say, sir, about his son, who was going to marry a shepherd's daughter.
If that shepherd be not in hand-fast, let him fly. The curses he shall / have, the tortures he shall feel, will break the back of man, the heart / of monster.
If that shepherd isn't already under arrest, let him run. The curses he'll get and the tortures he'll feel would break a man's back and a monster's heart.

Not he alone shall suffer what wit can make heavy and vengeance bitter; / but those that are germane to him, though removed fifty times, shall / all come under the hangman: which, though it be great pity, yet it is / necessary. An old sheep-whistling rogue, a ram-tender, to offer to have / his daughter come into grace! Some say he shall be stoned; but that / death is too soft for him, say I. Draw our throne into a sheepcote! All / deaths are too few, the sharpest too easy.

Not only will he suffer everything that wit can make heavy and vengeance bitter, but all his relatives, even fifty times removed, will come to the hangman. It's a great pity, but necessary. An old sheep-whistling rogue, a ram-minder, trying to get his daughter raised to royalty! Some say he'll be stoned, but I say that death is too soft for him. Dragging our throne into a sheep pen! All deaths are too few, the sharpest too easy.
Has the old man e'er a son, sir, do you hear, an 't like you, sir?
Has the old man got a son, sir, do you hear, if you please, sir?

He has a son, who shall be flayed alive; then 'nointed over with honey, / set on the head of a wasp's nest; then stand till he be three quarters / and a dram dead; then recovered again with aqua-vitæ or some other hot / infusion; then, raw as he is, and in the hottest day prognostication / proclaims, shall he be set against a brick wall, the sun looking with a / southward eye upon him, where he is to behold him with flies blown to / death. But what talk we of these traitorly rascals, whose miseries are / to be smiled at, their offences being so capital? Tell me (for you seem / to be honest plain men) what you have to the king. Being something / gently considered, I'll bring you where he is aboard, tender your / persons to his presence, whisper him in your behalfs; and if it be in / man besides the king to effect your suits, here is man shall do it.

He has a son, who'll be skinned alive, then smeared with honey and set on top of a wasps' nest, then left till he's three-quarters and a bit dead, then revived with brandy or some other hot drink. Then, raw as he is, on the hottest day the almanac forecasts, he'll be set against a brick wall with the sun looking down on him from the south, and stay there till the flies have stung him to death. But why are we talking about these traitorous rascals, whose miseries we should smile at, since their crimes are so great? Tell me (for you seem to be honest plain men) what your business with the king is. If I'm rewarded handsomely, I'll take you to where he is on board, present you to him, put in a word for you in his ear, and if any man besides the king can get your requests granted, here is the man to do it.

He seems to be of great authority: close with him, give him gold; and / though authority be a stubborn bear, yet he is oft led by the nose with / gold: show the inside of your purse to the outside of his hand, and no / more ado. Remember: "ston'd" and "flayed alive".

He seems to have great authority. Make a deal with him, give him gold. Though authority is a stubborn bear, it's often led by the nose with gold. Show the inside of your purse to the outside of his hand, and no more fuss. Remember: 'stoned' and 'skinned alive'.
An 't please you, sir, to undertake the business for us, here is that / gold I have. I'll make it as much more, and leave this young man in / pawn till I bring it you.
If you'll take on the business for us, sir, here's the gold I have. I'll make it as much again, and leave this young man as security until I bring it to you.
After I have done what I promised?
After I've done what I promised?
Well, give me the moiety. Are you a party in this business?
Well, give me half. (To the Clown) Are you involved in this business?
In some sort, sir: but though my case be a pitiful one, I hope I shall / not be flayed out of it.
In a way, sir. But though my case is a pitiful one, I hope I won't be skinned out of it.
O, that's the case of the shepherd's son. Hang him, he'll be made an / example.
O, that's the case of the shepherd's son. Hang him, he'll be made an example of.

Comfort, good comfort! We must to the king and show our strange sights. / He must know 'tis none of your daughter nor my sister; we are gone / else. Sir, I will give you as much as this old man does when the / business is performed, and remain, as he says, your pawn till it be / brought you.

Comfort, some comfort! We must go to the king and show our strange things. He must know she's not your daughter or my sister, or we're done for. Sir, I'll give you as much as this old man when the business is done, and stay, as he says, as your security till it's brought to you.
I will trust you. Walk before toward the sea-side; go on the / right-hand. I will but look upon the hedge, and follow you.
I'll trust you. Walk on ahead towards the seaside. Keep to the right. I'll just take a look at the hedge and follow you.
We are blessed in this man, as I may say, even blessed.
We're blessed in this man, I must say, really blessed.
Let's before, as he bids us. He was provided to do us good.
Let's go ahead, as he tells us. He was sent to do us good.

If I had a mind to be honest, I see Fortune would not suffer me: she / drops booties in my mouth. I am courted now with a double occasion: / gold, and a means to do the prince my master good; which who knows how / that may turn back to my advancement? I will bring these two moles, / these blind ones, aboard him. If he think it fit to shore them again / and that the complaint they have to the king concerns him nothing, let / him call me rogue for being so far officious; for I am proof against / that title and what shame else belongs to 't. To him will I present / them. There may be matter in it.

If I wanted to be honest, I see Fortune wouldn't let me. She drops loot into my mouth. I'm being courted now with a double chance: gold, and a way to do my master the prince a good turn, which, who knows, may come back to me as promotion. I'll bring these two moles, these blind ones, aboard to him. If he thinks fit to put them ashore again, and the complaint they have for the king doesn't concern him, let him call me a rogue for being so meddlesome. I'm hardened against that title and any other shame that goes with it. I'll present them to him. There may be something in it.

Sir, you have done enough, and have perform'd / A saint-like sorrow: no fault could you make / Which you have not redeem'd; indeed, paid down / More penitence than done trespass: at the last, / Do as the heavens have done, forget your evil; / With them, forgive yourself.

Sir, you have done enough, and shown a saint's sorrow. You could have committed no fault that you have not made up for. In fact, you have paid more penance than the wrong you did. At last, do as the heavens have done: forget your sin, and like them, forgive yourself.

Whilst I remember / Her and her virtues, I cannot forget / My blemishes in them; and so still think of / The wrong I did myself: which was so much / That heirless it hath made my kingdom, and / Destroy'd the sweet'st companion that e'er man / Bred his hopes out of.

While I remember her and her virtues, I cannot forget my faults towards them, and so I still think of the wrong I did myself, which was so great that it has left my kingdom without an heir and destroyed the sweetest companion a man ever placed his hopes in.
True, too true, my lord. / If, one by one, you wedded all the world, / Or from the all that are took something good, / To make a perfect woman, she you kill'd / Would be unparallel'd.
True, too true, my lord. If you married every woman in the world one by one, or took something good from every one there is to make a perfect woman, the one you killed would still have no equal.
I think so. Kill'd! / She I kill'd! I did so: but thou strik'st me / Sorely, to say I did: it is as bitter / Upon thy tongue as in my thought. Now, good now, / Say so but seldom.
I think so. Killed! She whom I killed! I did. But you strike me hard to say I did. It is as bitter on your tongue as in my thoughts. Now, please, say it only rarely.
Not at all, good lady. / You might have spoken a thousand things that would / Have done the time more benefit and grac'd / Your kindness better.
Not at all, good lady. You could have said a thousand things that would have done more good at this time and better suited your kindness.
You are one of those / Would have him wed again.
You're one of those who would have him marry again.

If you would not so, / You pity not the state, nor the remembrance / Of his most sovereign name; consider little / What dangers, by his highness' fail of issue, / May drop upon his kingdom, and devour / Incertain lookers-on. What were more holy / Than to rejoice the former queen is well? / What holier than, for royalty's repair, / For present comfort, and for future good, / To bless the bed of majesty again / With a sweet fellow to 't?

If you don't want that, you have no pity for the state, nor for the memory of his royal name. You don't consider what dangers may fall on his kingdom because his Highness has no heir, and devour the people standing by uncertain. What could be more holy than to rejoice that the former queen is at peace? What holier, for the restoring of royalty, for present comfort and future good, than to bless the king's bed again with a sweet partner?

There is none worthy, / Respecting her that's gone. Besides, the gods / Will have fulfill'd their secret purposes; / For has not the divine Apollo said, / Is 't not the tenor of his oracle, / That king Leontes shall not have an heir / Till his lost child be found? Which that it shall, / Is all as monstrous to our human reason / As my Antigonus to break his grave / And come again to me; who, on my life, / Did perish with the infant. 'Tis your counsel / My lord should to the heavens be contrary, / Oppose against their wills. [To Leontes] Care not for issue; / The crown will find an heir. Great Alexander / Left his to th' worthiest; so his successor / Was like to be the best.

There is no one worthy, compared with her who's gone. Besides, the gods will have their secret purposes fulfilled. For hasn't the divine Apollo said, isn't it the meaning of his oracle, that King Leontes shall not have an heir till his lost child is found? And that that will happen is as monstrous to our human reason as my Antigonus breaking out of his grave and coming back to me, who, on my life, died with the baby. It is your advice that my lord should go against the heavens and oppose their will. (To Leontes) Don't worry about an heir. The crown will find one. Great Alexander left his to the worthiest, so his successor was likely to be the best.

Good Paulina, / Who hast the memory of Hermione, / I know, in honour, O that ever I / Had squar'd me to thy counsel! Then, even now, / I might have look'd upon my queen's full eyes, / Have taken treasure from her lips,—

Good Paulina, who I know hold the memory of Hermione in honour, O, if only I had ruled myself by your advice! Then, even now, I might be looking into my queen's full eyes, taking treasure from her lips—
And left them / More rich for what they yielded.
And leaving them richer for what they gave.

Thou speak'st truth. / No more such wives; therefore, no wife: one worse, / And better us'd, would make her sainted spirit / Again possess her corpse, and on this stage, / (Where we offenders now appear) soul-vexed, / And begin "Why to me?"

You speak the truth. No more such wives, so no wife at all. One worse, and treated better, would make her saintly spirit take over her body again, and on this stage where we sinners now stand, come troubled in soul, and begin 'Why to me?'
Had she such power, / She had just cause.
If she had such power, she would have good reason.
She had; and would incense me / To murder her I married.
She would, and would urge me to murder the woman I married.

I should so. / Were I the ghost that walk'd, I'd bid you mark / Her eye, and tell me for what dull part in 't / You chose her: then I'd shriek, that even your ears / Should rift to hear me; and the words that follow'd / Should be "Remember mine."

I would. If I were the ghost that walked, I'd tell you to look at her eye and tell me what dull feature in it made you choose her. Then I'd shriek so that even your ears would split to hear me, and the words that followed would be 'Remember mine.'
Stars, stars, / And all eyes else dead coals! Fear thou no wife; / I'll have no wife, Paulina.
Stars, stars, and all other eyes dead coals! Don't fear a wife. I'll have no wife, Paulina.
Will you swear / Never to marry but by my free leave?
Will you swear never to marry except with my free permission?
Never, Paulina; so be bless'd my spirit!
Never, Paulina, as I hope my soul is blessed!
Then, good my lords, bear witness to his oath.
Then, my good lords, witness his oath.
Unless another, / As like Hermione as is her picture, / Affront his eye.
Unless another woman, as like Hermione as her portrait, comes before his eyes.

I have done. / Yet, if my lord will marry,—if you will, sir, / No remedy but you will,—give me the office / To choose you a queen: she shall not be so young / As was your former, but she shall be such / As, walk'd your first queen's ghost, it should take joy / To see her in your arms.

I've finished. Yet if my lord will marry (if you will, sir, and it can't be helped), give me the job of choosing you a queen. She won't be as young as your first, but she will be such that, if your first queen's ghost walked, it would be glad to see her in your arms.
My true Paulina, / We shall not marry till thou bid'st us.
My true Paulina, we will not marry until you tell us to.
That / Shall be when your first queen's again in breath; / Never till then.
That shall be when your first queen breathes again. Never till then.
One that gives out himself Prince Florizel, / Son of Polixenes, with his princess (she / The fairest I have yet beheld) desires access / To your high presence.
Someone who says he is Prince Florizel, son of Polixenes, with his princess (the most beautiful woman I have ever seen), asks to come before you.

What with him? he comes not / Like to his father's greatness: his approach, / So out of circumstance and sudden, tells us / 'Tis not a visitation fram'd, but forc'd / By need and accident. What train?

Who's with him? He doesn't come in a way that matches his father's greatness. His arrival, so sudden and without ceremony, tells us it is not a planned visit, but forced on him by need and accident. What followers?
But few, / And those but mean.
Only a few, and those of low rank.
His princess, say you, with him?
His princess is with him, you say?
Ay, the most peerless piece of earth, I think, / That e'er the sun shone bright on.
Yes, the most matchless piece of earth, I think, that the sun ever shone on.

O Hermione, / As every present time doth boast itself / Above a better gone, so must thy grave / Give way to what's seen now! Sir, you yourself / Have said and writ so,—but your writing now / Is colder than that theme,—'She had not been, / Nor was not to be equall'd'; thus your verse / Flow'd with her beauty once; 'tis shrewdly ebb'd, / To say you have seen a better.

O Hermione, just as every present time boasts that it is better than a better time gone by, so your grave must give way to what is seen now! (To the Servant) Sir, you yourself have said and written (but your writing is now colder than its subject) 'She has not been and will not be equalled.' That's how your verse once flowed with her beauty. It has ebbed badly, if you say you've seen a better.

Pardon, madam: / The one I have almost forgot,—your pardon;— / The other, when she has obtain'd your eye, / Will have your tongue too. This is a creature, / Would she begin a sect, might quench the zeal / Of all professors else; make proselytes / Of who she but bid follow.

Pardon, madam. The one I have almost forgotten (pardon me). The other, once she has caught your eye, will have your tongue too. She is a creature who, if she started a religion, could put out the zeal of every other believer and convert anyone she merely asked to follow.
Women will love her that she is a woman / More worth than any man; men, that she is / The rarest of all women.
Women will love her because she is a woman worth more than any man; men, because she is the rarest of all women.
Go, Cleomenes; / Yourself, assisted with your honour'd friends, / Bring them to our embracement.
Go, Cleomenes. You yourself, helped by your honoured friends, bring them to our embrace.
Still, 'tis strange / He thus should steal upon us.
Still, it's strange he should steal in on us like this.
Had our prince, / Jewel of children, seen this hour, he had pair'd / Well with this lord. There was not full a month / Between their births.
If our prince, the jewel of children, had lived to see this hour, he would have made a good pair with this lord. There wasn't a full month between their births.

Prithee no more; cease; Thou know'st / He dies to me again when talk'd of: sure, / When I shall see this gentleman, thy speeches / Will bring me to consider that which may / Unfurnish me of reason. They are come.
Please, no more. Stop. You know he dies again for me when he is talked about. Surely, when I see this gentleman, your words will make me think of things that may rob me of my reason. They have come.

Your mother was most true to wedlock, prince; / For she did print your royal father off, / Conceiving you. Were I but twenty-one, / Your father's image is so hit in you, / His very air, that I should call you brother, / As I did him, and speak of something wildly / By us perform'd before. Most dearly welcome! / And your fair princess,—goddess! O, alas! / I lost a couple that 'twixt heaven and earth / Might thus have stood, begetting wonder, as / You, gracious couple, do! And then I lost,— / All mine own folly,—the society, / Amity too, of your brave father, whom, / Though bearing misery, I desire my life / Once more to look on him.

Your mother was very faithful to her marriage, prince, for she printed off a copy of your royal father when she conceived you. If I were only twenty-one, your father's image is so exactly caught in you, his very manner, that I would call you brother, as I did him, and talk of some wild things we did together before. You are most dearly welcome! And your fair princess, a goddess! O, alas! I lost a couple who might have stood like this between heaven and earth, causing wonder, as you do, gracious pair! And then I lost, through my own folly, the company and friendship of your fine father, whom, though I live in misery, I long to see once more.

By his command / Have I here touch'd Sicilia, and from him / Give you all greetings that a king, at friend, / Can send his brother: and, but infirmity, / Which waits upon worn times, hath something seiz'd / His wish'd ability, he had himself / The lands and waters 'twixt your throne and his / Measur'd, to look upon you; whom he loves, / He bade me say so,—more than all the sceptres / And those that bear them living.

It is by his command that I have landed in Sicilia, and I bring you from him all the greetings that a king, as a friend, can send his brother. If weakness, which comes with old age, had not taken away some of the strength he wished for, he would himself have crossed the lands and seas between your throne and his to see you, whom he loves (he told me to say so) more than all the sceptres and those who hold them now alive.

O my brother,— / Good gentleman!—the wrongs I have done thee stir / Afresh within me; and these thy offices, / So rarely kind, are as interpreters / Of my behind-hand slackness! Welcome hither, / As is the spring to the earth. And hath he too / Expos'd this paragon to the fearful usage, / At least ungentle, of the dreadful Neptune, / To greet a man not worth her pains, much less / Th' adventure of her person?

O my brother (good gentleman!), the wrongs I have done you stir again inside me, and these duties of yours, so rarely kind, show up my own slowness! Welcome here, as spring is to the earth. And has he really exposed this paragon to the fearful, or at least rough, treatment of dreadful Neptune, to greet a man not worth her trouble, much less the risk to her person?
Good, my lord, / She came from Libya.
My good lord, she came from Libya.
Where the warlike Smalus, / That noble honour'd lord, is fear'd and lov'd?
Where the warlike Smalus, that noble, honoured lord, is feared and loved?

Most royal sir, from thence; from him, whose daughter / His tears proclaim'd his, parting with her: thence, / A prosperous south-wind friendly, we have cross'd, / To execute the charge my father gave me / For visiting your highness: my best train / I have from your Sicilian shores dismiss'd; / Who for Bohemia bend, to signify / Not only my success in Libya, sir, / But my arrival, and my wife's, in safety / Here, where we are.

Most royal sir, from there; from him, whose tears when he parted from her showed she was his daughter. From there, with a friendly south wind behind us, we have crossed to carry out my father's order to visit your Highness. I have sent most of my followers away from your Sicilian shores to Bohemia, to report not only my success in Libya, sir, but my safe arrival, and my wife's, here where we are.

The blessed gods / Purge all infection from our air whilst you / Do climate here! You have a holy father, / A graceful gentleman; against whose person, / So sacred as it is, I have done sin, / For which the heavens, taking angry note, / Have left me issueless. And your father's bless'd, / As he from heaven merits it, with you, / Worthy his goodness. What might I have been, / Might I a son and daughter now have look'd on, / Such goodly things as you!

May the blessed gods clear all infection from our air while you stay here! You have a holy father, a gracious gentleman, against whose person, sacred as it is, I have sinned. The heavens took angry note of it and have left me childless. And your father is blessed, as he deserves from heaven, with you, worthy of his goodness. What might I have been, if I could look now on a son and daughter as fine as you!

Most noble sir, / That which I shall report will bear no credit, / Were not the proof so nigh. Please you, great sir, / Bohemia greets you from himself by me; / Desires you to attach his son, who has— / His dignity and duty both cast off— / Fled from his father, from his hopes, and with / A shepherd's daughter.

Most noble sir, what I have to report would not be believed if the proof were not so near. If you please, great sir, the King of Bohemia sends you greetings through me, and asks you to arrest his son, who has thrown off both his rank and his duty and run away from his father and his prospects with a shepherd's daughter.
Where is the King of Bohemia? Speak.

Here in your city; I now came from him. / I speak amazedly, and it becomes / My marvel and my message. To your court / Whiles he was hast'ning—in the chase, it seems, / Of this fair couple—meets he on the way / The father of this seeming lady and / Her brother, having both their country quitted / With this young prince.

Here in your city. I have just come from him. I speak confusedly, as suits my amazement and my message. As he was hurrying to your court, in pursuit, it seems, of this fair couple, he met on the way this so-called lady's father and her brother, who had both left their country with this young prince.
Camillo has betray'd me; / Whose honour and whose honesty till now, / Endur'd all weathers.
Camillo has betrayed me, whose honour and honesty have stood up to every kind of weather until now.
Lay 't so to his charge. / He's with the king your father.
Accuse him of it yourself. He's with the king your father.

Camillo, sir; I spake with him; who now / Has these poor men in question. Never saw I / Wretches so quake: they kneel, they kiss the earth; / Forswear themselves as often as they speak. / Bohemia stops his ears, and threatens them / With divers deaths in death.

Camillo, sir. I spoke with him. He is now questioning these poor men. I never saw wretches shake so. They kneel, they kiss the ground, they contradict themselves every time they speak. The King of Bohemia stops his ears and threatens them with all kinds of deaths in one.
O my poor father! / The heaven sets spies upon us, will not have / Our contract celebrated.
O my poor father! Heaven has set spies on us and will not let our betrothal be celebrated.
We are not, sir, nor are we like to be. / The stars, I see, will kiss the valleys first. / The odds for high and low's alike.
We are not, sir, nor are we likely to be. The stars, I see, will kiss the valleys first. High and low fare alike in this game.
My lord, / Is this the daughter of a king?
My lord, is this the daughter of a king?
She is, / When once she is my wife.
She will be, once she is my wife.

That "once", I see by your good father's speed, / Will come on very slowly. I am sorry, / Most sorry, you have broken from his liking, / Where you were tied in duty; and as sorry / Your choice is not so rich in worth as beauty, / That you might well enjoy her.

That 'once', I see by your good father's haste, will come very slowly. I am sorry, most sorry, that you have lost his favour, when you were bound to it by duty, and just as sorry that your choice is not as rich in rank as in beauty, so that you might properly enjoy her.

Dear, look up: / Though Fortune, visible an enemy, / Should chase us with my father, power no jot / Hath she to change our loves. Beseech you, sir, / Remember since you ow'd no more to time / Than I do now: with thought of such affections, / Step forth mine advocate. At your request / My father will grant precious things as trifles.

Dear, look up. Even if Fortune, showing herself our enemy, chases us along with my father, she has no power at all to change our love. I beg you, sir, remember when you were no older than I am now. Remembering such feelings, step forward as my advocate. At your request my father would grant precious things as if they were trifles.
Would he do so, I'd beg your precious mistress, / Which he counts but a trifle.
If he would do that, I'd ask for your precious mistress, whom he thinks only a trifle.
Sir, my liege, / Your eye hath too much youth in 't: not a month / 'Fore your queen died, she was more worth such gazes / Than what you look on now.
Sir, my lord, there is too much youth in your eye. Not a month before your queen died, she was more worth such looks than the girl you are looking at now.

I thought of her / Even in these looks I made. [To Florizel] But your petition / Is yet unanswer'd. I will to your father. / Your honour not o'erthrown by your desires, / I am friend to them and you: upon which errand / I now go toward him; therefore follow me, / And mark what way I make. Come, good my lord.

I was thinking of her even as I looked. (To Florizel) But your request has not been answered yet. I will go to your father. As long as your honour has not been overthrown by your desires, I am a friend to them and to you. On that errand I am going to him now, so follow me and see what progress I make. Come, my good lord.
Beseech you, sir, were you present at this relation?
Please, sir, were you there when this was told?

I was by at the opening of the fardel, heard the old shepherd deliver / the manner how he found it: whereupon, after a little amazedness, we / were all commanded out of the chamber; only this, methought I heard the / shepherd say he found the child.

I was there when the bundle was opened, and heard the old shepherd tell how he found it. Then, after a short amazement, we were all ordered out of the room. Only this: I thought I heard the shepherd say he found the child.
I would most gladly know the issue of it.
I'd very much like to know how it ended.

I make a broken delivery of the business; but the changes I perceived / in the king and Camillo were very notes of admiration. They seemed / almost, with staring on one another, to tear the cases of their eyes. / There was speech in their dumbness, language in their very gesture; / they looked as they had heard of a world ransomed, or one destroyed. A / notable passion of wonder appeared in them; but the wisest beholder, / that knew no more but seeing could not say if th' importance were joy / or sorrow; but in the extremity of the one, it must needs be. Here / comes a gentleman that happily knows more.

I can only give a broken account of the business. But the changes I saw in the king and Camillo were real marks of wonder. They seemed almost to tear their eyelids, staring at each other. There was speech in their silence, language in their very gestures. They looked as if they had heard of a world saved or a world destroyed. A remarkable passion of wonder showed in them, but the wisest onlooker, who knew no more than what he saw, could not say whether it meant joy or sorrow. But it must have been the extreme of one or the other. Here comes a gentleman who perhaps knows more.

Nothing but bonfires: the oracle is fulfilled: the king's daughter is / found: such a deal of wonder is broken out within this hour that / ballad-makers cannot be able to express it. Here comes the Lady / Paulina's steward: he can deliver you more.

Nothing but bonfires. The oracle is fulfilled. The king's daughter is found. So much wonder has broken out within this hour that ballad-writers won't be able to express it. Here comes the Lady Paulina's steward. He can tell you more.
How goes it now, sir? This news, which is called true, is so like an / old tale that the verity of it is in strong suspicion. Has the king / found his heir?
How are things now, sir? This news, which they say is true, is so like an old tale that its truth is very much in doubt. Has the king found his heir?

Most true, if ever truth were pregnant by circumstance. That which you / hear you'll swear you see, there is such unity in the proofs. The / mantle of Queen Hermione's, her jewel about the neck of it, the letters / of Antigonus found with it, which they know to be his character; the / majesty of the creature in resemblance of the mother, the affection of / nobleness which nature shows above her breeding, and many other / evidences proclaim her with all certainty to be the king's daughter. / Did you see the meeting of the two kings?

It's absolutely true, if ever truth was made plain by evidence. You'll swear you see what you hear, the proofs agree so well. Queen Hermione's cloak, her jewel round its neck, the letters of Antigonus found with it, which they know are in his handwriting; the majesty of the girl, so like her mother; the nobility that nature shows in her beyond her upbringing; and many other proofs declare with complete certainty that she is the king's daughter. Did you see the meeting of the two kings?

Then you have lost a sight which was to be seen, cannot be spoken of. / There might you have beheld one joy crown another, so and in such / manner that it seemed sorrow wept to take leave of them, for their joy / waded in tears. There was casting up of eyes, holding up of hands, with / countenance of such distraction that they were to be known by garment, / not by favour. Our king, being ready to leap out of himself for joy of / his found daughter, as if that joy were now become a loss, cries "O, / thy mother, thy mother!" then asks Bohemia forgiveness; then embraces / his son-in-law; then again worries he his daughter with clipping her; / now he thanks the old shepherd, which stands by like a weather-bitten / conduit of many kings' reigns. I never heard of such another encounter, / which lames report to follow it, and undoes description to do it.

Then you have missed a sight that had to be seen; it can't be described. There you could have seen one joy crown another, in such a way that it seemed sorrow wept to leave them, for their joy waded in tears. There was casting up of eyes and holding up of hands, with faces so wild that they could be recognised only by their clothes, not their features. Our king, ready to leap out of himself with joy at finding his daughter, cries, as if that joy had suddenly become a loss, 'O, your mother, your mother!' Then he asks the King of Bohemia's forgiveness, then embraces his son-in-law, then smothers his daughter with hugs again. Now he thanks the old shepherd, who stands by like a weather-beaten fountain statue that has seen many kings' reigns. I never heard of such another meeting. It lames any report that tries to follow it, and defeats any description that tries to capture it.
What, pray you, became of Antigonus, that carried hence the child?
Tell me, what became of Antigonus, who carried the child away from here?

Like an old tale still, which will have matter to rehearse, though / credit be asleep and not an ear open. He was torn to pieces with a / bear: this avouches the shepherd's son, who has not only his innocence, / which seems much, to justify him, but a handkerchief and rings of his / that Paulina knows.

Still like an old tale, which has more to tell even when belief is asleep and no ear is open. He was torn to pieces by a bear. The shepherd's son swears to it, and he has not only his innocence, which seems great, to back him, but a handkerchief and rings of Antigonus's that Paulina recognises.
What became of his bark and his followers?
What became of his ship and his men?

Wrecked the same instant of their master's death, and in the view of / the shepherd: so that all the instruments which aided to expose the / child were even then lost when it was found. But O, the noble combat / that 'twixt joy and sorrow was fought in Paulina! She had one eye / declined for the loss of her husband, another elevated that the oracle / was fulfilled. She lifted the princess from the earth, and so locks her / in embracing, as if she would pin her to her heart, that she might no / more be in danger of losing.

Wrecked at the same moment their master died, in sight of the shepherd, so that everyone who helped to abandon the child was lost at the very moment it was found. But O, the noble battle between joy and sorrow that was fought in Paulina! She had one eye lowered for the loss of her husband, the other raised because the oracle was fulfilled. She lifted the princess from the ground and locked her in such an embrace, as if she would pin her to her heart, so that she could never be in danger of losing her again.
The dignity of this act was worth the audience of kings and princes; / for by such was it acted.
The grandeur of this scene deserved an audience of kings and princes, for it was acted by them.
