One of the prettiest touches of all, and that which angled for mine / eyes (caught the water, though not the fish) was, when at the relation / of the queen's death (with the manner how she came to it bravely / confessed and lamented by the king) how attentiveness wounded his / daughter; till, from one sign of dolour to another, she did, with an / "Alas," I would fain say, bleed tears, for I am sure my heart wept / blood. Who was most marble there changed colour; some swooned, all / sorrowed: if all the world could have seen it, the woe had been / universal.

One of the most touching moments of all, which fished for my eyes (and caught the water, though not the fish), was when the queen's death was told, with the way she came to it bravely confessed and mourned by the king. How listening wounded his daughter! Until, from one sign of grief to another, she did, with an 'Alas', I'd almost say, bleed tears, for I'm sure my heart wept blood. The most marble-hearted there changed colour. Some fainted, all grieved. If the whole world could have seen it, the sorrow would have been universal.
Are they returned to the court?
Have they gone back to the court?

No: the princess hearing of her mother's statue, which is in the / keeping of Paulina,—a piece many years in doing and now newly performed / by that rare Italian master, Julio Romano, who, had he himself / eternity, and could put breath into his work, would beguile Nature of / her custom, so perfectly he is her ape: he so near to Hermione hath / done Hermione that they say one would speak to her and stand in hope of / answer. Thither with all greediness of affection are they gone, and / there they intend to sup.

No. The princess heard of her mother's statue, which Paulina keeps, a work that took many years and has just been finished by that rare Italian master Julio Romano. If he were immortal and could breathe life into his work, he would steal Nature's customers, he imitates her so perfectly. He has made Hermione so like Hermione that they say you would speak to her and wait for an answer. They have all gone there with eager love, and mean to have supper there.

I thought she had some great matter there in hand; for she hath / privately twice or thrice a day, ever since the death of Hermione, / visited that removed house. Shall we thither, and with our company / piece the rejoicing?
I thought she had something important there, for ever since Hermione died she has privately visited that remote house two or three times a day. Shall we go there and add our company to the rejoicing?
Who would be thence that has the benefit of access? Every wink of an / eye some new grace will be born. Our absence makes us unthrifty to our / knowledge. Let's along.
Who would stay away who is allowed in? Every blink of an eye some new wonder will be born. Our absence wastes our chance to know. Let's go.

Now, had I not the dash of my former life in me, would preferment drop / on my head. I brought the old man and his son aboard the prince; told / him I heard them talk of a fardel and I know not what. But he at that / time over-fond of the shepherd's daughter (so he then took her to be), / who began to be much sea-sick, and himself little better, extremity of / weather continuing, this mystery remained undiscover'd. But 'tis all / one to me; for had I been the finder-out of this secret, it would not / have relish'd among my other discredits.

Now, if I didn't have the stain of my old life on me, promotion would drop on my head. I brought the old man and his son aboard to the prince and told him I'd heard them talk about a bundle and I don't know what. But he was too taken up with the shepherd's daughter (as he then thought she was), who began to be very seasick, and he was little better himself, as the storm went on, so the mystery stayed hidden. But it's all the same to me. If I'd been the one to find out this secret, it wouldn't have gone down well with all my other bad deeds.
Here come those I have done good to against my will, and already / appearing in the blossoms of their fortune.
Here come the people I've done good to against my will, already blossoming with their good fortune.
Come, boy; I am past more children, but thy sons and daughters will be / all gentlemen born.
Come, boy. I'm past having more children, but your sons and daughters will all be born gentlemen.

You are well met, sir. You denied to fight with me this other day, / because I was no gentleman born. See you these clothes? Say you see / them not and think me still no gentleman born: you were best say these / robes are not gentlemen born. Give me the lie, do; and try whether I am / not now a gentleman born.

Well met, sir. You refused to fight me the other day because I wasn't a born gentleman. Do you see these clothes? Say you don't see them, and still think I'm no born gentleman. You'd better say these robes aren't born gentlemen. Give me the lie, go on, and see whether I'm not a born gentleman now.
I know you are now, sir, a gentleman born.
I know you are a born gentleman now, sir.
Ay, and have been so any time these four hours.
Yes, and have been any time these four hours.

So you have: but I was a gentleman born before my father; for the / king's son took me by the hand and called me brother; and then the two / kings called my father brother; and then the prince, my brother, and / the princess, my sister, called my father father; and so we wept; and / there was the first gentleman-like tears that ever we shed.

So you have. But I was a born gentleman before my father, for the king's son took me by the hand and called me brother, and then the two kings called my father brother, and then the prince, my brother, and the princess, my sister, called my father father. And so we wept, and those were the first gentlemanly tears we ever shed.
We may live, son, to shed many more.
We may live, son, to shed many more.
Ay; or else 'twere hard luck, being in so preposterous estate as we / are.
Yes, or else it would be bad luck, being in such a preposterous position as we are.
I humbly beseech you, sir, to pardon me all the faults I have committed / to your worship, and to give me your good report to the prince my / master.
I humbly beg you, sir, to forgive me all the wrongs I have done your worship, and to give a good report of me to the prince my master.
Prithee, son, do; for we must be gentle, now we are gentlemen.
Please do, son, for we must be gentle now we are gentlemen.
Ay, an it like your good worship.
Yes, if it please your good worship.
Give me thy hand: I will swear to the prince thou art as honest a true / fellow as any is in Bohemia.
Give me your hand. I'll swear to the prince you're as honest and true a fellow as anyone in Bohemia.
You may say it, but not swear it.
You may say it, but not swear it.
Not swear it, now I am a gentleman? Let boors and franklins say it, / I'll swear it.
Not swear it, now I'm a gentleman? Let peasants and farmers say it. I'll swear it.
How if it be false, son?

If it be ne'er so false, a true gentleman may swear it in the behalf of / his friend. And I'll swear to the prince thou art a tall fellow of thy / hands and that thou wilt not be drunk; but I know thou art no tall / fellow of thy hands and that thou wilt be drunk: but I'll swear it; and / I would thou wouldst be a tall fellow of thy hands.

However false it is, a true gentleman may swear it on behalf of his friend. And I'll swear to the prince you're a brave fellow with your fists and that you won't get drunk. But I know you're no brave fellow with your fists and that you will get drunk. But I'll swear it, and I wish you would be a brave fellow with your fists.
I will prove so, sir, to my power.
I'll prove one, sir, as far as I can.

Ay, by any means, prove a tall fellow: if I do not wonder how thou / dar'st venture to be drunk, not being a tall fellow, trust me not. / Hark! the kings and the princes, our kindred, are going to see the / queen's picture. Come, follow us: we'll be thy good masters.

Yes, by all means prove a brave fellow. If I don't wonder how you dare get drunk when you're not a brave fellow, don't trust me. Listen! The kings and the princes, our relatives, are going to see the queen's image. Come, follow us. We'll be good masters to you.
O grave and good Paulina, the great comfort / That I have had of thee!
O wise and good Paulina, what great comfort I have had from you!

What, sovereign sir, / I did not well, I meant well. All my services / You have paid home: but that you have vouchsaf'd, / With your crown'd brother and these your contracted / Heirs of your kingdoms, my poor house to visit, / It is a surplus of your grace which never / My life may last to answer.

What I did badly, sovereign sir, I meant well. You have paid in full for all my services. But that you have agreed, with your crowned brother and these betrothed heirs to your kingdoms, to visit my poor house is an extra kindness that my life may never last long enough to repay.

O Paulina, / We honour you with trouble. But we came / To see the statue of our queen: your gallery / Have we pass'd through, not without much content / In many singularities; but we saw not / That which my daughter came to look upon, / The statue of her mother.

O Paulina, we honour you only by troubling you. But we came to see the statue of our queen. We have walked through your gallery, and taken much pleasure in many rare things, but we did not see what my daughter came to look at: the statue of her mother.

As she liv'd peerless, / So her dead likeness, I do well believe, / Excels whatever yet you look'd upon / Or hand of man hath done; therefore I keep it / Lonely, apart. But here it is: prepare / To see the life as lively mock'd as ever / Still sleep mock'd death. Behold, and say 'tis well.

As she lived without equal, so her dead likeness, I truly believe, is better than anything you have ever looked at or any hand of man has made. So I keep it alone and apart. But here it is. Get ready to see life imitated as vividly as still sleep ever imitated death. Look, and say it is good.
I like your silence, it the more shows off / Your wonder: but yet speak. First you, my liege. / Comes it not something near?
I like your silence. It shows your wonder all the more. But still, speak. You first, my lord. Isn't it rather like her?

Her natural posture! / Chide me, dear stone, that I may say indeed / Thou art Hermione; or rather, thou art she / In thy not chiding; for she was as tender / As infancy and grace. But yet, Paulina, / Hermione was not so much wrinkled, nothing / So aged as this seems.

Her very pose! Scold me, dear stone, so that I can say you really are Hermione. Or rather, you are her in not scolding me, for she was as gentle as infancy and grace. But still, Paulina, Hermione was not so wrinkled, not nearly as old as this seems.
So much the more our carver's excellence, / Which lets go by some sixteen years and makes her / As she liv'd now.
So much the greater our sculptor's skill, which lets some sixteen years go by and makes her as she would be if she were alive now.

As now she might have done, / So much to my good comfort as it is / Now piercing to my soul. O, thus she stood, / Even with such life of majesty, warm life, / As now it coldly stands, when first I woo'd her! / I am asham'd: does not the stone rebuke me / For being more stone than it? O royal piece, / There's magic in thy majesty, which has / My evils conjur'd to remembrance and / From thy admiring daughter took the spirits, / Standing like stone with thee.

As she might have been now, it would have comforted me as much as it pierces my soul now. O, this is how she stood, with just such majestic life, warm life, as it stands coldly now, when I first courted her! I am ashamed. Doesn't the stone rebuke me for being more stone than it is? O royal work of art, there's magic in your majesty that has called my sins back to memory, and taken the spirit from your wondering daughter, who stands like stone with you.
And give me leave, / And do not say 'tis superstition, that / I kneel, and then implore her blessing. Lady, / Dear queen, that ended when I but began, / Give me that hand of yours to kiss.
And let me, and don't say it's superstition, kneel and beg her blessing. Lady, dear queen, whose life ended just as mine began, give me that hand of yours to kiss.
O, patience! / The statue is but newly fix'd, the colour's / Not dry.
O, wait! The statue has only just been set up. The paint is not dry.
My lord, your sorrow was too sore laid on, / Which sixteen winters cannot blow away, / So many summers dry. Scarce any joy / Did ever so long live; no sorrow / But kill'd itself much sooner.
My lord, your sorrow was laid on too thick if sixteen winters cannot blow it away nor as many summers dry it up. Hardly any joy ever lived so long, and no sorrow that did not kill itself much sooner.
Dear my brother, / Let him that was the cause of this have power / To take off so much grief from you as he / Will piece up in himself.
My dear brother, let the man who caused this have the power to take away as much grief from you as he can carry himself.
Indeed, my lord, / If I had thought the sight of my poor image / Would thus have wrought you—for the stone is mine— / I'd not have show'd it.
Indeed, my lord, if I had thought the sight of my poor statue would affect you like this (for the stone is mine), I wouldn't have shown it.
No longer shall you gaze on't, lest your fancy / May think anon it moves.
You mustn't gaze at it any longer, or your imagination may soon think it moves.
Let be, let be. / Would I were dead, but that methinks already— / What was he that did make it? See, my lord, / Would you not deem it breath'd? And that those veins / Did verily bear blood?
Leave it, leave it. I wish I were dead, if I didn't think already... Who was it that made it? Look, my lord, wouldn't you think it breathed? And that those veins really carried blood?
Masterly done: / The very life seems warm upon her lip.
Masterly done. Life itself seems warm on her lip.
The fixture of her eye has motion in 't, / As we are mock'd with art.
Her fixed eye seems to move, so art fools us.
I'll draw the curtain: / My lord's almost so far transported that / He'll think anon it lives.
I'll draw the curtain. My lord is so carried away that he'll soon think it lives.
O sweet Paulina, / Make me to think so twenty years together! / No settled senses of the world can match / The pleasure of that madness. Let 't alone.
O sweet Paulina, make me think so for twenty years on end! No sound mind in the world can match the pleasure of that madness. Leave it.
I am sorry, sir, I have thus far stirr'd you: but / I could afflict you further.
I'm sorry, sir, I have stirred you so much. But I could afflict you more.

Do, Paulina; / For this affliction has a taste as sweet / As any cordial comfort. Still methinks / There is an air comes from her. What fine chisel / Could ever yet cut breath? Let no man mock me, / For I will kiss her!

Do, Paulina, for this affliction tastes as sweet as any comforting medicine. Still I think there's breath coming from her. What fine chisel could ever carve breath? Let no man laugh at me, for I will kiss her!
Good my lord, forbear: / The ruddiness upon her lip is wet; / You'll mar it if you kiss it, stain your own / With oily painting. Shall I draw the curtain?
My good lord, don't. The red on her lip is wet. You'll spoil it if you kiss it, and stain your own with oil paint. Shall I draw the curtain?
So long could I / Stand by, a looker on.
I could stand by and look on for that long.

Either forbear, / Quit presently the chapel, or resolve you / For more amazement. If you can behold it, / I'll make the statue move indeed, descend, / And take you by the hand. But then you'll think / (Which I protest against) I am assisted / By wicked powers.

Either stop, leave the chapel at once, or prepare yourselves for more amazement. If you can bear to watch, I'll make the statue really move, come down, and take you by the hand. But then you'll think (which I deny) that I am helped by evil powers.
What you can make her do / I am content to look on: what to speak, / I am content to hear; for 'tis as easy / To make her speak as move.
Whatever you can make her do, I'm happy to watch. Whatever you can make her say, I'm happy to hear. For it is as easy to make her speak as move.
It is requir'd / You do awake your faith. Then all stand still; / Or those that think it is unlawful business / I am about, let them depart.
You must awaken your faith. Then everyone stand still. Or anyone who thinks what I am doing is unlawful, let them leave.
Go on. No one shall move a foot.

Music, awake her: strike! [Music] / 'Tis time; descend; be stone no more; approach; / Strike all that look upon with marvel. Come; / I'll fill your grave up: stir; nay, come away. / Bequeath to death your numbness, for from him / Dear life redeems you. You perceive she stirs.

Music, wake her: play! (Music) It's time. Come down. Be stone no more. Come closer. Strike everyone who looks at you with wonder. Come, I'll fill up your grave. Move. No, come away. Leave your numbness to death, for dear life rescues you from him. You see, she moves.

Start not; her actions shall be holy as / You hear my spell is lawful. Do not shun her / Until you see her die again; for then / You kill her double. Nay, present your hand: / When she was young you woo'd her; now in age / Is she become the suitor?

Don't start back. Her actions will be as holy as you hear my spell is lawful. Don't shun her, unless you see her die again, for then you would kill her twice. No, give her your hand. When she was young you courted her. Now, in age, has she become the suitor?
[Embracing her] O, she's warm! / If this be magic, let it be an art / Lawful as eating.
(Embracing her) O, she's warm! If this is magic, let it be an art as lawful as eating.
She hangs about his neck. / If she pertain to life, let her speak too.
She hangs about his neck. If she belongs to life, let her speak too.
Ay, and make it manifest where she has liv'd, / Or how stol'n from the dead.
Yes, and let her make it clear where she has lived, or how she was stolen from the dead.

That she is living, / Were it but told you, should be hooted at / Like an old tale; but it appears she lives, / Though yet she speak not. Mark a little while. / Please you to interpose, fair madam. Kneel / And pray your mother's blessing. Turn, good lady, / Our Perdita is found.

That she is alive, if you were only told it, you would jeer at like an old tale. But it seems she lives, though she hasn't spoken yet. Watch a little while. (To Perdita) Please come between them, fair madam. Kneel and ask your mother's blessing. (To Hermione) Turn, good lady. Our Perdita is found.

You gods, look down, / And from your sacred vials pour your graces / Upon my daughter's head! Tell me, mine own, / Where hast thou been preserv'd? where liv'd? how found / Thy father's court? for thou shalt hear that I, / Knowing by Paulina that the oracle / Gave hope thou wast in being, have preserv'd / Myself to see the issue.

You gods, look down, and from your sacred jars pour your graces on my daughter's head! Tell me, my own one, where have you been kept safe? Where have you lived? How did you find your father's court? For you shall hear that I, knowing from Paulina that the oracle gave hope that you were alive, have kept myself alive to see the outcome.

There's time enough for that; / Lest they desire upon this push to trouble / Your joys with like relation. Go together, / You precious winners all; your exultation / Partake to everyone. I, an old turtle, / Will wing me to some wither'd bough, and there / My mate, that's never to be found again, / Lament till I am lost.

There's time enough for that, in case they want to spoil your joy at this moment by telling their own stories too. Go together, all you precious winners. Share your happiness with everyone. I, an old turtle-dove, will fly off to some withered branch, and there mourn my mate, who will never be found again, until I am lost too.

O peace, Paulina! / Thou shouldst a husband take by my consent, / As I by thine a wife: this is a match, / And made between 's by vows. Thou hast found mine; / But how, is to be question'd; for I saw her, / As I thought, dead; and have in vain said many / A prayer upon her grave. I'll not seek far— / For him, I partly know his mind—to find thee / An honourable husband. Come, Camillo, / And take her by the hand, whose worth and honesty / Is richly noted, and here justified / By us, a pair of kings. Let's from this place. / What! look upon my brother: both your pardons, / That e'er I put between your holy looks / My ill suspicion. This your son-in-law, / And son unto the king, whom heavens directing, / Is troth-plight to your daughter. Good Paulina, / Lead us from hence; where we may leisurely / Each one demand, and answer to his part / Perform'd in this wide gap of time, since first / We were dissever'd. Hastily lead away!

O, peace, Paulina! You should take a husband with my consent, as I take a wife with yours. This is a bargain, and made between us by vows. You have found mine, but how is still to be asked, for I saw her, as I thought, dead, and have said many prayers in vain at her grave. I won't look far (for I partly know his mind) to find you an honourable husband. Come, Camillo, and take her by the hand, whose worth and honesty are well known and here confirmed by us, a pair of kings. Let's leave this place. (To Hermione) What! Look at my brother. Forgive me, both of you, that I ever put my evil suspicion between your innocent looks. This is your son-in-law, the king's son, who, by heaven's guidance, is betrothed to your daughter. Good Paulina, lead us from here, where we can take our time to ask and answer each one's part in this wide gap of time since we were first separated. Lead us away quickly!
